I come from a DDR background. I also have enjoyed plenty of music related games. The idea of putting these into this setting, and in VR no less, intrigued me. Once it came out, I saw the price and couldn't pass it up. 

I will say, it is simple in its design, to which there is room for improvement. For example, the system for picking your song is hard to use, and using the scroll bar on the side doesn't always work for me. Also, I can't seem to get the special to work after getting the swords to glow, but that may be because I'm playing it on an Oculus instead of the vive. and finally, I can't quite figure out how it senses music. Some songs I think will be extremelyt hard (Through the Fire and Flames for instance), aren't, and vice versa. 

All that aside, I still will give this a thumbs up, because when it comes to actual gameplay, it's a blast! Me and my son have been playing with it for a little bit now, and it's quite the workout as well. Although, like my kid, you can play this by just swinging your swords around wildly an do pretty good, the idea of being able to "slice" through multiple blasts at once, and do it intentionally, is quite rewarding. 

edit: There has been an update, and the problems of scrolling through the music, as well as not being able to fire the special, have been fixed. The UI where you pick your songs has improved as well.

I really don't like discouraging small VR developers because I want more games, but this one just doesn't cut it.

The idea is that it uses your music library to generate the rhythm components, but at best it's just using the tempo to generate the volume of orbs. It really doesn't feel like it has anything to do with your song choice.

It also doesn't come with any pre-loaded music. I know the developers didn't want to license any music, but you at least needs a tutorial song because as it is right now you start the game up for the first time, then have to immediately take off your headset to move music into the correct directory.

I could live with it if those were the only issues, but it's not at all. Compared to so many other VR experiences out there, including free ones, it doesn't look great. And the hit detection on the swords is terrible. I sliced my sword through many orbs that seemed to ignore it completely and I had the best luck trying to poke at them with the tips. Overall, the control schemes need a lot of work and need to be much more accurate (just navigating through the instructions is annoying). Nothing is intuitive and you can't move around at all without moving in the physical world.

It's cheap and seemed like an interesting idea so I gave it a try, but unfortunately Sword Samurai needs a lot more polish to be worth playing.

Staring at the grid of colorful blocks, you quickly realize that matching the left side with the right isn’t tough in the way political maneuvers are. Clicking a block changes its color and the colors of its neighbors, but it’s all predictable, thanks to a set sequence. The challenge is more about following a known pattern than dealing with unexpected surprises. You know what will happen each time you click, which takes away some of the tension but still demands careful planning to get the blocks just right.

As you race against the clock, gold, silver, and bronze medals are handed out based on how fast you finish. But since each puzzle has only one solution, the timer feels unnecessary. You can’t really outsmart the game or come up with a faster way to solve things, so the rankings seem more like a formality than an actual achievement. The time-based rewards do little to make the game feel more competitive or meaningful.

The puzzles themselves are short and straightforward, with little variation. The vibrant visuals and catchy soundtrack give the game life, but the lack of complexity holds it back. More challenging levels or user-generated content could have added replayability, but as it stands, it’s a brief and predictable puzzle game, fun for a while and sometimes that’s all it needs to be.

A remarkably unique take on the space trading genre, Helium Rain is doing Early Access right.  You'll find bugs, typos, all the old favorites, but the developers are extremely receptive (they even have their own Redmine server you can log and track bugs in) and quick to turnaround fixes and enhancement.

Past the Early Access considerations, you're left with a very compact, but utterly hypnotic space trading/combat game.  "Compact" because HR eschews the current trend of "fifteen trillion stars!" for just a handful of planets and sectors, but those planets and sectors are never without plenty to do, from running simple courier missions to building space stations, developing a trade fleet, commanding an economic empire.  Fly one ship while the rest of your fleet is own doing your bidding (and hopefully making some money while they're at it.)  For me it's almost reminiscent of something like Euro Truck Simulator 2 in that regard.  Except in space.  And with guns.

On the surface, look at the screenshots.  The washed out, high-contrast colors and dreamlike music confer one of the most "chill" space games I can remember.  The clean UI is occasionally fiddly, occasionally brilliant, and while it might look a bit too much like your cable box UI, it does the job and continues to improve.

Even this early, I find it one of the more compelling space games in my library.  And unlike some games that provide an entire galaxy but leave you wondering what to do next, more than once I've forgotten what I'd planned to do because something else more interesting came up, and then forgot I was doing THAT because something even more interesting than that came up.  Even while you're blissing out to the celestial look and feel, you'll never be bored.

If any of this sounds good to you, and you don't mind the vagaries of Early Access, I'd say, hit that Buy button immediately.

The game is fantastic. Don't get discouraged by the grinding in early game, it gets much more complex and diversified as soon as you get a fleet. There will definitely be some hauling to get through first, but manual docking takes only 10 seconds once you're used to it and seeing your progress in that task will make it very rewarding, even without a HOTAS. Or you can buy an autodocking technology to make it as easy as a click, but in my opinion, it just lowers the potential and depth of the game; if you're into space simulations and piloting, then no need to make money faster by doing more trips thanks to the autodocking, it's not a competitive multiplayer game, take your time and play each trip. Hauling is more fun in HR than in Elite from my perspective, and fortunately it won't be your main task for weeks.

At the beginning, after a few hours, I thought myself that this game was beautiful and felt great, but unfortunately was going to be repetitive and lack content. I'm happy to say it proved me wrong (but the game can definitely use more content of course), however it all depends on how you play and how you expand your colony, it's possible that the game could evolve in more or less interestings ways depending on your actions.

As soon as you get a fleet, it is much easier to make money since you can specialize a ship into trading (and the trading routes system is complex enough, I was expecting something much simpler, very good surprise here), or start using fighter ships with contracts that tend to pay better rewards. Overall, the money/docking ratio increases quite fast as soon as your fleet and company build up, and the diversity of the gameplay as well.

The UI looks great and is actually convenient once you mastered it, but it takes some getting used to. A few more hints on where to find specific functions would help sometimes, it's not always obvious that the warning about missing components for building a ship would be in the orbital map for instance, or that you'd have to go check the shipyard in its sector screen to know what is missing, I was initially just looking into my Company screen to check the status of the ship I ordered. More filters in the Economy screen, and a way to show which stations buy what in that same screen would be useful, as well as a Search field for specific ressources in the Sector screen. But all that is really rather minor, the UI is already nice to use and feels a lot less crippled than Elite's sy-fy/immersive UI for instance.

So if the beginning of the game looks repetitive and boring to you, try to hang on, it gets better and the game has a great potential. I have played or backed many space sims, from KSP to Elite: Dangerous, Star Citizen or Rogue System (very recommended if you are into hardcore DCS-like sims). KSP is a jewel, but is admittedly quite a different game. Helium Rain is the game I didn't see coming, and yet it's the single best space opera I've played so far. Beautiful, several things to do, good flight models that feels just right, real physics (no cap on velocity as long as you keep burning; only saw it in KSP and Rogue System so far), deep if you care about the company system, real sandbox with an impact on the world, and I have to add that the orchestral music is beautiful and fits perfectly the pleasant ambiance of the game. Playing this game feels like watching [i]2001: A space odyssey[/i]; not that the music or assets are similar, but your brain and eyes will feel the same.

If you are into space sims and not necessarily intense shooters with fancy effects everywhere, you will like it (even the fights are nice, much calmer than fights in other space games, and it's not a bad thing). If you're into intense shooters, think twice, but give it a try, you may like what you'll see. If you're into trading, you may like it, but you will have to go through some piloting first. In any case, don't expect an AAA game with 52 billions stars or a mix of FPS/Fight/Exploration and 160M funding, but do expect a game beautifully made with a great attention to the details. The game is not expensive and is well worth that price, or more. The team have opened their source code, have a public bug tracker (with visible progress), communication is great, and their first game is good, it's encouraging to see development going this way.

There is a minor bug in the current build with UE4 on Linux with AMD mesa drivers, basically there's no bright sunlights on my computer. Sad. And then, looking at screenshots and videos, I realized I much prefer the game this way, looks more realistic and just more "space" when the bright anodized paints are more subtle in the shade. Now I'm not sure I want the bug to be fixed!

Buy this if;
-You always wanted a very cold hard sci fi space game.
-You want an economic engine more than a story or battle sim
-you are happy to pay its price for ~5-20hours of game.

I think its excelent, but its not a story game, it's a sandbox about building your space company through trade routes and space stations. After the initial start from nothing about 80% of your time will be in the interface rather than the cockpit.

Battles are very good, but full neutonian physics might put off some. 

It is a small focused game, it is not X3, so don't expect lots of techs and infinite space to explore.

The AI is pretty weak. It is good at economic efficiency, but if you step over to a more aggressive strategy the different factons do not adjust well. As such I played the game twice and I am probably done with it, but I still rank it was one of the best in the genre.

These "real economy" games usually dont work as well as this one.  Really nice.  Any time you can manage trade fleets and send them off on their own semi-automated trade routes, I'm pretty much hooked.

A little bit like the X series (X:BTF, X2, X3, etc) where you can build production chains that extract raw materials and produce goods.  

The AI factions follow all the same rules that you do, so you can buy out all the plastics to grind production lines to a halt.

The realistic spaceflight, optional manual docking (sort of KSP-light with RCS thruster control for coupling with docking hatches), newtonian physics, and Heinlein / Atomic Rockets style future all makes a really rich setting if you like that sort of sci-fi.

I'm not very good at the combat, but it is also great sci-fi.  You hear the echo of your guns fireing, and you hear shots hit your hull -- but there are otherwise no sounds in space.  It really feels great, and playing around with the different sized ships in the simulator they all feel different.

Spaceflight isn't too hard, either.  Often newtonian motion and such makes that difficult, but the ships auto-stabilize your motion towards whichever way you point.  You can still strafe by things, but it helps to keep you from flying off out of control.

First off, this isn't an adrenaline pumping high combat space sim.
It's like Elite:Dangerous and the X universe had a minimalist baby with the UI from most of the episodes of Black Mirror.  Feels almost like the universe came out of Ben Bova's planet series of books, or is a logical extension thereof.  Those were great books for scientists who want to read sci fi without having an anneurism.  This game is kinda the same.  

And to me, that's pretty awesome.  I've had the itch for a space-trading light combat sim for a while now, and Helium Rain did not disappoint.

The lighting's a little harsh (as space should be)
The economy sim has a few bugs (it's early access, devs seem very intent on fixing this)
The ship selection looks good for the size of the game.  (To be fair, I've only bought light ships so far, haven't got the creds for a heavy yet)
Combat is dog-fighting style, which would probably be my one complaint.  They're space-ships not space-planes.
Not story-driven but there are some story elements, which are nice.

The idea of a single solar system (multiple planets/sectors) makes the scale feel good for a single player game.  Some expansions incorporating slow FTL (like a 30 day cost to travel time) and another few systems to round up to around a hundred sectors would be a nice addition, and push the scale up to a comfortable max for a single player experience in my opinion.  Big enough to stay interesting for a while, small enough to keep the game pretty casual.

When utilizing any of the shipyards in the game to build a ship, the shipyard will sometimes require materials to begin construction on whatever ship is in queue - which is fine.  What's not fine is when the shipyard requests materials but doesn't have the money to pay for them - and there's no option to trade them for free.  What you end up with is a deadlocked game where all the shipyards have your ship in the build queue but can't begin construction, no matter what you do.

I looked for and found comments from the developers about this exact problem, but both of them have since moved on to other projects and don't seem interested in fixing what is essentially a campaign breaking bug.

Bad form.  Do not buy this game unless and until this is fixed - if it ever is.

At first, I was not a fan of Helium Rain. I judged the game to be too shallow. The absence of a cockpit or bridge combined with the absence of VR, since a few titles in the same genre had this - for example: No Man's Sky and Elite Dangerous. 

Then, somehow, its relaxing atmosphere, unique ship design and Newtonian flight model combined with its modding options tipped the balance in its favor. The dev team gave us a complete modkit to shape Helium Rain's 3d models to whatever you want them to be. With a lot of patience you could create your own game, designing your own ships, but using Helium Rain as an engine itself.

It's a sandbox game and should be seen and played as such. The negative reviews of some people here are a result of comparisons with other games or expectations that were never fulfilled. Expectations usually never get fulfilled, so who's to blame there?

There is no 'story', this is not 'Wing Commander' 'Starlancer', 'Freelancer' or 'The Darkening'. It was made by a devoted indie team that made a completely finished product that is playable and does not have any game breaking bugs.

Its beauty is in its barebones, realistic approach regarding ship and station design, which id does extremely well. There are no exotic hull designs here like you see in some titles like X3 Terran Conflict and X3 Albion Prelude. It makes even more sense than the ship designs from the TV series The Expanse, which would really feel at home here.

The combat is very raw and pure. No shields, no cloaks, just maneuverability, speed and numbers vs firepower and mass. 

Overall, I spend more than my fair share of time in this sim and in its dev kit. I purchased the game on Steam, and also on GOG. I wanted something DRM free that I could play without the need for a steam client and at the same time support the devs and thank them. Funnily enough, the game itself is not for sale on the EPIC store, where you can download the mod kit free of charge and start modding.

So, would I recommend this? Definitely YES

If you are a nerd that like me loves the 'simulation' aspect of a game and you don't need any 'hand holding' in ways of a 'playable story' and just love the possibilities of a sandbox game, where depth means Newtonian physics without micromanagement, this is for you. 

Helium Rain succeeded where Elite Dangerous or the X3 franchise failed, because it is complex, without being complicated. There is not quite another game like it.

The art style. The setting. The level of just-right balance between sci-fi and realism. The connected economy, and AI playing by the same rules as the player. Nothing appears out of thin air - if no ore is mined, no steel will be made and no new ships will be built in shipyards. With some smart moves you can beat the AI and become an industrial giant in the system. Prices move up and down with supply and demand, and unbalanced economy will create resource shortages.

The setting sets the mood of the game nicely - as one of the colonists who arrived at the blue gas giant Nema, you along with others in the colony ship wake up from stasis to discover that the moons that promised new home are barren or flat out hostile. With no options left, humanity established a series of outposts around Nema nad its moons, harvesting important gasses and resources from the gas giant and encircling asteroid fields. 

You start with a little basic ship to haul some tools or people around with.  You can take on contracts from established corporations, or seek good trading deals. Every new sector around the gas giant or its moons that you discover is added to your economy screen, so it becomes easier overtime to find good deals. Money allowing, you can build stations and trading fleets to expand your empire, and combat fleets to protect what is rightfully yours.

Ladies and gentlemen, this game is a must-play for 4x/space sim geeks, for this indeed is a true gem among gems. It saddens me that so few people seem to have actually played it. As an amazing bonus, the game is open source and available on github!

I have somewhat mixed feelings about giving this a negative review, because it is actually a good game.
The reason it gets a negative review are just a few things that drag the game down, and I'll list these problems here. There are plenty of other reviews talking about the good stuff so I'll skip over that.

1: The tutorial doesn't really teach you jack shit (reminiscent of the X series tutorials, really fucking bad)
2: There is no save system, or rather, the game is played in ironman mode only, and relies exclusively on an autosave function. I don't know fully how that autosave function works but if you just quit the game, then start it up again, you will be in the same spot as before. This means that if you make ANY kind of mistake, you're locked into them, and there are so many big mistakes to be made in this game because...
3: Lack of detailed information about just about anything in the research tree. (EVEN IF YOU LOOK ONLINE!) this makes it really easy to say research something, like a tier 4 tech, that actually requires resources that can only be obtained from tier 5 tech factories that no faction in the game owns early in the game, (Which means you have to make it yourself, which means some tech is useless until you have a higher tier tech in order to be able to produce it!). This is just one of many huge cases where lack of information only allows you to be wise of something after you've messed up a save you may have spent hours or days in, and ruined your entire playthrough. At which point, back to point 2; you would have to restart from the beginning, which is just not ok.

There's a workaround to save, by copying your save files manually to another folder when you want to save; but why the fuck should users have to go through so much trouble for a function that has existed in video games since the very beginning of video game history?! This is just utterly retarded.

These are 3 problems that compound to make the game terribly much worse than it otherwise would be.

Lack of information could have been solved with a good tutorial, and an actual save system could have mitigated just how painful it is for a user to make mistakes due to that lack of information, since they could just save everytime before they research something or make otherwise big in-game decisions like building certain factories or ships.

But combined, these 3 seemingly not that huge issues, become a profoundly huge (and extremely easily fixable) issue that honestly the developers have no legitimate excuse for not doing something about.

If it wasn't for these 3 issues however, the game is great. It's a space sim sandbox based entirely around the idea of building a trade empire and achieving world domination with it, It's great but it doesn't matter how great it is if it's borderline unplayable for beginners.

Helium Rain is a must-play Space Economy Sim for fans of the genre. If you enjoyed X³, Elite:Dangerous or EVE Online, or if you just wanted to build your own industrial empire in space, I’d highly recommend you give Helium Rain a try.

[h1]What do I get to do in this game?[/h1]

You start out in a scrappy little shuttle, hopping from station to station, flying with 6DoF and Newtonian flight physics, and spinning and lining up your ship to perform docking manoeuvres. For those of you who prefer more economics and less flying, Autopilot and Auto-dock are also available.

You’ll work your way up towards purchasing freighters and building a trading fleet, making money hauling goods from A to B. As you buy low and sell high to corner the market, you’ll amass enough wealth to start building your mines and factories of your own, cutting your competitors out of the market.

But beware! Pirates and less scrupulous corporations won’t stand by watching idly. You’ll have to invest in your own defense fleet to escort your haulers and protect your assets from the greedy paws of others who are after your hard earned coin.

[h1]Pros:[/h1][list]
[*][b]Economic simulation:[/b] every good and asset in game is produced by a factory, supplied with goods produced elsewhere. 

[*][b]Fleets:[/b] the game is built around the player owning multiple fleets spread across the system. You can choose to micromanage or set up preset trading routes

[*][b]Flight model:[/b] No speed limits: you can accelerate as much as you want, just remember that you’ll need to decelerate unless you want to overshoot your target and drift into space. At your disposal are forward/backward thrust, pitching, yawing, rolling, and lateral/longitudinal strafing.

[*][b]Dev feedback:[/b] The game is actively being worked on and the developers regularly provide feedback both on here and on the game’s website.

[*][b]Graphics:[/b] The game has a beautifully polished aesthetic going for it. It adds a lot of character that really make it stand out from the crowd.[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [i]Not so much cons, but features that still need a bit of dev love before the game leaves Early Access:[/i] [list]
[*][b]User Interface[/b] has a few niggles here and there that begin to manifest in the mid to late game when you have large amounts of assets to keep track of. Especially noticeable is the lack of a Journal recording your cash flow.

[*][b]AI corporations[/b] feel like they lack differentiation. Shipyards will gladly take orders to build fighters for pirates, only to the summarily attacked by them. Peaceful corporations seem to just turtle and amass wealth.

[*][b]Simulation speed[/b] begins to slowdown in the end game due to corporations expanding without enough resistance.[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Personally, I am a dozen hours into my first playthrough in the first 2 days of buying the game. I’ll still play Elite:Dangerous for the combat, atmosphere and immersion of the spaceships, and EVE Online has its niche as the MMO for space economies, but Helium Rain has established itself as my go-to option for single-player spaceship economy tycoon empire building.

Helium Rain (HR) is an atmospheric Economy/Management simulation game, set in a "hard sci-fi" space setting.

The atmosphere of HR gives off a bit of a lonely and relaxing vibe. The game setting taking place entirely in the orbit of a gas giant named "Nema". The station and ship designs are great in HR, I like the more realistic designs here which is a bit of a departure from the majority of games set in space. The overall setting being in orbit of a gas giant gives a lot of opportunities for a nice backdrop. There is no sound in space which HR portrays.

While HR is fundamentally a Space-Sim most of the time (at least in my experience) flying was done on auto-pilot while going through full-screen menus and sorting out some odds and ends for my budding empire. In a sense the majority of the game is played through the User Interface (UI). While there are a few Quality of Life (QoL) things missing overall it's consistent and wonderfully streamlined, suffering slightly in the late stages though in terms of ease-of-use.

There are no fantasy style propulsion systems in HR, so travel takes days between different sectors. Due to the time scales involved the game understandably introduces simulated time. Days can be processed/skipped and events processed along on the sector map and when done going through the days we're back in our ship in space again. I feel like there's a little bit of a disconnect here between the space-game and the simulated part of the game but many alternative approaches have their own downsides too.

There is a simulated economy system which has multiple layers, it's quite neat really. Ships and stations require different resources to be built which ultimately had to be mined (by stations rather than ships), processed and freighted to their respective destinations. Each time resources changes hands from one company to another currency will be exchanged, and at times transactions can't be completed due to certain companies running out of liquid currency. Staff on stations gets paid for their work, this money goes to the local sector population. The population will use this money to try to buy goods from their local Habitation domes to keep themselves fed and happy. If they get what they need they will go on and multiply at which point more money gets added into the games overall economy, constantly cycling through different companies and then back to the population again.

Upon starting a game you will start with a simple trade vessel but as you play you'll gain more ships, stations and possibly even eventually have formed a monopoly or even wiped out all the other factions completely, dependenant upon playstyle and goals. HR is purely a Sandbox game. There are contracts (basically missions/objectives) that popup including a unique set which could be considered a story-line but fundamentally it's all about the pure sandbox and simulation.

Combat takes place over rather long ranges. Often to the point of not really being able to make out enemy ships. Components on ships can be damaged and rendered inoperable/destroyed. Incoming rounds can ricochet off the hull of a ship. The visuals and audio for combat are a real joy.

There is a Mod-Kit for the game over on the [url=https://www.epicgames.com/store/en-US/p/helium-rain]Epic Games store[/url] which can be used by creators to add extra content (such as ships and/or stations) and then share their results on the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/681330/workshop/]steam workshop[/url]. In addition to this the [url=https://github.com/arbonagw/HeliumRain]source code is open-source[/url]. It is certainly not common for a game to be open-source which I am certainly [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/681330/discussions/0/2149847423922759328/]
thankful for[/url]

I would definitely recommend this game.

I have been looking for a game that recaptures the magic of X3 for a long time. It is rare to find a space sim that has the same ethos as X3: your goal is to build an empire, and you build fleets to protect that empire, rather than the more common philosophy of "it's fun to blow stuff up, so that's the main goal". But the devs are well on their way to delivering this, even though the game is VERY early access. I'm really quite surprised at how much there is since it was released (in EA) like a week ago. I really, really hope they continue to develop this game. So if you like space trading sims, it is playable as is but will no doubt get better and better. Probably its biggest advantage over X3 is a pretty sane interface.

The rest of my review is notes and suggestions to the devs:

- The number of sectors is just too small for a long-running game. It is nice to start, though.

- More goods, more stations, more ship types, and more weapon types are needed. I'm sure these are all forthcoming, although the current content is great for the current stage of development.

- I haven't done any combat yet although I couldn't easily find commands for a military fleet to "patrol this sector" (with all my stations) and so on. There is apparently no need or purpose to build a military fleet to protect my traders from pirates etc. I'm pretty nervous to try combat actually, as to do that I'd have to declare war, and there is apparently no "revert to save" option. (EDIT: I was right about "no revert to save" being a problem, because once you get into a war with one company, you'll shortly find yourself in a war with everyone...but wrong about the "no combat ships needed", as it turns out)

- If research is supposed to be a key part of the game, there needs to be a lot more to research. In particular, (more) ship upgrades, tiers of ships/weapons, and so on.

- Contracts do not seem to scale with reputation, ship capabilities (other than military), or anything else. So later game, contracts become useless and too small to bother with really. (EDIT: I think it does scale with the needs of the factories, so that as NPC factories level up, contracts get bigger. If so, scratch this one).

- Not sure about how I feel about the "you have to discover new sectors via VIP or telescope" mechanic. Seems a bit contrived.

- The diplomacy system seems underdeveloped, at least at this point in my playing. I'm not sure why it benefits you to curry favor or hurts you to lose it (as long as you lose favor with less powerful corps).

- No incentive for exploration. I'm all about the trading sim obviously, but it would be nice to have more things to do while you wait for your factories and trading fleets to make you obscenely wealthy.

- It hurts me to say this because I fear it will get nerfed, but the Atlas seems overpowered to me. Basically the cost difference between bad and awesome ships is too small IMO.

- I built a habitat thinking it would make me credits from taxes or something, but it seemingly consumes resources for no reason. Is there some benefit to population?

- Sometimes I am in the middle of autodocking and it cancels for no apparent reason. It may be because I frequently ALT-TAB (or the Linux equivalent) out of the game while I'm waiting to dock. Speaking of autodocking, it should just be built-in, not researchable. Manual docking at the beginning is annoying as balls, and it was the first thing I researched anyway.

- I think instead of in-game tutorials, at least for the intermediate concepts, like making a trade fleet, there should be an in-game wiki or something. I got halfway through "making a trade fleet" and then forgot how to do the first few steps of it.

- Oh, BTW, thanks for Linux support. I only buy Linux games so this expanded your audience by at least 1.

- Are there audio settings? I'd like to disable the music sometimes (EDIT: found it, didn't look hard enough, wasn't in an Audio menu but just general settings).

In general, I'm so excited about this game and wish I could give you more money, if I knew it would result in more development. Very good work so far.

I wanted to like Helium Rain, I really did. It is a smaller space sim, confining the player to one (albeit beautifully rendered) star system. The space visuals are somewhat starker and colder than, for example, those of Elite Dangerous, but the quality is very similar if not the same. I also immediately took a liking to the spaceship design: no silly transparent airplane cockpits, very few aerodynamic shapes, and a very utilitarian vibe to most if not all of them. Overall, the setting and the art direction very much reminded me of the Expanse (the books, not TV series), albeit one can argue that the shiny, colorful metallics of the ships and space stations may be a bit TOO shiny.

The flight model, too, is different: there is no maximum speed, and once you get going, you have to make an effort to slow down (Sir Isaac Newton is, after all, the deadliest man in space). You are free to accelerate, decelerate, pitch, yaw and strafe in every direction if you so desire, and you quickly learn the value of careful thrust application, counterthrust and small motions. All that said, as much fun as I had flying manually, unlocking autodock was a time-saving blessing.

In fact, things go very well while you putter around the system in a single ship. As mentioned, you are confined to one starsystem with a large, Saturn-like planet and four moons. The playable area is divided into "sectors" - clusters of stations orbiting the bodies together, each specializing in something (fuel production, metallurgy, gas extraction, etc.).  You begin as a customary nobody, in possession of a single shuttle capable of ferrying 100 tons of goods and an untold number of VIP passengers. The game does a decent job explaining to you what's what and what there is to do through a series of tutorial missions, which are all reasonably helpful. One standout is the combat tutorial, which eventually has you declare war on one of the factions. This ultimately results in a suicide mission - considering that by that time you probably have 1-2 combat ships to your name, you're liable to get thrashed by whomever you antagonize. Fortunately, there are no lasting consequences - your ships get disabled, but can be repaired, and you take a bit of a reputation hit with your target faction, which can be remedied through some trading.

The gameplay starts to fall apart when you expand beyond your initial one-man, one-ship operation. Setting up trade routes for an automated trader is a wise idea; except they seem to break for no reason (the trader started skipping stops on route, and nothing I did could fix that). The interface becomes more and more of a hindrance as your operation gets more complex. For some reason, it has a very console-like feel to it, and traditional PC tools like context menus are nowhere to be found. Commanding multiple ships quickly becomes a chore. It isn't possible, for example, to order all ships in your fleet to dock with the same station - you must individually take control of each of them, and order them to dock while sitting in the ship. You can't order a ship to dock and then switch to another fleet member - this causes the first ship to aimlessly fly off into the distance. If you have multiple freighters in your fleet, you cannot load them all up at the same time - again, you have to hop from ship to ship and load/unload them manually. After a while, you start noticing problems with flying individual ships as well. The instrumentation is remarkably poor - there is no radar, and no way to quickly look at what spaceships are present in the system (or target them) without going into the "sector detail" screen. This takes you away from the action in the cockpit, which can be deadly when under fire.

Another disappointment that soon reared its head was the fact that while you can, in fact, accelerate to ludicrous speeds, you have neither the time nor the room to do so. Each sector is a bubble approximately 20-30 km in diameter and stations are very close to each other; by the time you build up any appreciable velocity, you already have to start braking or overshoot (in fact, while flying on autopilot, you will rarely exceed 100 m/s). If you decide to wave goodbye to civilization and take off into he black... unfortunately, once you approach the edge of the sector bubble, the game informs you that you got too far from the sector and must return via the travel function.

All in all, after your operation acquires enough complexity, gameplay becomes too much of a chore to put up, at least for me. Which is disappointing, considering the dearth of good space sims on the market. Unfortunately, Helium Rain is "feature complete" at this point, so any bug fixes or UI rework are highly unlikely.

And so, in year 7, day 125, and I just declared war on the universe... Wait, let me step back..

I loved Frontier II: Elite (90's predecessor to Frontier:Dangerous) which was a great open world trading combat game with real Newtonian physics (well, 90's real).  Helium Rain has the same feel--I enjoy this. I played one initial game to get a feel for it--the economics, combat, etc. And then re-started to do some work...

I made my money exploring, running escort contracts, and trading. Before long I was able to buy a few trade ships and began establishing trade routes (a good function that is thoughtful without being overly complex like other games with larger scale, such as the X-series). It was all going well.

I invested heavily in research so I was able to build a a few complexes with the goal of becoming self sustaining (generate fuel to run my mines, mines to run my foundries, and ultimately--supply a shipyard that I can use to then create the mightiest fleet in the universe...Well, it all worked to plan. Except, once I completed my shipyard i found that the rest of the universe (all other corps) were basically broke.

You see, the Helium Rain Economy is a closed loop system. There are no artificial ways that the game creates capital (Cash is generated basically by habitats of people who purchase supplies). So, as I built up my stations (each costs 40-80k) i was essentially milking every dime out of the economy. Therefore, by the time I could create my battlefleet--there was no cash left for my enemies to be able to even dream of stopping me. I controlled all the capital and i didn't need any of them to build my fleet.

So, I declared war on the pirates with the mission to eliminate their kind from the universe! I defeated their fleet with ease, and chased them back to the Boneyard, where lay siege on their facilities. I captured all but their last solar farm--because--well, because I couldn't. The game would not let me. I did not let this deter me: So, I ordered my fleet to attack the last station. They did, and then stopped with it at around 80%. Again, not to be deterred, I spent way more time than I care to admit sitting in my capital ships hammering away until i FINALLY was able to blow it up... Now there was one ship left.. and.. I can't find it.

So, i declared war on my next strongest competitor--this war went quickly. I disabled their ships, and took many of their stations..

And so, with an overwhelming fleet and the only functioning industrial complex in the universe, I deployed my fleets all over and declared war on the universe. Nobody could stop me... my victory, while grand, was hollow...

So, yeah, this may have sounded negative--it's not. The game is well put together, and (obviously) was able to keep my attention as i saw how far I could go. Once I finish off this last fleet of freighters that I'm mopping up, I'll likely put it back on the shelf and wait for the next update (which dev notes have said are centered on the economy.

Assorted thoughts:

1. Combat is not action-packed, this is more about trade than pew-pew.
2. There are tactics in the economics, but not a lot of high strategy. Supply and demand, flooding some systems causes problems--it's good, but not horribly complex (again, like the X-series that WAY overcomplicates it).
3. The universe is right-sized. Part of me wants more, but the system wouldn't be manageable. They did a solid job of realizing the world in a playable scale.
4. I like it. It's clean, it's pretty, it's got a great feel to it--and, I say all this noting it's all in early access (though late-stage).
5. Fleet control is somewhat clunky, there could be a better way to organize and view the fleets. Also, the game gets bogged down late-game, taking several seconds to load the Company tab.

Notes on the Early Access:

The game did not like the way I was trying to play it. I never found that last pirate to kill off, and it REALLY didn't want me to destroy that last pirate station. The devs seem to want to develop a persistent world that can keep rolling. I respect that. However, there needs to be a late-game solution to economic domination. After all, I had taken complete control of the universal economy completely by accident!! All i did was trade and build, and that pulled all the cash out of the economy. Thoughts to this end:

1. Perhaps implement a "Bank" where the player and or the NPCs can get late-game cash infusions? If not a bank, than some other 'random event' based system where money can be injected into the economy to boost both players and/or NPCs as needed (this could be some kind of low-cash in the market trigger on the dev-side).
2. Consider creating gameplay elements based upon settled regions--there is really no advantage that I found to settling around any of the celestial bodies in particular--and the other corporations didn't seem to be too particular. Maybe have some of the corps be territorial (Corp X claims the systems around Adena, and if you want to trade there you have to pay a tax, fight, etc.)
3. Also, what is the damned noise in Daedalus?!? I couldn't figure that one out, is it nothing? Is it something secret that can be discovered that I didn't figure out? I want some more mysteries in the game... alien life, artefacts (maybe this is how to create the cash?) loot dropped from meteors or something.


Overall, I enjoyed it. But, I broke it without meaning to :) Looking forward to the next update, i'll pick it back up for sure..

TL;DR: Superb vision for a game, but my recommendation comes with some caveats.

PROS
+++Hard Sci-Fi (Game steers clear of unknown physics; game word feels very near-future, perfect for physics nerds)
++ Scenery is stunning (and takes into account the changing relative positions of the star, and I think other moons too)
+Fairly easy to get into. Infinitely easier than X (at least the 3rd entry in that series)
+Building up sectors and establishing supply chains felt satisfying
+Economic simulation is great (until you discover auto-trading)
+Combat was satisfying
+Investigating signal beacons felt like an interesting introduction to new sectors

CONS
-Before you do anything, you WILL research autodocking!  X-D
---The UI is a bottleneck to both economic and military domination
-Once you research auto-trading, the supply chains feel irrelevant
-Some minor bugs
-Narrative doesn't seem to fully leverage the amazing setting

In Detail...

Pros first. I feel Deimos Games nailed the setting. Playing the game truly feels like you are living in an (admittedly lonely) astronautical colony. Even more impressive, Deimos take a hard-science approach so -even as a physics lecturer-, there was generally nothing that I could point at and say "that is just impossible". Nothing to pull you from the immersion. Not even any wormholes or FTL. Hell, even the sound effects feel right: rather than a ridiculous "pew pew", it truly sounds like the weapon fire is resounding through the hull of your ship; low pitch and gritty. It is truly "The Expanse" of space economy sims. The position of the star also alters slightly each day and (I've not checked rigorously, but I think) the moons also seem to alter their relative positions, so the natural environment feels real, too.

Helium Rain is fairly easy to get into. I have played 50+ hours of X series games, and rarely spend more than a few hours in those before I get fed up with them, but Helium Rain was much easier to get started and start actually building stuff. If I get the itch for this kind of game, I will probably come here in future. I don't think the other pros really need any more explanation...

Combat was fairly satisfying, the pace is somewhat slow once you get into the larger vessels, since you often start 10 km from the enemy and the big ships move somewhat slowly. While I'm not a fan of the wait while heading into combat, it feels satisfying to pummel an opponent with heavy cannons. My main gripe is that your fleet will stop firing once they disable a ship, and if you want to finish the job, you have to do it yourself, which can be time consuming.

...so on to the cons. The UI is okay at first: if you are doing simple things and don't own much, it is really easy to get going and put in 20-30 hours. However, without planning, the UI then quickly becomes inadequate. Want to move your war fleets? Rather than select the fleet directly as it is displayed on the map, you have to open the sector screen for your destination, and pick the fleet from a dropdown box, which gives _no_ information of what each fleet contains, so let's hope you remembered to rename your fleets to something recognizable! What to merge/split fleets? No dragging and dropping, you have to remove each ship manually, which puts each removed ship into a new fleet, which must then be merged one-by-one into the destination fleet. Want to change the destination of a trade route? You can't edit the destination, so you'll have to make a new waypoint and delete the old one.

These UI tasks are tedious, and subtract from the enjoyability considerably. I'll probably try the game again with better management (renaming fleets), but I think even the most diligent efforts by the player will still find them eventually grinding against the UI as their business expands.

The next issue I have is auto-trading. Until you research auto-trading, the game feels very strategic. You start so far behind the top companies that it makes you think how you can build optimal stations to make the most profit. However, once you research auto-trading it seems far more profitable to retask all freighters to auto-trading, and suddenly be earning a million credits in mere minutes of game time. So, either you want to get auto-trading as soon as possible, or pretend it doesn't exist.

Finally, while the game sets up a superb setting, and even a decent framework for the backstory, it doesn't really seem to follow through. You get the "Pendulum" questline, but the missions seem to do their utmost to avoid building on the story. While enjoyable little errands, they were presented in a fairly bland, concise manner. While this makes the missions easy to understand and execute, it doesn't pull you any further into the world. Of course, I guess that in games like this, I think few people play for the storyline or even the setting. The story is set up as much as it needs to be, and you're free to make your own thereon.

Bottom line, fantastic space sandbox for hard-science fans. If you are methodical and don't rush, the game will reward you for many hours. But beware! If you do rush, the UI will eventually drown you.

(EDITS on May 1, 2020: Having finished the Pendulum mission and had some more combat experience, thought I'd update my comments on those)

I've put a lot of hours into Helium Rain, so decided to give a better review on what the game is, as I'm once more putting it on the shelf. 
 
In essence, this game is an elaborate spreadsheet simulator, with a fluctuating economy based on rival company's own needs and goals. That is not a bad thing, although there are a couple things to note: Actual gameplay is little more than flying to docks. Combat exists, although outside shooting meteors rarely comes up, and almost any aggressive action ends in a sea of headaches. Companys will fight amongst each other, expand, and trade with themselves and you.
 
There is some amount of management. You can buy multiple ships, arrange them in fleets, and maneuver around the systems. You can do trade routes, although do not do this with ships that are too large, or you will cause a lot of issues I'll address later. You can have some large bands of roving attack ships, which in my case was just the opportunity for a bit of money if I happened to be sitting in a system with incoming meteors. A research system exists, but the only research that truly changed anything meaningful was 50% less travel time, and being able to construct foundries, since apparently no other company can make electronics but me now. Robust tools are offered to assemble fleets and automate basic things, as long as you name your fleets and routes properly so you don't forget which ship is the one you want. Manual action is rewarded with time efficiency as your AI ships take a day to dock and do anything, while you can dock an unlimited amount of times in a single system in a day. 
 
However, my primary issue is the lack of immersion. Although the world moves around, it mostly ignores you. Nobody picks fights with you or truly competes. Even the pirates are friendly. As such, it has been me taking advantage of the larger companies who are rather inept at keeping their own supply chains going. Using fleets of Omens on automated trade routes, I was shunting thousands of resources around keeping all the cogs lubricated, but my income was not high enough to play with the big toys, such as battleships or massive stations.
 
And that is when I realized the real enemy in this game is the enemy company's being inept the longer the game runs. They have a fixed amount of money in their corporate pockets, and seem to be fairly ignorant on using it efficiently. I inadvertantly bankrupted a number of companies by upgrading my trading ships to Atlas and Sphinxes; these can carry 1,600 and an impressive 16,000 cargo, while an Omen carries 400. The problem is that the enemy companies spent every last credit they had on me supplying a few stations that could hold many thousands, and then...
 
I had nobody to sell to. Not only that, but the entire economy fell apart. With the enemy companies broke, their supply chains collapsed from the bottom up, and eventually every station they had in the solar system needed things they couldn't afford to supply. Buying resources from them does not seem to increase their coffers, even 50-100k worth of water and fuel. Day by day they hemmorage up perhaps 500 credits total, which I use to try and cram pieces of steel to finish my latest ship, which despite taking hundreds of thousands of credits for me requires steel that they cannot buy from me to complete it. Looking at the diplomacy now, all companies are -10k+ credits in the bank, although Nema Heavy Works is hanging on with a positive balance of 28. Axis Supplies has 400k until I wipe them out, and the pirates are happily sitting on a million, so maybe I'll buddy up with them since they don't hate me. 
 
I'm not sure if destroying the economy of the solar system is an intentional danger in this game, but given it took 20 hours to happen, that's a little rough. My game is not dead, as I can construct my own habitats to sell to, and my own shipyard, but what for? If my goal is to defeat all the other companies, they are pretty much dead, with whole systems floating with the broken corpses of ships they cannot afford to repair. 
 
I found the game relatively cathartic as an idling game. Purchasing auto dock then doing other stuff while my ship tuddled around slowly docking made it more enjoyable. Although I spent 20 hours in it, I never got to accomplish anything in the endgame I desired, like a large self-sufficient complex hidden away in the ruins or a fleet of battleships. It was just far too easy with no particular conflict, and now I'm the only one floating around with a positive balance and the burden of destroying a poor system struggling to survive on it's own. 
 
I admire what the devs have done with this game, and it had a strange charm that kept drawing me back to poke at it even if not with my full attention, but until the difficulty and the ability of companies to sustain themselves without me keeping them afloat or accidentally destroying them, I'll put the game on ice. Since there's no neutral vote, I'll do recommend, but be wary of tutorials that don't cover all the bases or recommend insanity like waging war on people, and may the lord bless you in your first attempts to figure out how automated trade routes work, as that was a nightmare.

This game is early access. That's something to keep in mind.
I've encountered a couple of very minor bugs, none of which interrupt the game. It runs stable, great frame rate, and haven't had a crash at all. Which can't be said for a lot of other games in early development on Steam (and in full release too).
The game itself feels like the X series with Elite and mildly inspired Kerbal Space Program. The physics make it interesting and while at first I was concerned it would be a chore to fly around with the momentum, the game is good about adjusting to your controls and where your mouse is pointing (or where you adjust your view if you use a gamepad).
The game does feel sparsely populated and stations are relatively close together. I haven't played very long (4 hours in), but there doesn't feel like much reason to explore just yet. On the other hand I'm still doing tutorial contracts and understanding the game, so there might be a lot that opens up. There appears to be a story/plot that you can follow, but seems to be ultimately an optional contract to start.
Trading works like you would expect. Stations require specific resources. Some produce specific resources. You purchase the products and sell them to places that have them in demand. One unique aspect in the game is a live economy. It's a welcome aspect that causes natural changes in prices and I look forward to using this to my advantage as I progress in the game.
While the interface seems relatively bland and light, it works very well. The docking information is very helpful in lining up your ship and feels satisfying to have the magnetic bonding occur when you get close. Finding the right information in the menus is a bit of an issue. It feels cumbersome to look up where locations are, how long it'll take to fly there, then enter another menu to look up economic information. On one hand I'd hate it if it made it extremely clear since half the fun of a game like this is finding a trade route, not just having it handed to you. On the other, I'd like to see this design improved in the future. As you start to get additional ships, this sort of management process is more crucial. However there is an option to make trade routes that I assume send your other ships out to do the route automated. If that's the case, then there isn't much issue once they go on their merry way.

Ultimatly I'm happy with this game at this price point. The game feels light on polish and interface, but feels relatively solid in features and content. I'm hoping to see a wider variety of locations, ships, equipment, and items to move in the future, but there's a lot of potential here and the developers are very active on Reddit and on their own forum. This is cleary a work of love, not for a quick buck.

This game, while admittedly still in Early Access, is everything that EVE, No Man's Sky, and the X series strived for. This is a heavy corporation simulation game, with space-battle elements. The point is to create a company, build it up from nothing, and take over all commerce in known space.

The trade system, including setting up trade routes, is fairly complex and requires some tutorials (or blundering around like I did). Once you have your trade networks setup, you can start raking in some serious cash. The market is dynamic and has a finite number of goods. It's possible for the game to run out of a particular good, until more are made. Also, if you take too long to deliver goods to a station, you may show up finding that someone else already sold the station what they needed... now you're left holding onto some cargo you can't sell right away. This makes the commerce aspect of this game incredible!

The flight system is lovely. Newtonian physics rule the game and so you need to get a handle on the controls or you'll find yourself smashing into space stations. Buy the "Automatic Docking" technology as soon as you can. It makes life easier.

The game is heavy on grinding, and if that's your thing, then you're in for a treat. I'm not super far in just yet, so I don't know what all there is to do, but I'm uncovering more and more story-arc style missions. Also, after several hours of playing I'm still working through 'tutorial' missions!

I'm curious to see what elements are added to the game over time. So far it's surprisingly well polished for an EA game and I have yet to encounter any significant bugs.

UPDATE:
I do feel that some more exploration, systems, planets, stars, etc... would be nice. However... considering the technology in the game, I understand that this is not likely to happen, which is unfortunate. One planet and its 4 moons are hardly enough to keep me going.

Also, once you've reached a certain level of development, the game slows to a crawl. The AI will match you ship-for-ship once you start building a large battle fleet. When that happens, performance takes a nose-dive. 

I'm not sure if these last two points can or will be addressed, but they're kind of stopping me from playing any further. That said... I did put 20 hours into this game, and for $12, that's really good.

During a time when magical FTL travel, sound in vacuum and "energy shields" are standard in space fiction settings. This grounded space opera game is a breath of fresh air in the space sim genre. The fully-featured Newtonian fly model and the lack of sound transmission in vacuum really make the space combat feel unique, instead of being just a WW2 dogfight reskin. The setting is also sensible for the near future, a bunch of colonists stranded on a system far away from home struggling for survival in the void around a bountiful gas giant is a much better story to show the desolation of space than galactic empires warring for power.

Being an indie game made mostly by one developer, the game certainly comes with limits, I feel a tiny bit of lack of immersion by the fact that I couldn't drink some space rum made with CH4 mined from a gas giant in a zero-g space bar in a space station with my loyal crews, looking at the blue ring of gas giant thinking about whether our old Earth has the same hue of blue, since loneliness seems to be a part of this game's personality, but that's just cherry-picking. I would definitely be pleasantly surprised tho if the sequel comes with interior and character interaction. Definitely look forward to whatever this talented developer makes next.

This game nails the lonely deep space colony feel 100% with the graphics, art and music. The UI is clean, functional and I also found it intuitive so far.

Gameplay-wise, it seems very similar to a cleaned up X3. I attribute a lot of that cleaner feel to the way the game handles trading and travel. There are no gates, and transfering to different orbits takes days, but days can be fast forwarded through. Days also act as turns for resolving automated trade activities and constructions (and other events during war or metorite intercepts).

The combat was responsive and fun. It seems like it can be easy to disable parts of ships, but destroying them takes a lot more. This turns out to be a good thing since the combat ends when ships are disabled rather than destroyed. So even if you loose a fight, you likely will only need to pay to repair your drifting damaged ships instead of having to construct entirely new ones. I haven't tried combat using larger ships yet.

Definately can recommend this one. The developers are also very active, listen to observations/suggestions, and are willing to discuss them. In some cases they have implemented suggestions very quickly. The game already feels mostly finished and it runs great (no stuttering/performance issues, and no crashes).

So, to me, it feels like you're just playing in different rooms. No feeling of distance, or traveling. When it comes to space games, you're talking distance and traveling. The way this is set up, it just feels wrong. 

Some of the missions just make no sense. In the real world, today, you wouldn't give a stranger a ride to the store just so you can get some reputation increase from him. Well in this game some of the missions will reward you with research or reputation gain. Please correct me if I'm wrong, that is just how i seen it while in game. Yes, many missions do reward you with monetary rewards, and some would argue that the research rewards can be worth it as well. fair enough.  Still, if I was creating a business, the last thing i would want to do is give a free ride to someone who will feel better about me by doing so. 

That really is my big gripe with the game. It has many good things as well. Trading feels rewarding, ship movement does not have speed restrictions, it really feels like you are navigating in space.  Granted, this is only in each sector. Not sector to sector travel. Again that is obtained by simply skiping time into the magical future.

How about organized crime in space? Not pirates, not (just) pew-pew, but robbery in space, capturing a money transport, hacking to enemy stations, stealing corporate secrets, smuggling, being a crime boss? How about hiding your identity, using stolen transponder codes, otherwise you'll get caught by the police? This is quite the little gem. While it has a smaller scale than many of its counterparts, when you consider how many of those counterparts don't quite live up to their ambitions, it's a more than fair trade off. Instead of taking place in a vast galaxy full of numerous alien races you are living in a single solar system populated only with fellow humans who all came from the same colony ship that was lost in a civil war. Without a central government or any habitable planets, you and your fellow humans are left to live and work in orbit of a gas giant and it's moons. 

Most games in this genre sell themselves as having a living, breathing economy, but don't always live up to it. This game seems to have taken great care into this aspect. Missions in this game are needs-based. If one sector is short on food and another short on steel, those will be the hauling missions available. In fact, as far as I could tell, when the game starts your rival corps already have some stations up, but not entire supply chains working. For instance, by the time I could afford my first new ship, I only knew of 1 shipyard. That shipyard already had 3 ships in queue to build from other corps, and those ships weren't being built yet because there weren't nearly enough steelworks to fullfill all the demand. By the time I found the next shipyard, my ship at the other still hadn't been built, but I could already afford another, so I queued it up there. Went to check on it a while later and discovered they had either been attacked by pirates or hit by a meteorite. In either case, not only was my ship still in queue without enough steel to produce it, but the station was so damaged it could only work at 1/10th the speed. I took a short break from my regular mission grind and got the needed steel to the shipyards, set my new ships on some automated trade routes, getting some of those resources moving where they need to be, and started building my own stations. 

I still haven't made it to combat yet, and may update my review after I've gained some experience in that respect, but I can talk a little bit about the flight system itself. Neutonian physics was one of the big selling points for me, and while I do enjoy the feel of it,  any KSP fans will get a laugh out of its "realistic" model. While it has a similar feel to real neutonian physics, it only really works in close proximity. Transfering from one planet/moon to another is fully automated. Every station is in a geostationary orbit and your ship can come to a complete stop in space at any point without the gas giant you're orbiting sucking you in. Docking is not only incredibly easier than in KSP or Orbiter, but can also be automated with one of the first available techs. Apart from a signal hunting mini-game and the combat I still haven't gotten into, you don't actually need to do any flying. That said, the automated function isn't perfect. If you set autopilot to undock from one station and dock at another in the same sector, which also happens to be directly behind the station you just undocked from, autopilot will slam you right into the station. There was even a station I undocked from that was shaped like a giant tube with gravity rings spinning inside. I immediately thought "this will be neat to fly through" and just as immediately, my ship started bashing it's face against an invisible wall that makes it impossible to fly through the tube. All that said the bugs are fairly minor and if they actually made flying realistic you would spend 99% of your game trying to properly dock or being sucked into gas giants. 

If you're looking for something similar to, but more casual than the X or Evochron series, it doesn't get much better than this.

The game has several uniquely skinned zombies- almost doubling those from Arizona Sunshine; and there seems to be some script on top of that which also changes the color of their shirts and clothing; never giving me the feeling of "Oh, I'm shooting at an endless horde of the same asset" vibe I've got from other zombie VR games.

Enemy mechanical variety

The game doesn't stop at having differently skinned zombies that all just waddle up towards you like Arizona Sunshine- alongside the walkers, runners, and ones that inch together at you using their hands with broken legs, you also get ones that explode, buff fellow zombies, shoot radiation around, have guns; among others that go so far as to burrow underground, come up, and attack you at intervals- you need to change your strategies depending on the enemy you're facing- adding so much more depth and complexity to the game. This is on top of the 4 unique bosses mind you- each that are skinned and behave significantly different to each other.

Map variety

There are a total of 7 maps, each which are completely unique, largeish, and that vary with lighting, and even enemies. On the urban setting for instance- you'll get biohazard themed zombies (CDC outfits) thrown into the mix, whereas on the Texan setting, you'll get cowboy zombies with a unique wild west music. 

Weaponry and Progression System

The game has over 20 unique weapons that once again, aren't just reskins of eachother- but behave and sound differently too; from katanas, to RPGs, shotguns, and assault rifles that you can dual wield in a Wolfenstein-esque way, the game lets you murder your way through the hordes in whatever way you please.

This is on top of the progression system to acquire stronger weapons, perks like multishot and increased damage, and an adorable cat you can summon that grants you buffs like temporary infinite ammo and double damage. You need to strategize- do you spend money on better weapons, or invest it into research to get those perks? 

Optimization

I'm playing this on a Ryzen 1700, GTX1080 FE, 16GB of RAM, and SSD for the boot with an Oculus Rift; no stuttering or crashes to report.

This is easily the best wave zombie-shooter in VR I have played. Forget about Kiling Floor Incursion, this is what that game should have been. In my opinion this really wipes the floor with the opposition in terms of playability.

The game consists of waves of zombies and boss waves. The killed enemies can drop ammunition, money or experience, or even power-ups like damage boosts, unlimited ammo for a few seconds or invulnerability. After each wave there are short periods of time that can be used to spend your hard-earned cash and purchase new weapons and ammo, just like Killing Floor. Except you can go shopping any time you like, even during a wave! You can also drop weapons and share them with each other.

The gun play is good, especially in bullet-time mode, with automatic or manual reloading for each weapon. In casual mode you just basically press a button to drop the mag, and pull weapon close to your chest to reload.
In "hardcore" mode the weapon damage is doubled, but the weapons need manual loading. In this mode you can either drop the magazine with controller button, or pull it out and then insert a new one from the ammo belt manually. If you fired all the rounds you will need to pull back the bolt, but if you didn't then you can continue firing as soon as the magazine is replaced.

You can even mix these two so that your co-op partner could be playing "casual" mode while you play "hardcore", without effecting each others gameplay.

There are dozens of weapons to choose from, from knives and pistols grenade launchers (and a minigun), and they all look, sound and feel good. The MP5-equivalent of the game even has the notch for the bolt to catch it! This is a nice touch. As you complete levels you unlock more weapons and they level up as you play and improve their stats (permanently) which increases damage and magazine size. 

Completing levels and leveling up your character gives you perk points which can be used to increase crit chance, ammo pool, bullet time cooldown/duration, available stamina/HP and even trader prices and power-up drop chances.

Weapon unlocks, character and weapon leveling and perk system all feel rewarding and you never really feel you wasted your time.

You can customize your UI to your liking, the locomotion options are varied and you can use free locomotion or teleporting, or mix of the two, depending on your preference. You can even fully customize your holster positions to your liking along X, Y and Z axis!

There aren't too many levels to choose from but I am pretty sure that if you like shooting games in VR, this is a must-buy!

Aside from some minor gripes I can't really think of any major faults in this game.

This is a wave/arena shooter. You're in small maps, attacked by waves of zombies, at the end of the way there are boxes with supplies, which you collect, and you also buy weapons and ammo between the waves in the shop.

Like some other reviewer mentioned, there's decent enemy variety and multiple zombie types, plus there are bosses. The developers also tried to make sure they won't all look the same, so there are recolored shirts/clothes/etc.

There are issues however.

* The store page claims the game supports seated play, that is a lie. No seated play support, meaning there's no height offset, and while you COULD play in a chair, you'll be playing an angry hobbit with a shotgun, as your eyes will be at seated level.
* At the start of the game my controls didn't work, and that required using ocmmunity control mapping through steam settings, which is very unobvious thing to do.
* At the start of the game, the guns in my hands were facing 45 degrees upward and were hard to aim. THis can be configured in the settings, however...
* You can't go into settings/options from the game. You're either in the level, or you're in the settings.
* Smooth turn technically exists, but is comletley unusable, as turning speed is too low and cannot be raised to a decent value.
* Some parameters are configured via sliders and there's no way to precisely adjust numerical value. For example, turning speed is a slider, locomotion speed is a slider, and if you accidentally move locomotion slider from its default value, then it is unlikely that you'll be able to move it abck to its 300 spot. (the range is 0-600, and the slider is small, meaning you'll simply miss the value).
* There are some awkward translations here and there, as developers were apparently asian.
* Smooth locomotion uses acceleration during movement, that might trigger VR sickness in some people quite quqickly.

The biggest problem for me was lack seated support and smooth turn support. When I finally played it standing, I found that it isn't as awful as it seemed, and is actually not bad. However I also realized that it is not what I'm looking for right now.

If you're a zombie game fan, have standing play space and no knee problems, I think it is worth checking out.

Now in terms of the core gameplay, I think they have things really well balanced overall but I have a few suggestions which (if the devs ever came back) should be implemented to take this to a full price game level experience.

1. Allow a sprint button. Rather than set a fixed movement speed just give us a fixed walk and run mechanic.
2. For hardcore mode, place magazines and holsters where they should be - on your vest or belt rather than floating in front of you. Yes - I have adjusted the placement for weapon holsters in the options but you can't adjust where ammo is held. Give us a virtual vest like Pavlov or Onward and this would also increase immersion. 3. Allow the auto grip of second hand in Hardcore mode or allow it to be hold to grip rather than toggle. Toggle is not intuitive.

BIG STUFF
5. Allow some larger maps and integrate a story mode. This game could become a RE style game with a little narrative or NPC allies. Protect a VIP or transport something etc from a central safe house as you head out to the open city on various objectives.
6. Allow us to choose our loadout at the gun range and take these weapons with us. We've earned them by levelling up so let us choose what we start with.
7. Add unlimited ammo to the gun range and let us have more fun. Maybe an zombie spawner or sandbox mode would be a great little time waster.
8. ATTACHMENTS!!! Yes some guns come fitted but allow us to customise our weapons like the last Pavlov update. 
9. Player model. This needs serious work as the current model does not compare at all to the AAA zombie models.
10. Base/barricade building. Give us a map or add to an existing one where we can fortify a stronghold. We can use money to buy upgrades and this adds another level of core gameplay.
11. More maps! We currently have 4 maps but there is so much more that could be done. The progression of maps currently has no relation to a story beyond a brief blurb.

Alright, 22 hours in to the game, here's what I've got to say.
Super fun game. High replay value.
ZomDay offers a wide selection of guns and various skills to invest in to make different builds to use which makes every level feel different. By builds I mean this, pistol, shotgun, assault rifle, sniper ad melee. It took me about 12 hours (give or take) to max out my level being 100. Upon leveling and beating missions and challenges on various difficulties you get skill points which you can re-spec at a small cost of special tokens called snake coins. Snake coins are used to unlock new skills as well as purchase special strong weapons in a mission (which you can refund at the end of the game). So Let's say you buy a gold 1911 pistol for 6coins, you can refund it for 3. The drop rate on the coins is vey reasonable, considering you need about 100 to unlock good skills.
At level 100 I have about 300skill points (another 50 if I could beat 2 of the missions that are super hard)

This is a mindless zombie arena horde wave shooter. You can play online coop multiplayer or you can play single player. You can use different weapons from pistols, shotguns, SMGs, ARs, grenades, mines, and melee weapons. You'll be up against a horde of zombies that includes zombies with special abilities such as exploding zombies, zombies that heal other zombies when they explode, zombies that throw poison gas at you, and boss fights at the end of the waves. 

You have full locomotion and smooth turning options (as well as teleportation and snap turning or no turning). There's different graphical, HUD, and sound settings as well. You can two hand weapons and it does help a little bit with weapon stabilization, but you can also 1 hand 2 handed weapons. This is not a sim, it's 100% full arcade action. You reload weapons by bringing them close your body and then pressing a button (varies depending on headset).

It's obviously better played with friends. The thing holding back this game is that it very much does feel like a VR game from 2017, which it is. In fact, I bought it on sale back in 2017 and while there is more here than there was in 2017, a lot of the core gameplay is essentially the same. Sadly, it's still better than most horde shooters in VR with all the variety it has in weapons and zombie types.  

However, weapons don't handle all that great. The maps are pretty small. Zombies just seem to pop out of nowhere and they come from all sides. You'll clip through zombies and some objects. While you do get to use different weapons and you can get upgrades and level up certain skills .. it's still just mindless shooter action. Run and gun and melee as often as feasible seems to be the only strategy. The major challenge in this game is just not running out of bullets. The only times I died is because I ran out of ammo or in the boss fights because they are bullet sponges.

There's only 5 maps although they do vary the objectives, the gameplay loop is very similar from one to the next. Even the challenge mode doesn't feel all that different from the normal "story" mode gameplay. And yeah, there is no story. You see a zombie, you shoot it fast and quickly in the head. Rinse and repeat.
