Zombie Army 4: Dead War – A Gory, Glorious Nazi Zombie Slaughterhouse

Rebellion’s Zombie Army 4: Dead War is a masterclass in horde-based third-person shooting, blending the precision of Sniper Elite with the relentless chaos of Left 4 Dead. Whether you’re playing solo or with a squad, this game delivers a thrilling mix of strategic sniping, close-quarters brutality, and wave-based mayhem that never gets old.

Combat – Satisfying Gunplay with Brutal Precision
The core shooting mechanics in Zombie Army 4 feel fantastic, especially if you love precision shooting. The signature Sniper Elite kill-cam is back, rewarding well-placed shots with slow-motion X-ray destruction. Watching a round shatter a Nazi zombie’s skull—or explode a ribcage with a well-placed rifle shot—never gets old.

You start with a basic arsenal, but weapons can be upgraded in creative ways. The M1 Garand with incendiary rounds? Deadly. The Trench Gun upgraded with an electric charge? Pure carnage. Even the PPSH-41, an already high-rate-of-fire SMG, can be turned into a zombie-shredding machine with explosive rounds. Each weapon has a noticeable weight and kick, making every kill feel impactful.

Melee combat is just as satisfying. A well-timed stomp can crush multiple zombies, and performing takedown kills refills your health—encouraging aggressive play even when you're surrounded. Special abilities like shockwave punches or fire-based axe melee strikes add another layer of depth to close-quarters combat.

Campaign – Cinematic Set Pieces and Spooky Atmosphere
The campaign spans nine missions, each packed with cinematic moments, eerie settings, and a variety of enemies that keep things fresh. One moment, you’re battling through a flooded Venice overrun with the undead; the next, you’re escaping a crumbling fortress or fighting a zombie tank in a fiery war zone.

Standout levels include:

"Zombie Zoo" – A twisted, abandoned zoo filled with grotesque experiments and terrifying zombie tigers.
"Hell Base" – A secret Nazi bunker where dark experiments have gone horribly wrong, culminating in one of the game’s toughest fights.
"Molten Nightmare" – A volcano-infused battlefield where lava flows through the streets, forcing you to fight both zombies and the environment itself.
The environmental design is top-tier, balancing horror elements (creepy abandoned buildings, sudden ambushes) with high-energy action sequences.

Enemies – More Than Just Your Average Zombies
Sure, there are classic shambling zombies, but Zombie Army 4 throws a lot more at you:

Suiciders – These explosive zombies charge at you and detonate on impact, forcing you to stay alert.
Elite Zombies – Armed with LMGs or flamethrowers, these tanky enemies require teamwork (or heavy firepower) to bring down.
Butchers – Massive, chainsaw-wielding monstrosities that can tear you apart in seconds.
Necromancers – These guys resurrect fallen zombies, turning even a cleared-out area into a nightmare if left unchecked.
Zombie Sharks – Yes, there are actual zombie sharks. Need I say more?
Boss fights, like the Zombie Tank and Hitler’s Final Form, are intense, requiring smart use of explosives, teamwork, and constant movement.

Horde Mode – Pure Survival Madness
If the campaign wasn’t enough, Horde Mode offers an endless challenge. You start with basic gear and must scavenge for better weapons and upgrades as increasingly tough waves of zombies attack. Maps change dynamically, with new areas unlocking as rounds progress, keeping things unpredictable.

One moment, you're holding the line in a bunker, barely holding off an elite wave. The next, you’re running for your life as an entire street collapses behind you. The escalating chaos makes for some of the most intense moments in the game.

Co-op – The Real Way to Play
Zombie Army 4 is enjoyable solo but thrives in co-op. The difficulty scales dynamically, meaning more players means more enemies, more chaos, and more chances for hilarious team-based disasters.

Reviving teammates under pressure, setting up synchronized sniper shots, and using electric traps to wipe out an entire wave of zombies is pure fun. Plus, the emote system and character skins, add a layer of ridiculous charm to the experience.

Final Verdict – A Must-Play for Zombie Fans
If you love games like Sniper Elite, or Left 4 Dead, Zombie Army 4: Dead War is a no-brainer (literally). With its precise shooting mechanics, grotesque enemy designs, pulse-pounding set pieces, and chaotic co-op action, this game delivers some of the most fun you can have mowing down hordes of the undead.

Other examples of bad mini gaming are that they give you the answers instead of clues in your book.  Othertimes, like the hidden door lock, you pull a piece of paper out of the trash with the solution but you can't interact with that paper and look at it after you already seen it the initial time. This is a point and click adventure game though I sort of use "adventure" lightly.  It was developed by RSK Entertainment, an Iranian based game company.  I mostly decided to purchase it because I want to support more developers from the Middle East.

It's not likely to top anyone's top 100 list of games but it does have it's own... charm.

The graphics are a childish 2D drawn/cutout style that I think is evocative of the childish nature of the story and character so while I wouldn't be nominating the graphics for any awards it was certainly fitting for the game.  I liked that the backgrounds depicted more modern and typical sorts of views of life in Iran (as opposed to orientalist fantasy).  The settings seemed fairly representative of modern day Iran's homes and towns.  The animations were okay for the style of the game but not very impressive.  They were however fairly smooth and well transitioned animations with no visible glitches.

The background music was good, it had some tunes that I'm sure I've heard before but cannot quite place.  The background musi certainly helps you to feel the Iranian flavor of the game.  The voices are all in Persian/Farsi it seems so I can't attest too much to the quality of the voice acting but the sound quality was good and the story seems to be done in the form of some sort of poetry (a common element to both Arab and Persian storytelling and culture).  The meter sounds good, though I understand very little of what's being spoken.

Though though the game's audio is in Persian/Farsi there are English subtitles.  While I get the jist of what's being said the translation quality is absolutely terrible.  It's almost comically bad!  Problems range from simple spelling errors, to different terms for the same thing being used, to poorly worded sentences.  You'll likely understand most of it but its going to be a very awkward read.  I think they may have been trying to maintain some of the poetry's meter and perhaps rhyme?  But it doesn't translate well that way.  It could use another pass over by an English translator or at least have an English speaker re-write the phrases so they could be better worded and understood even if it's translation of the idea more than the specific words.  

The story and dialogue are definitely reflective of Iranian values and culture.  Unfortunately it's cultural charm are not enough to save it from a slightly unclear story line.  It's not exactly clear what Alimarden is supposed to be doing though there are occasional clues as to how he should use his inventory.  But the story itself is a little bland.  Basically you are Alimarden and for often no good reason you just want to do bad things that make problems and get you into trouble.  The first half of the game is spent destroying things being a little mean and possibly abusive to animals and making messes... the second half is spent with Alimarden seemingly wanting to make amends and cleaning up his messes and making apologies.  I guess in that sense it has some morality teaching players about redemption.

The interface is fairly simple there's a main menu where you can stat a new game, save a game, get instructions on how to play (basically just click on everything with a hotspot, click inventory to desired location).  In game you can see all hotspots by clicking the spacebar.  Items will pop up their title when you mouse-over them.  Your inventory is accessed simply by bringing the mouse cursor to the top of the screen.  There's also a little circle with a brain pictured on it in the upper right hand corner.  I thought at first it was like a checklist of things you had to do but by halfway through the game I started to think it's actually more intended as hints if you get stuck.  I think this might be one reason why I played through it so quickly.


My time spent playing was probably around 1-1.5 hours making this $4-$6/hour of game play.  That's pretty pricey.  If you want to experience a game from the Middle East or give it a try for any reason... wait for a sale.  It does go on sale frequently during steam seasonal sales.  I wouldn't recommend purchasing it at full price though.  When purhased cheap you might enjoy it as a quick quirky game to play one afternoon or something.

Alimardan's Mischief is a simple 2D point and click adventure game with a comedy theme as you control a bratty kid that is a nuisance and causes a lot of problems.  Gameplay involves clicking around on your screen to make the kid misbehave by putting down banana peels and other bratty behaviour. 

This game has been translated from some other language into English... badly.  If this was done through Google Translate, Google Translate should feel ashamed of itself.  Regardless, the language in this game is broken and will put off a lot of gamers.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, left handed gamers or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 2 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Alimardan's Mischief has the gamer gouging price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.  For comparison, the $5 asking price for this game could get you games like the Tomb Raider remake, "Mass Effect 3" or "Portal 2".  Yeah, Mass Effect 3, or this.  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.  There's also thousands of free, superior quality games on Steam.

This game is one if not the best multiplayer game for VR thanks to 2 things :

1) Movement

The movement system feels a lot like the one from Climbey but better. Once you understand how it works it's incredibly precise and rewarding. Throwing yourself across the map with the "muscle up" card and using the grappling hook midair to get behind an unsuspecting enemy with your "skirmisher gun" is an amazing thing to do. I've spent 30 minutes, just swinging myself around the map, being amazed at how fast you begin to master the movement system. 
Incredible on this aspect and very unique.

2)The Cards

Once again, a cool unique feature. You build a deck of 20 cards when you're in the main menu, during the match these cards appear on your arm and you use them by throwing them on the ground.

Cards are divided in 4 categories :
-Offense = Weapons (burst rifle, almost OS rifle, dual shoulder mounted miniguns, homing rockets etc...)
-Buffs = Shields, get tiny or big, be super strong, reduce gravity for you only etc...
-Utility = Flying dragon, create a wall to take cover, create a black hole etc...
-Movement = cool stuff like grappling hooks, gravity vortexes, jetpacks, wings to fly like a bird etc...

When you start the round you have 6 cards on your left arm. When you cast one of them it adds time to a timer on your right wrist. When that timer reaches 0 your hand is"refilled". Some cards add more time than others. If you want to you can discard a card (it adds only 2 secs to the timer).

The card system makes it so that you can have plenty of different gaming styles in one match.
One second you're using the skirmisher to take out somebody from behind, the next second you're launching rockets from the sky thanks to your handmounted jetpack. 

Basically this systems ensures that you're never getting bored.

Oure is a gentle beautiful ethereal game which lovers of flying will enjoy.  It has a good mixture of zen flying, finding collectables, solving puzzles and battling to calm the Titans to fulfil their role.  This is a non-violent game, but you can be killed if you stray in the wrong area.
You play a dragon-child whose parents have sent you to the land in the skies to save the dying and stricken world below.  You can choose between a girl and a boy.  Your main role is to activate ancient machinery and puzzles which will awaken the eight Titans who have the power to restore the world.  You have to calm each Titan down and restore them to their full glory.  Only then will they trust you and aid you in bringing restoration to the world below.
Along the way, you will discover relics of the past.  There are also glowing orbs which give you more stamina and empower you in other skills.  I managed to find all 750 of them!!  The clouds themselves can restore your energy too by simply flying through them.  Some people will find it laborious to track down all the collectables and relics.
I love flying in games and this was the best flying game I've played.  It has a gentle ambiance to it and you can go your own pace.  The devs captured the movement of the flying dragon well.  You can see the love they poured into this game. 
The lovely and interesting environments are backed by a sublime orchestral soundtrack which soars around you on your journey.  When you're following the Titans the music becomes more strident and urgent.  Great stuff!
Gameplay was good, but I did have some frustrating moments controlling the dragon in tight spots underground and with the Titans on keyboard.  I'm hoping it is better with a game pad which is recommended.  Some other reviewers said these problems are caused by the camera's position. 
The 'battles' with the Titans can be frustrating because some of them are quite hard, but perseverance and thinking outside of the box will pay handsome dividends.  I did find these 'battles' a bit jarring to the rest of the game which is very relaxing.   Plus the similar actions required for the Titans became repetitive.
You can be killed by hidden rays in the ground but this game is extremely forgiving and you respawn very quickly.
There is no map for this game despite a very large world.  But by turning your dragon into a circle it highlights the areas to be explored, so that was extremely handy.  This could be done anytime.
Voiceovers are by British child actors and they did a good job with the minimal dialogue.
Graphics were really lovely, gentle, ethereal with surprises popping up here and there.  The devs created a very original world in the skies and this old dragon approved.  
The ending did feel a bit of a anti-climax after all your hard work.  Sadly, this game never seems to go on sale.
Highly recommend for those who enjoy floating around at a leisurely pace amidst a calm environment.  8.5/10

[h1]A fantastic little cracked gem of a game.[/h1]

You'll probably know if Oure is your 'thing' from the description, and if it is there's a lot to love. The world is simply gorgeous, and the controls work well with them to make this a very Zen experience. It really captures the feeling of flight in a way that makes it intuitive to play around and pull off graceful manoeuvres with ease. While this might be the dragon nerd in me talking, I really think Oure beautifully captures how a creature like this would move, and because of that the dragon is a joy to control. On top of the gorgeous overworld, the Titan segments are visually spectacular and consistently creative mechanically.

But, I did mention this was a cracked gem and your enjoyment of Oure will really depend on your ability to deal with some of the niggles the game can throw at you. 

The largest wish I had was that game had a bit more confidence in itself and what it was trying to be. I felt the overly generous scattering of collectable orbs, text based UI prompts and opening explanitory voice acting were attempts to try and justify its ‘gamey-ness.’ Oure is very rapid to give you objectives and explanations, when I feel a subtler approach that let you explore and form some of your own conclusions could have really upped the imersiveness of the experience. For example, turning off the stamina bar and using nothing but the contextual tattoo on your dragon’s back is a beautiful immersive touch, but you get pulled out of it a little every time you collect an orb and the word ‘saving’ flashes up and the number of orbs you’ve collected displays on the screen; two things that could have easily been conveyed in a way that didn’t use obvious text. This is something that drastically improves over the course of the game, though, as the game lets go of your hand a bit and leaves you to explore after the first few titans.

Another potential problem is the small elements of polish that are missing. The game shows its humbler origins than, say, Journey or Abzu by some of the small niggling technical complaints. There are quite a few small issues like the DoF being a bit too aggressive, moments where the physics-based animation would jitter out in confined spots, and the camera needing wrangling particularly in the Titan segments. They didn’t bother me much, but I can see them causing death by a thousand cuts for some with less patience for them. However, these are very much fixable problems that could be addressed in the future, making the game a wholehearted recommendation.

However, I really feel these complaints are overshadowed by the many things the game does right. There’s clearly a lot of love that’s been put into Oure, and it shows in the world that has been created. The moments when the cloudscape moved into sunset, or a cool night, or a grey overcast were breathtaking. It also feels well paced, not overstaying its welcome and not making its overworld too big or daunting. Oure nails its atmosphere, and soaring through clouds, only to find a small entrance that leads to a hidden cloud cave filled with an ancient ruin was an exploration dream come true.

If relaxing, exploration focused experiences are your thing, then Oure is a fantastic labour of love, so long as you have patience with its rougher side.

Goblin and Coins II is an old-school, 2D pixel art platformer game, with nice, hand-drawn graphics, fluid animations and simple, yet responsive control system. The main character is unarmed, so the trick is to avoid enemies or squish them by jumping on them. The game features 25 levels, filled with various enemies and environmental obstacles, along few boss fights in between. There's also a bit of puzzle elements thrown in for good measure.

It's challenging, but not too hard and you can adjust the difficulty by allowing more continues when you lose all lives. However, the game is not over even if you have spent all your continues: you spawn in the Underworld and if you manage to escape it, you will be ressurected with additonal continues.

Goblin and Coins II is an unique nostalgia trip to the 8-bit era, but it could also be a perfect introduction into the world of video games for your kids.

This is quite an improvement from the original which was charming but had several elements which made it a rather conditional recommendation. While it won't convince anyone who's not already a platformer fan to get into the genre, it is rather well built. While there's a live system that does have you frequently quitting to menu instead of risking a death, it's not a true game over so it's up to you as a player to play as you consider best. Levels are simple enough with occasional key hunts, but they are moderately memorable in layout and design. While the game is linear, there are incentives to replay, especially with some of the unlockable upgrades which add a minor Metroidvania flavour while also making things easier. 

My only complaint so far is that when going to full coin runs, the game expects you to find all the coins in the stage at once (instead of remembering which coins you've picked before). This is easy enough in most stages, but on some of the larger ones with plenty of branching paths the search can get exhausting.

Looking forward to the standalone expansion.

As of now, I've given Goblins and Coins II a quick run on the Steam Deck. I've completed three maps so far. So, plenty of game left to go, but I thought I'd offer a few quick thoughts on the game so far.

1: The game plays perfectly on the Steam Deck, which is my only PC gaming venue ATM, so Deck compatibility is important to me. No issues there at all and I haven't needed to tweak anything. There was one prompt for interacting with an in game object so far (B button), but beyond that, it's been all move and jump, choose a map, or scroll through upgrades. Easy peazy.

2: The game itself has even more charm than the first game and is definitely suitable for gamers of any age.

3: I'm "die terribly because I misjudge jumps" guy when it comes to platformers, but I find the platforming challenges in this game to be pretty intuitive.

4: It's a really nice looking game and the level design is sensible.

5: It's also very much a pick up and play type game. Have 5 or 10 minutes available? You can accomplish something, and you'll never forget how to play it if you take a break for whatever reason.

Anyway, that's my budget review of Goblins and Coins II. I do know the developer, but I purchased Goblins and Coins II myself with the intention of playing it at a casual pace with no obligations, so know in reading this that you are getting a review of the game rather than a fluff piece for the dev.

I'd recommend giving this game a look. It's fun, cute, inexpensive, and Steam Deck compatible.

Rain of Reflections does not tell you too much at the start of the game. Leaving it to the player to discover this beautiful world was a clever move from the developers. The more you find out, the deeper the game pulls you into its story.

I remember enjoying point an click adventures very much as a teenager and young adult. Since then point an click adventures have changed and often don't seem as enjoyable to me as in the past. Rain of Reflections revived this long lost feeling of a through and through exciting and intriguing adventure.

The game is a mixture of an adventure, a turn-based strategy game, and a puzzle game. In order to hack computers, security systems, or electronic devices you need to solve different types of puzzles. Although this is the weakest part of the game it's still fun.

Enemy encounters have to be solved in turn-based strategy mode, which is very exciting and doesn't need to hide behind AAA titles like XCOM or Shadow Tactics. In my opinion, 'Rain of Reflections' actually does a better job than XCOM. It's amazing!

'Rain of Reflections: Set Free' is actually the first episode of a three-episode game and was released on October 4th, 2019. This means that in order to experience the full story, we have to wait for two more episodes to be released. 

Rumor has it that the game has been abandoned because the developers didn't share updates on the progress of the next episodes for quite some time. Officially the game hasn't been abandoned and frankly, even if episodes 2 and 3 won't be released, episode 1 is very much worth being played anyway. 

Yes, there is an open ending, but it's not too bad because the first part of the story comes to a conclusion. In my opinion, it's absolutely worth playing this episode no matter if additional episodes will be released or not.

The game/episode has a rather short play-time. It took me 4 hours and 40 minutes to finish the game. But right after finishing the game I started a new play-through. This time aggressive and attempting to do everything different than the first time. Decisions in the game make a difference and change the outcome.

There's a sequence in the game where you steal a taxi and fly to your next destination. This part is so relaxing and feels so real, I simply didn't want to get out of the taxi anymore. The music on the radio is fantastic and together with the rain, constantly falling on your windscreen and the colorful neon billboards passing by, puts you right in the cyberpunk mood. It creates a very relaxing moment.

'Rain of Reflections' is a must-play for every cyberpunk fan. Even if only the first of three episodes has been released and even if the other two won't come, which is not sure yet, the game is very much worth playing. I love it!

[h1]That said, I think this game is pretty unique.[/h1]
Described succinctly, Rain of Reflections is a point and click adventure game with grid puzzle [hacking] and turn-based stealth sections.
[b]Sections:[/b][list]

[*] Hacking mini-games.

Breach is a turn-based physics based 'get-the-ball-into-the-hole' with momentum minigame. You'll need to control its inertia and utilize the landscape to succeed. There is also a 3D rotational block puzzle where you've got a limited number of turns to match it to a 2D shape. And a third hacking puzzle that uses sound waves to navigate a plane. This is also turn-based.

[*] 'Encounters' and 'Confrontations'.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2413129043
Stealth is paramount to these sections, as you're largely be ill-equipped to deal with the threat that befalls you. However, you'll have a battery powered stealth device available to you. Narratively, some of the enemies are trying to capture you. But you will eventually obtain weapons.[/list]

[h1]Huh, whose footprints are these?[/h1]
'Encounters' can turn into 'Confrontations' rather abruptly upon being spotted. And while the game does allow you to fire at enemies, no one actually has any [i]'health'[/i] bars. Instead, everyone has a “motivation” bar. Wherein status effects alter their “motivation”. Upon losing “motivation”, they'll flee. Wilona specifically losing motivation will result in a game over. You can lose motivation from being spotted, being exposed, being suppressed etc. And you're able to speak your to partner or the enemies during a fight, this will encourage or annoy them—something of that ilk, gaining a small bit of 'motivation' back for the former. If an enemy shoots at you, you'll have a chance to move the character out of the way. And vice versa. This action is performed at the cost of a lot of motivation. So don't get caught. As mentioned, you will eventually have two people to control in these sections but only Wilona has stealth. She's able to hack things mid-fight (be it an encounter or confrontation) and obtain more charges for her stealth device.

Typically the objective is to get from one place to another in these sections and “killing” or “taking out” enemies is not required. You can complete it pacifist. In fact, there's an achievement for not resorting to violence.

[h1]The Gist:[/h1]
The game is not complete, this is 1 of 3 purported sections of a game that show little evidence of being in the works. It's not that long, but it's very polished for what it is. I would like to see more episodes, but I don't think they're coming. Beyond this, I feel the 'game' is decently priced at $10 USD. It does end on a cliffhangar that will probably never be resolved. It's a familiar sci-fi narrative but it's well told or at least interesting and different enough to hold your attention for its 4 hour duration.

I enjoyed it. 

Though, I'd have liked to see a 'restart encounter' option. Story decisions are one thing to lock someone into once made. But encounters, especially in a hybrid like this, should have some flexibility—at least in my opinion.

Tough one. But I'll give you my honest opinion on this "game" and its pricing model. I bought this after its price was reduced to 10 bucks (5 on sale). For that I got a 2.5 hour long experience. The developers want to release 2 more chapters with other characters and probably other gameplay features. This idea in itself is interesting, hooooowever. Some mild spoilers might follow:

Chapter 1 or Wilona's chapter starts off quite interesting. There's a bit of world building, a bit of character building and some tutorial stuff about her remote hacking and cloak abilities. Remote hacking is a kind of puzzle. You either have to guide a ball around a level to an end point, have to locate a sound source or rotate some geometric shapes to fit into a grid.
Let's start off with the fact that 90% of the puzzles are about the ball. And that puzzle is mostly fine...if you could scroll the map and knew where you were going to plan your route accordingly and not fall into nothingness. The sound location puzzle is also mostly fine, but there are only like 2 or 3 in the whole game. The rotating shapes puzzle on the other hand is just terrible. You're supposed to fit a 3D object into a 2D frame by rotating and flipping it, however you only have a very limited number of moves to do so. Any failure in anything results in, well failure. No option to repeat, nothing. Might be realistic, but then again, these are puzzles, you're not actually "hacking" anything...

The 2nd part of the game is "encounters". These usually start off with you being unspotted and having to escape a situation. Which is fine, since Wilona is not a hardened fighter, I'd assume, being the daughter of the minister and a doctor...as well as being a doctor herself. So you gotta sneak away and use your "cloak" ability, which turns you invisible for a turn, but needs to be recharged. You will do this 2 or 3 times...then you meet up with another character who doesn't have a cloak and the whole gameplay mechanic is obsolete. You then have to basically fight your way through every encounter, and of course you now have a gun. Gotta be honest, the game was a lot more fun without the guns. By then it devolved into your typical XCOM experience, just instead of shooting to kill you're primarily shooting to demoralize and make the enemy flee, but then you can shoot them dead anyway. Whether that has any positive or negative effects on the game I don't know. Didn't seem like it. It would have been interesting to have the game adapt to your play style (only playing Wilona, not the other douche), whether you accomplished your goals through sneaking, talking or violence and whether you actually killed people or not...but nah...

The 3rd part is the "adventure" part. And I put this in quotes, because this is not an adventure. You're just going from screen to screen, interacting with things...i.e. hacking and talking. That's it. The game claims that it has multifacetted characters and each and every line is unique and yet I am pretty sure that everyone playing this game will have mostly the same experience. It doesn't matter whether I ignore a call from my mother, the bloody minister, she's gonna do the same thing at the end either way. It doesn't matter whether I steal a car and lie to someone about it being stolen, because that person is never seen again, etc. You are NOT interacting with any character for more than a minute then they're obsolete.

This is supposed to be a "full" game, yet nothing is fleshed out. How am I supposed to care for any of the characters when the story is so obscure and there's no connection between anyone? To be honest, the game feels pretty soulless. Dark Souls characters have more background.

What they SHOULD have done instead, is combine all their planned chapters into 1 game, give each character 2 or 3 alternating chapters and gradually introduce new gameplay elements for each character in each chapter, while spinning a continuous story. What they did instead was create a boring character with gameplay features that are barely being used, it's basically a glorified tutorial, yet the next chapter won't even be related to this character anymore. So, her story is over? The story, that at the end, by the way devolved into a total mess to be honest. Like, "oh we don't care anymore now, let's just throw stupid stuff at the screen no human would ever say". I'm just confused and irritated. Wait for all the chapters to be released and then take a long look if you really want to buy this.

Oh wow, this game is a gem! It took me a while to start playing it, but this game has an interesting concept and a couple innovative fresh new features.

To roughly break it down, the game combines two genres. One is an adventure game with walking around, interacting with stuff and doing some dialogues. The other part is a turn-based tactical "combat" on a grid. I've put "combat" in exclamation marks, because you actually try to avoid fighting.

Adventure part:
The adventure part isn't actually that original. When you walk near interactive objects, you see an Eye-icon popping up to indicate you can interact with. Dialogues are also clearly marked with a Chat-icon. The dialogues also let you know via icon, if the option is a decition to make, which branches off into different story outcomes, or if it is a topic you can talk about and still got the option to talk about the other topics. I wouldn't call it innovative, but actually I think it helps to have more control over a conversation. You also can hack various electronics via 3 different minigames. You sometimes have two different routes to choose from and sometimes you can do them all, to hack 2 different things on the same terminal. The minigames are a bit hard to explain, but they are somewhat innovative, not that hard, but still are fun enough to enjoy doing.

Tactical part:
The tactical part is where this gem starts to shine. But not necessarily because it's high quality, but because it feels somewhat new. The tactical part basically is a stealth game, where you try to avoid enemies and clear your objectives. Get to a specific spot, deactivate electric devices, hacking a terminal etc.

You got 2 actions to spent on Movement, Attack and Talk. At least these are the options so far, 3 hours into the game. You can't attack twice, but you can move twice and also talk twice, as long as you got some dialogues to choose from, more on that in a bit.

Movement costs one action and requires you to pick a spot on the marked grid in reach, which shows you a preview of your movement on the first click. If you are happy, you can confirm that action. If an orange indicator is shown on your path, it means you moved over something that startled the enemies, like a puddle or something, so the enemies will start scout the area towards that spot. If a red indicator shows up on your path, it means they have visual contact and start a confrontation, which basically is combat. So when you make some noise that spot will be marked for the enemies, so you know where they are going to. If they saw you, they will go towards that spot where they last saw you, which isn't necessarily the spot where you ended your movement at. So whenever you have Line of Sight to someone and then lose sight to that target, the target will be shown at it's last known location. So enemies will not just magically know where you are, if they lost sight on you. I think this is a brilliant mechanic.

Attack costs one action and I believe you need some sort of weapon. I'm not sure yet if there are any melee or fist attacks. So far I can only speak about pistols. Pistols need ammunition, which you can collect from various ammo boxes, scattered around the tactical map. Interacting with those require no additional action, just have to get next to it. I'm not exactly sure how the range of a weapon is indicated, because so far I haven't noticed any radius or something. To attack you have to open a radial menu, pick Attack and then a target. Not the most comfortable way to attack, but since attacking isn't your main goal, it's not that bad. You can also attack various interactive objects to disable an electric trap or something.

The tatical part uses a Cover-system. Cover 1 means it gets destroyed in 1 attack and Cover 2 lasts 2 attacks. So you can destroy all cover in game I think. The number is a bit small and I think they simply should have used different icons instead. Maybe a shield for 1 and an outlined shield to indicated it's reinforced or something for 2. You can either attack the enemies cover, or the enemy directly, which will be affected by his cover. But since the game uses Motivation instead of Health, attacking the enemy directly isn't always the best choice. Destroying his cover maybe can harm his motivation way more than shooting him. But more on that Motivation thing later.

The 3rd action I've encounter so far in the game is Talking, which also costs 1 action. You either can talk to your allies or the enemies. Not all enemies have dialogue options to choose from, but on some they can be unlocked somehow during the Encounter. Each Chat Line have different effects. You can encourage your allies of example, or even yourself to gain benefits. Or you can try to talk your way out with the enemy, or simply lower his Motivation in various ways. This is one of the most unique things I've seen in the genre for a while and can be a lot of fun to find balance between talking, moving and attacking.

Oh and I almost forgot about the main characters special free-action, the Invisibility Cloak. Activating it costs 1 battery charge and will last till your next turn starts. You can recharge your battery by draining some energy out of other devices around you.

So as said earlier, this game doesn't use Health but a Motivation system for the characters. So you don't kill a person, but lower his Motivation or Morale if you like. The game tutorial suggests you hold the fate of the enemies in your hand, so maybe you can also choose to kill at a certain point. When Motivation runs out, the character will try to flee. I guess this is where you can keep shooting to kill I guess. If an ally tries to flee, you can use a motivational Chat-line to bring him/her back to the "fight".

And that's basically it. This game also has some flaws, like outdated graphics and the controls feels a bit clunky. The biggest flaw I think is the save system tho. The game uses autosaves at specific checkpoints, but there is no option to restart at the last checkpoint. I even had to quit the game to re-try an encounter without combat, because I couldn't find an option to go back to the Main Menu. So there is definitely room for improvements there, but overall I think this game is totally underrated and deserves more fame.

From announcement to release this game was at least three years in the making, in reality much longer than that. The developers created an interesting world and sowed the seeds for a lot of different stories to take place, none of which actually turned into anything but the storytelling version of a faceplant. There’s under 3 hours of gameplay here, mostly padded by tedious “hacking” mini games and point-and-click exploration with no real reward. Combined with the total of maybe five combat encounters you’ll finish the game asking yourself what the developers were doing for all those years.

The combat consists of a very simplistic turn-based system where you have two actions and some limited movement each turn. The characters all start with a  health bar of sorts called “motivation” which gradually moves up or down depending on how the encounter goes. Sounds good enough but in reality you end up with the absurd scenario where the main character can run low on motivation and flee the battle by the enemies yelling mean things about them from across the room, causing game over. I would spend many restless nights wondering who in the world thought that would be a fun idea if this game was memorable in any way at all.

With the two types of actual gameplay both being duds you might think there’s anything else here; Not really. The animations all scream of corners cut with the characters only moving in straight lines and doing janky emote-like animations in the few cut scenes that’s there. It reminds me a lot of PC-games around 2001 in the worst possible way. The dialogue system gives the early impression that choices matter but no, most of them have a predetermined outcome and no matter what you’ll have to press the option you didn’t care for to progress the story. 

In the end you have a somewhat interesting story that’s poorly told through gameplay that feels like padding. A game where the developers gave up, released the 3 hours of game they had while leaving in all the teasing for the non-existent remaining two episodes and not even caring enough to patch out the “To be continued” when they abandoned the game. I wouldn’t recommend this even on sale.

Lionbite Games takes a crack at the puzzle turn based story telling genre that Telltale games, and Daedelic Ent. have been pumping out for many years. Not an easy task for much can go wrong in putting all the elements together into a strong presentation and release. Rain of Reflections does a lot right and still has some things that can be improved on, so let's get to it:
PROS
Presentation: First thing is clearly the passion of the developers in telling their story is visible from the start. The action is front and center, animation, colors, sounds, and execution clear and defined. I was impressed with the atmosphere, scope, and the science fiction characters that many gamers take advantage of today. A nice start
Controls: Both controller friendly and mouse with clean options in choices, movement, and selections that never make you feel out of control. The Puzzles are not difficult to pick up and game play not hard to follow. That is a good thing.
Cinematics: They do an excellent job of presenting their story with good camera movements and smart scenes. The concept artwork comes together nicely.  
Battles: If you love turn based tactics, they do a nice job of not just combining strategic puzzle elements with clear stealth and combat interactions. The isometric style is nicely done without pulling you too far away from the action. It compliments the story. An interesting fatigue system. Plus
Sound: Whether the computer, voice acting, and music. It gives Rain a strong presentation. 
Game play: Plenty to do, whether hacking, puzzle map solving, interactive choice dialog, combat, even dialog penalty interactions, as well as a solid template to build on. Instead of looking at Rain as a short tale, I see it as a set up to additional content and different story lines. Smart.
CONS
System: I caution that you follow the system requirements. The game had some distorted slow motion distortions and freeze ups the motion and some bugs that they need to get cleaned up. Slight Con for me
Limited: The combat does compliment the story line, but is not grand enough to be a true strategic multiple player tactical turn base men 4 vs chess implementation. Now this may change with additions and multiple story plot lines of other characters, but for now a slight con for me. 
Plot lines: It gives the illusion of multiple plot lines and consequences, but certain encounters in dialog clearly push you in one direction. The story moves along to get you to the end regardless. Short and sweet, slight con for me. 
Adult Themes: Graphics, language and content is in full force here. I can only caution for the young.

Overall: Lionbite Games has a great start in creating their introduction franchise that they can build on for years. Rain of Reflections takes what other point and click story adventures do right and dresses it up wisely. It is great to see Telltale Games influence here and whether Life is Strange, Telltales Tales of the Borderlands, and Daedelic's Pillars. Rain of Reflections honors the science fiction futuristic genre with a smart short adventure that I am sure they will expand on. If you truly love these type of games then Rain of Reflection is worth the price of admission. It is not just what those developer's did right, but what is the next step. The answer is multiple plot multi universe storytelling. See the VIDEO gameplay above discussion to see if Rain is for you. A solid entry. My Score 3.5 out of 5

The game mixes several genres: point'n'click Adventure, turn-based Combat, and turn-based Stealth. In addition, it allows you to talk in battle and influence your allies and enemies with your words. It is also giving you choice and it's possible to finish it without anyone dying because of your actions. Another cool idea is that you don't lose your "health", rather, you lose your "motivation" to fight and survive.

Basically, it's an action-adventure mix that can give a lot to the player. But it failed. I don't know why the game failed financially. Was it a lack of marketing? Was it the bland face of the protagonist? Was it the forgettable title that uses very common words? Or maybe most people don't want to play rich games that mix more genres and thus tell a more varied story through their gameplay?

Now, for the verdict. It's not a "yes", or a "no", sadly, the story was a bit "meh", even though some of the scenes reminded me of The Longest Journey. Since there's no "meh", I'm giving it a thumbs up - but only for people who really love the game design ideas that I described above. It is painful to say it, because I really liked the intention behind the game, even if the execution wasn't that exciting. I don't regret buying and playing it. I'd buy and play the next episode, but there probably will never be another episode. This is sad, because more rich games with layered gameplay like this have to exist.

Rain of Reflections is an atmospheric, dystopian adventure game with an identity crisis, it doesn't know if it wants to be an adventure game or a tactical combat game, and ends up falling between the two genres.

The derivative grid-based xcom system many developers are overusing these days, has a twist with allowing conversation prompts to buff or debuff friends and enemies, but ultimately it proves rather stale, as it doesn't know whether it wants to be a puzzle solving non-combat sequence, or a tactical combat sequence and emphasizes neither.

The game also has a hacking system that proves entirely too repetitive with the frequency of its occurrence, while providing little challenge but an abundance of tedium.

Gameplay aside there's a classic sci-fi world there, one that drops the protagonist in the middle of an ongoing story and forgets to tell the reasoning or background of the characters involved, leading to more questions than answers after the 2.5H gameplay that makes up what would have been the first of three episodes of the game.
That is if it hadn't been abandoned, with no words from the developers since 2020.

There's a lovely crafted atmosphere and soundscape, with solid voice work that serves to lift an otherwise middling experience.

Rain of Reflections is ultimately a game with potential seeping from it like the pouring rain in the games scenes, but as they say about potential, if it isn't realized, it doesn't mean much.

This game is a nice surprise as it takes some very different gameplay elements and mixes them well together.
At its core it's a point and click game focused on story telling (dialogue options and different outcomes depending on your actions). 
It also has a strategic side similar to the Xcom franchise but with a twist on it: you aren't forced to use violence or kill your opponents so that player choice is still present and relevant even during action phases.
Lastly you'll encounter the "hacking" mechanic during the point and click part of the game. It is very similar to the one present in the Deus Ex franchise. Basically three different kind of minigames you'll have to complete in order to progress. Those minigames aren't too hard but still offer a challenge and the game often gives you the possibility to choose which type of minigame you want to play to hack a certain device.

I was really impressed by the art direction as well as the soundtrack of the game. The voice acting and animations are in my opinion very well executed. All those elements really help immerse the player in the story set in a dystopian future where humankind can't procreate anymore.

The only cons that I could find are that the fixed camera sometimes hindered my ability to move around or to interact with some objects in the world (it's just a minor annoyance, not a game breaking bug). And as it stands right now you can play only one chapter of the game (out of the three "promised" in the game menu) and production on the remaining chapters seems to be at a standstill unfortunately.

Regarding playtime it took me 5 hours to complete the first chapter once. As the game offers some replayability it may take a player 10 hours or more to explore every alteration in the storytelling of the game.

All in all a nice and refreshing experience but one can only hope that the other chapters will be released.

Rain of Reflections is an immersive game set in a dystopian future.  You play the main character Wilona and make decisions as her as you go along.  All conversations have different ways to answer and lead to different results, so sometimes you can talk your way around things instead of shooting.  Decisions are not groundbreaking though, so replay value is small.  Nice if you screw something up though, the game keeps going and you have to get out of the mess you just got yourself into!

Encounters turn to a tactical based grid where you can move and act.  Every encounter can be handled many ways.  I was able to stealth almost all the encounters and when spotted, was still able to run off the map after dodging a shot.  Encounters are not the meat and potatoes of the game though.  This is more story driven and immersive.  The encounters DO have that X-Com look and feel to them, with cover and shots, but also have a touch of Metal Gear Solid where if you make a noise you can still move away and recover your stealth before being seen.  It's up to you how to handle them.

The graphics are excellent and the music is great too.  The game plays with that Resident Evil feel, where you have a set background and run your character through it (getting different camera angles when you run, etc).  You have search points to examine things and a full hacking system.  Environments are top notch overall and I did appreciate the voice acting.  When you have the chance to hack a system, it goes to a mini game of sorts where you need to solve different puzzles to unlock a way to open the system up.

The story was pretty good.  I am interested to see where it goes next, there is plenty of groundwork set here, but still plenty of holes to fill.  Characters, though few, were interesting.  There's not much in character development outside the main character here at this point and no way to immerse yourself in the world either.  You only get what progresses the story.  Don't expect to be able to buy a bowl of noodles, or read a newspaper, or talk with random people.  There is also no inventory, only story.

Now, while I recommend the game, there are still some drawbacks.  

First, while the price is great for this game quality, this is only chapter 1.  You can finish this in 4-6 hrs easily, maybe less if you don't look around at things.  If there are 3 chapters at 5 hrs a piece, not sure 30 bucks is worth it for 15 hrs of play unless the story gets way more interesting.  That is assuming further chapters are released at the same price.  I liked it a lot, but it was so short I am on the fence right now on the pricing.  I got it on sale for 5 bucks, so I am still happy with it.

Outside of that, I did have an issue with some of the dynamic camera jumps.  This game is one in which the camera changes angles during conversations and during scenes such as being in an elevator to give you a more theatrical feel.  But the angle jumps are very fast and too frequent.  It works most of the time, but for example, that conversation with Luc by the boat had the camera changing twice a sentence while they stood still and really became noticeable.

Lastly, there is no direction.  No objective marker of such.  While you can't really get that lost, I did have an issue at the end with the pods.  Wasn't sure what the heck I was doing until I clicked everything in the room and found where to go.  This was brought about by going to sleep just before the room (didn't know I was at the end already!) and forgetting where I was supposed to go when I came back.  Something to think about devs..

Overall about a 6.5-7/10.  Needs more character development on secondary characters, needs more to explore and do, and needs a bit more at stake. [spoiler] Seems mom/dad save you or stop you no matter what you do. You can escape any shot, etc. 
 [/spoiler]  Still a good game and a good start.

‘Rain of Reflections’ is a story taking place in a dystopian future, in a world where humans have become infertile. The whole story appears to have been split into several chapters, each chapter being an individual game and having a different protagonist. For now, it seems at least 3 chapters have been planned for the whole story. ‘Set Free’ is the first chapter in this series that introduces us to the setting and the conflicts happening within it. The game fuses together deep narrative and world building with tactical isometric battles.

This first chapter revolves around a young scientist Wilona and a fellow member of a rebel group, Luca, both of whom are on an important mission. The game has a good world-building, and many parts of the environment and conversations with NPCs give us a good idea of what the world is like. 

There are 4 main aspects to the gameplay.

1) There are dialogue choices and role-playing to do that alter the tone of the conversations. Most of these do not have a big impact on the story progression, but generally they're a great addition.

2) There are point-and-click interactions with the environment and a few simple puzzles to solve to make progress.

3) Tactical encounters. These are akin to XCOM-style battles, but with a fresh take. Instead of gunning down everything, we have to use alternate ways of dealing with enemies. We have to use stealth where we can to avoid being seen, and where this is unavoidable we need to de-motivate the enemies, and it's even possible to win the encounters by simply making the enemies flee in terror after you've destroyed their cover enough times. You can also motivate allies and de-motivate enemies with dialogue one-liners during combat, which is a very nice idea.

4) Hacking mini-games. There are 3 different ones. Firewall, in my opinion the weakest mini-game by execution, requires aligning 3D shapes to 2D frames. Breach, which is the most common mini-game, has a lot of depth and a great idea, where we navigate a virtual ball towards a node and fleeing security on a turn-based basis. The ball, however, gains momentum and so we need to think each move through carefully so to stay within the available tiles and not fly off the edge. The third mini-game is the Transmission, where we have to locate the tile from which the signal is coming from based on which direction the visible sound waves have the strongest amplitude.

The game has an excellent visual design. The dystopian cyberpunk world is put together quite beautifully. There are many elements of gritty industrialism, as well as obvious vibes of inequality in how different areas are designed. The designs of enemy soldiers also give an impression that the city has a somewhat authoritarian regime with a lot of indoctrination. The main character, Wilona, has a pretty realistic look, resembling more an average woman with a modest dress sense rather than a busty hottie with barely any clothes on. 

The music is great and atmospheric. The game's main theme, 'Into the Night', which has vocals in it, is fantastic, very pleasant to listen to, and gives the game a very strong sense of its own personality.

The game is generally well-polished and appears to have had a lot of passion put into it. It manages to offer a lot of different gameplay elements in its fairly short overall length. It's packed with content and there's almost no padding whatsoever. As far as narrative, gameplay, and presentation, this game does a great job with each one, and perhaps its only real drawback is the short length, which is not exactly a problem in itself, but the story in this chapter does seem to end rather abruptly and feels incomplete as a standalone game. So, I hope we'll get to see the future chapters fairly soon, because there's a lot of promise here for a great series with interesting characters and a captivating setting.

For a more in-depth review, especially on each gameplay element, check here: https://saveorquit.com/2020/01/20/review-rain-of-reflections-set-free/

Fjong is a very simple Angry Birds style mobile app-like Clickteam copy + paste job that's been dumped on Steam as if it was a PC game.  Gameplay consists of putting your finger on your iPhone screen to fling a pixel blob at various candies to eat them.  Eat enough and the level is over.  So yeah this is dumbed down even compared to Angry Birds, at least that has structures to destroy, etc.  This is shallow compared to that.  Worth pointing out Angry Birds is free on the app stores but the developer here wants your cash money for this garbage.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game only displays in mobile phone style ultra-pillarboxed aspect ratio.  This is just one of many indications this was developed to be a mobile app and not a serious PC game.  It's not acceptable for developers to dump garbage like this on Steam when it's not even formatted or designed to run properly on modern PC gaming displays, to the point that this could be considered insulting.

Some of the defects in the game can be attributed to the choice of using the Clickteam Fusion game engine/toolset - the "No-Code" construction kit that "Anyone can make games with!!".  Including, you know, people who aren't game developers.  Which is a problem.  This is a very poor quality toolset sometimes used by amateur developers as it's free (so they don't have to pay for GameMaker Studio) and doesn't require advanced game development skills, but unfortunately has very limited capabilities (it's arguably worse than GameMaker Studio).  Just as you can't make a silk purse out of a sows ear, you can't make a great video game if you use a terrible engine.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes "Fjong" might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected in the general public reception.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 8 players.  That's right, only 8.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in the game is to be expected.  Gamers just didn't take this low quality game seriously, and for good reason.

Fjong is relatively cheap at $2 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

twickles is a minimalistic puzzle game published by assemble entertainment, who have a pretty decent-sized library of games published, but none are anything particularly good. twickles, however, is one of their older games, yet it probably is one of their top-five games overall even though it's an extremely basic puzzle game. it's more a testament to how bad most of the other games they've put out since are. twickles is very basic in gameplay, but the puzzles are fun and unique. overall, this game is a decent puzzle game and grabbing this for 69 cents when it's 90% off (which is frequently) is really the only way i'd recommend this, despite it being one of the publisher's better titles.

[u]In short:[/u] Twickles is a short but clever, somewhat traditional puzzle game. With interesting mechanics and cleverly designed bite-sized levels you get a nice satisfying brain-teaser. The looks, sounds and technical aspects are perfectly functional, but unfortunately nothing to write home about. With a bare-bones game like that and barely 3 hours of content I'm having a hard time recommending it for full-price, but on a discount this is a very easy recommendation from me.

[u]In long:[/u] The [b][u]gameplay[/u][/b] is physics-based and revolves around guiding a small ball from start to finish. Every level you are presented with a grid of square tiles. Clicking a tile rotates that tile, which is a "free" move you can do without limit. Arrows below the grid allow you to rotate the whole grid, which adds to your move counter. You can technically beat levels any way you want, but the true goal is to use the least moves possible which completes the level with a trophy. There is no time pressure, it's just a classic puzzle game about planning out the correct sequence of moves. And I mean that literally as there is no undo functionality. Thankfully this is not a big concern as the levels are generally quite short (no level requires double digit moves) and I actually enjoyed not being able to blindly use trial-and-error. The same goes for the game never telling you what the target number of optimal moves is, which - again only given the brevity of each level - adds a nice puzzling layer how far off from the minimum number you still might be.
There is a total of 75 [b][u]levels[/u][/b] across 5 level packs, each pack introducing a new mechanic (basic rotations, fixed tiles, physics blocks, fans, portals). Some of the later challenges combine mechanics in really ingenious ways, but levels are generally short and sweet. I completed the first 2 worlds in about 30min total while the other three worlds are a definite step-up in difficulty and took me 50 minutes each. Usually the majority of time would be spent on 1 or 2 particularly hard levels where the optimal solution was not obvious to me.
I found the game to be over-all quite enjoyable. If you find the optimal solution instantly you feel smart, but completing a hard challenge is equally satisfying. Some of the zero-moves solutions were quite beautiful. With just 15 levels per pack the game never gets old or stale. Every new mechanic opens up some interesting interactions. But the lack of content might honestly be my biggest complaint. Some of the levels are really good and tough, and I wish there were more of them as 3 hours feels barely like a teaser (and somewhat over-priced if you buy without a discount if I'm being honest).

The [b][u]presentation[/u][/b] is fairly weak. The visuals are minimalist-ish, but not really. Everything is quite functional, but lacks in style. The sound effects are not great. The single ambient background track at least is fine and suitably unobstrusive.

The [b][u]technical side[/u][/b] is also fairly bare-bones. For graphical settings you get either full-screen or one of 4 pre-set windowed resolutions. Dark mode is available (and always nice to see), but the game is dim enough where I never felt the need to even try it. On the audio side you get mute buttons for sound effects and music but no volume control. The physics are clearly non-deterministic, but intended solutions never rely on this randomness. Apart from that I've thankfully never encountered a bug or glitch.

In [b][u]conclusion[/u][/b] this is a fun but brief classic puzzle experience. I enjoyed the aspect of optimizing solutions until I found the shortest one. Sadly, apart from the clever level design there is not a lot going on and I wish the game were longer than 3 hours, especially considering its regular price. I bought this on sale for -89% which was well worth the money, so this is still an easy recommendation from me if you can wait on a sale.

This is a lovely par-based puzzle game. In a clever bit of design, there's a par count for rotating the whole level, while individual tiles can be rotated without penalty. This makes for some very clever puzzle designs (including puzzles with a par of 0 moves).

Puzzles seemed trivial at the start of part 1, but quickly get really challenging. I ultimately needed walkthroughs for the par times on 3 of the 75 levels.

The game has a lovely minimalist aesthetic. Music and sounds are also satisfying. Even the loading screen icon is shaped like an actual puzzle piece in the game. Altogether, the game reminds me a bit of those old wooden marble labyrinth games.

I do have some criticisms, though. There's no undo feature, which isn't a huge deal but was annoying at times. The game doesn't tell you the par count of a level until you reach it, so a suboptimal solution only tells you that you could be faster, without an indication for how close you are. Overall I don't love the philosophy behind this par-based system, since it elevates "perfect" solutions while barely recognizing "imperfect" ones. Rather than a winner-takes-all trophy system like this one, I much prefer a stars system à la Divide By Sheep (where a perfect solution grants all stars, but any valid solution grants at least one star).

Finally, a small number of the later puzzles involve puzzle physics, which has some really unintuitive edge cases. Some of the behavior is almost idiotic. Please, devs, do not implement game-engine physics in your turn-based puzzle games, just script the behavior. Then you won't have to deal with levitating blocks, occasionally glitchy acceleration, etc.

I did enjoy this game overall, though.

Twickles is a 2D puzzle game based on a 5x5 (later, 6x6) grid. Some of the grid squares have path sections, like straight lines, or T-sections. There is a start block, with a ball, and an end point, and the ball obeys gravity. You have to make a path for the ball from the start to the end. You can rotate a grid square clockwise or anti-clockwise, and you can also rotate the whole grid.

There are 75 puzzles, and new mechanics are introduced: unrotatable blocks, blocks which occupy the same path sections as the ball, fans which blow the ball, and linked pairs of teleporters. The game knows the minimum number of moves necessary to complete each puzzle, and you earn a trophy if you do that (and achievements for getting certain numbers of trophies). But you don't need to do that to progress - just complete the puzzle, however many moves it takes.

The puzzles are well designed, and some are simpler than they look, while some are real head-scratchers. The interaction between puzzle elements leads to considerable variety in puzzle solutions, and there are enough puzzles to keep you going for a reasonable time, especially with trying to do all 75 in minimal moves. This is one of those minimalist games, with a simple, clean design and small file size. I highly recommend it for puzzle game fans.

Coffee Pixes is an Adobe Flash tier block placement puzzle... think Tetris, but the developer couldn't work out how to make the blocks fall down the screen, so you just have to drag and drop them from the side of the screen.  Make a horizontal or vertical row to eliminate those blocks.  That's all there is to this, an incredibly shallow, lazy effort that handles worse than free browser/Flash games, but the developer wants your money for this on Steam. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The game features somewhat lazy, simplistic 2D graphics, of the type you normally expect to see in low effort Flash/browser games and mobile apps.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The implementation here is of such poor quality, the developer couldn't work out how to make the game display in fullscreen, it only runs in a window.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just point and click stuff like a browser/Flash game.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

Some of the defects in the game can be attributed to the choice of using the GameMaker Studio construction kit/toolset.  This is a very poor quality toolset favoured by amateur developers as it's cheap and requires little in the way of development skill, but unfortunately has very limited capabilities.  Just as you can't make a silk purse out of a sows ear, you can't make a great video game if you use a terrible engine.  GameMaker Studio is most commonly used to make retro pixel shovelware and cash grabs.

Pyromind takes a simple mechanic and executes it well. It's not particularly complex, but it doesn't have to be. Each turn one or more bombs appear on the field. Each bomb explodes after a certain number of turns, and their explosions can cause surrounding bombs to explode as well. You play a "mind" that runs around the field defusing bombs while avoiding explosions.

The trailer doesn't adequately convey what gameplay is like, and the still images don't help either; in practice gameplay is much more straightforward than the trailer might make it out to be. The tutorial takes about 30 seconds and you're good to go.

The game feels responsive. Interface is minimalistic and the field is easy to parse, which is helpful to get you into that flow state where you just react without thought. Each "mind" has some variance to its playstyle, though not by much.

However I do feel that the difficulty is a little overtuned. The last couple levels for each mode felt pretty much impossible. I think while the game is presented in a series of increasingly more difficult levels, you're really intended to think of the game in more of like a score attack fashion.

For a couple dollars I think it's a worthwhile pick for sure.

Out of all the Steam reviews that I've done, I've think that PyroMind has gained my recommendation the quickest of all, since I've had this game in my library for less than 4 days at the time of this review.

This interesting puzzle/action game starts as a quirky, turn-based title where you move space by space on a grid, defusing bombs for points while staying out of the blast zones of bombs that you can't reach in time. Different "minds", or characters that you play with each having a different perk, are unlockable with progress and/or a currency earned through gameplay, and there's also a fun little mini-game in the main screen.

In my book, when a game stops me from complaining about what I don't like, you can't get a more positive review out of me than that.

[b]captain backwater[/b] is a sliding game with a pirate theme and a matching element. the goal isn't to reach the exit but to bump two (sometimes more) of the same items together. not for upgrade purposes like in [b]2048[/b]-likes, but to make them disappear. [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1070250/]notes[/url] is an example that comes to mind, but I'm sure there are others.

[b]100 levels[/b] unlocked one by one, and besides the sliding action there are a bunch of mechanics. arrows, dynamite and bombs to clear treasure faster, various means of changing treasure color, spikes activated after moving over them (they just block, don't cause game over), the occasional rapier to destroy any tile, etc. [b]teleporters aren't great[/b], their animation is slow and part of the puzzle is unfortunately figuring out which leads where.

[b]coins and bananas serve as very annoying collectibles.[/b] coins are invisible and appear out of nowhere as the items sashay around (if you even use the tiles hiding them) and you [b]have to mouseover each quickly before they disappear[/b]. bananas are thrown all over the screen by a monkey, appearing after matching two goblets, same collection method.

I don't mind optional challenges and annoyances, but [b]collectibles unlock levels 81-100 one by one[/b], so they're kinda mandatory. nothing wrong with a bonus level pack put behind collectibles either, but then make them puzzly, not some arcade bullshit. they can't be farmed by replaying the same levels, of course, but [b]level select doesn't show where you have some left[/b] either.

[b]undo is available but it counts as a move.[/b] good enough to simply solve levels, useless if you go for high scores, which are only local and meaningless anyway, [b]no par for the levels[/b], so why bother. no on-screen timer but completion time is shown on the level complete screen, along with all sorts of other stats and your score. found and missed coins and bananas would be somewhat useful info but [b]the counter is usually incorrect[/b], possibly messed up by undo, so even though [b]I kept completing levels and grabbing coins, my counter often didn't go up, so I couldn't unlock more bonus levels[/b].

[b]controls are mouse-only[/b], no hotkeys besides esc bringing up the pause menu. since you're not controlling a single entity, it's fine, but undo and reset should still have their keys.

non-widescreen graphics are the usual casual-colorful kind, stretched to fill the screen on widescreen monitors, which I'm sure were available back in 2017 as well. [b]music is surprisingly good if very repetitive, but the same annoying soundbites all over the place are incredibly grating[/b]. there are separate volume settings but not for speech, so [b]I tried replacing audio files in the install folder, but then the game didn't start[/b]. english and german languages, full screen toggle for a small non-resizable window, in-game cursor and achievements and a 'high-quality visuals' toggle that removes some unnecessary effects, so it's not too bad. [b]not being able to go back to the map from a level is less than ideal.[/b] quitting shows the high score list first, gotta close that, then click play to be able to choose another level.

[b]core gameplay would be fine, shame about the bugs, annoying speech and collectibles.[/b] there have also been [b]pricing shenanigans over the years[/b]. it was $10 on release back in 2017 both on steam and itch, then [b]went down to $1 permanently[/b] on both platforms only a year later, followed by [b]an increase to $6 in late 2021, but only on steam[/b], it's still $1 on itch and both are drm-free. very much a dick move.

what's more, they [b]essentially re-released the same game 5 years later under a different company and title[/b] ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1839600]pirate's gold[/url]), but without mentioning this game or the differences and similarities (meaning the same exact levels) anywhere on the store page. even more ridiculously, [b]5 years weren't enough to add a speech slider[/b], so you don't even get a better experience for double the current price of this, just some slightly different graphics. they're not denying the connection, even offering owners of backwater a free key for pirate's gold on discord, but then why not release it as backwater remastered or a simple patch? even if it's a trademark or similar issue, they should be able to mention it on the store page, like every half-assed first-person puzzler does with the witness and portal.

[b] Captain Backwater [/b] is a pirate puzzle game that requires you to launch pieces of the same type either horizontally or vertically causing them to disappear when they collide. Your mission is to wipe all pieces off the board. There are hidden coins in most levels that you can collect and in some levels a monkey that throws bananas that you have to catch. The game has some quirky mechanics like arrows, stop signs and rapiers that you can utilise to complete the level. While the game has a good puzzle concept, visuals and music, I cannot recommend it for the following reasons:

- There are a 100 levels with linear progression and if you get stuck on one, you are REALLY stuck. I personally got stuck on level 37 and got bored after that.

- Coins and bananas don't seem to have any value at all (except for opening levels beyond level 80 which requires a measly amount).

- There are only 8 trophies and I already got 5 by playing less than an hour.

- Undoing a step counts as a step and is a completely superfluous implementation.
