Bought this game on a whim and enjoyed the first half of the game. The end was however unfortunately not as fluid as the beginning of the game. The main problem this game suffers from is it's poor game mechanics. 

Dodging is good but often enemies track you to an insane degree ensuring you'll always be hit no matter how good you think you are.

There is almost no visual indication that you are hitting an enemy. They just freeze up instead of having a stagger animation.

There is a wide variety of weapons but unfortunately they all deal about the same amount of damage with no single weapon being a direct upgrade if you don't count their attack animation with has wider reach or faster speed than others. 
This made it very hard to calculate which weapon would be effective against different enemies. Since the tooltips for blunt weapons indicate they lower enemy armor, I assumed this would mean that my weapon would deal more damage overtime against single opponents or bosses since I would keep hitting them or maybe I would deal more damage against knights who are by all definition wearing armor.

This is not the case. It is just a part of the weapon lore. The game would very much benefit a detailed menu for damage or atleast the exact effects of accessories and items since the game does not tell you that very well.

Secondly the endgame is a slog and feels very, very rushed. Most of the bosses deal insane amounts of damage on a single hit and can one hit kill you leaving little room for error. That does not even account for the amount of pits in this game that emulate the classic Castlevania death.

The best part about the game and most unique is the fact that outfits change your entire character. While this has very little effect on actual moves as they remain the same, it does change a few animations which are unique for each outfit. I found myself using the starting Danache Summoner outfit due to it's tiptoe animation for jumping.

I also found the easter egg items in this game to be a nice addition.

I will sadly not replay the game due to it's sheer difficulty in the endgame. Hmm, well first of all I recommend this game, I've had tons of fun with it, enjoying every game so far.

Found Horror Game 11.exe is an odd anthology sort of game where each game in the whole is released sometime after hidden objects (shapes) in the previous game are found by the community. There are some genuine scares and the story can certainly be intriguing at times.
That said it is a mixed bag with different styles. Some games more frustrating than others, some very gamey, some more akin to a walking sim, though all mostly rooted in the gameplay of what you'd expect from an RPGMaker horror game. Because of that I imagine there will be some who like every bit of it like me and some who like none of it, but I think the majority will find some things they like and some they don't.

It's also worth noting the puzzles, as you can clear the game and get all the endings without straining your brain too much. However if you want to dig deeper and join the community hunts for shapes in each game, the puzzles suddenly get extremely cryptic. There are still some shapes found and not, that even the community a long time after the release of that individual game do not know exactly how to get. I do think that is a strong point, having something there for those that enjoy a challenge, while making the game accessible to the average player who just wants to finish the game and enjoy the story.

Quite a large complaint is how long it takes for each game to be finished even if all the shapes are found. And that is a fair citicism, be warned you will likely have to wait a fair bit of time once you catch up. However, I believe the current content is more than worth the price and with much more to come I can't complain too much, as much as I want to play more now.

So yes, definitely recommended, I hope if you choose to buy that you enjoy the game and get sucked into the yaiverse and enjoy the rest of the games by the dev.

RPG Maker strikes again!

Reformers is one of hundreds of low effort retro-looking RPG Maker asset/construction kit flips spamming the Steam catalog, made with the RPG Maker video game construction kit... in their own words, "Our easy to use tools are simple enough for a child."  Like all RPG Maker "games", this is essentially a bunch of low quality/canned assets from RPG Maker coupled with a cringeworthy high school anime club fan fiction.

As with all RPG Maker games, the poor quality engine displays badly in fullscreen and doesn't have full HD support or any graphics tweaking options, making this unacceptable for any dedicated modern PC gamer.  The point can be made that the intention of RPG Maker is to make demos and small games to pass around friends, and shouldn't be used for "professional" game development.

Like most RPG Maker shovelware and asset flips, the game features extremely low quality copy + pasted 2D retro art, looks awful, and has even worse gameplay.  RPG Maker is an absolutely terrible construction kit, and never results in games of any reasonable quality or value to gamers.

This shovelware is only differentiated by the "developer" copying + pasting assets from a slightly less often used RPG Maker template, resulting in slightly different looking graphics... but RPG Maker is crap to the core.  

This is also badly translated from Chinese, I guess Google Translate should be ashamed of itself.  But is that what we signed onto Steam for, crap translation in badly written RPG Maker asset flips?  Of course not. 

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 5 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Reformers has the utterly unrealistic price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.  Gamers who want a good retro JRPG experience would be better off playing the originals, like Final Fantasy, Star Ocean or Chrono Trigger.

This game has a LOT of raw potential, but it comes up short in a variety of ways. My hands-on review of this game can be found here, but my general ideas are written down below:

Pros:
- Game has a nice aesthetic.
- Being able to customize the look and equipment of not only your robot but your hideout is a huge plus for any title.
- The music is pretty decent.

CONS:
- I can almost never find anyone to play with online.
- The combat in this game is very bland and hollow. The special abilities you have range from absolutely broken and overpowered to pointless and dull. The lack of special combat options like blocks, parries or dodge mechanics means most fights with enemies devolve into spamming attack and running away, then going back in over and over.
- The bosses are obscenely difficult if you're doing a single player run. The only way to do them is to very slowly whittle their life away while avoiding them and the enemies they spawn as much as humanly possible, meaning any up-close hack n' slash build you've made is going to be about useless
- Leveling up feels pointless. It unlocks some gear, but other than that, there are no upgrades or stat points that you can use from leveling, meaning that getting experience feels like a grind for a piece of equipment you're probably never going to use anyway.
- Enemies look mostly the same. The variety is a little lacking.

📌 Visão Geral
Overcooked! 2 é um jogo de cozinha cooperativa e multiplayer, onde os jogadores devem trabalhar juntos para preparar e servir pratos dentro de um tempo limitado. O jogo é ambientado em uma série de cozinhas temáticas, que incluem desafios e obstáculos únicos, tornando cada nível uma experiência única de caos e diversão.

A principal premissa do jogo gira em torno de colaboração e coordenação. Em um cenário típico de cozinha, é preciso cortar ingredientes, cozinhá-los, montá-los e serví-los aos clientes. A diferença aqui é que a dinâmica do jogo exige comunicação constante e uma boa divisão de tarefas entre os jogadores, já que os níveis rapidamente se tornam complexos.

🎮 Jogabilidade e Mecânicas
🔹 Cooperação e Trabalho em Equipe
O cerne de Overcooked! 2 é a cooperação, e o jogo brilha quando jogado com amigos. É possível jogar com até 4 jogadores, seja localmente ou online, o que aumenta o caos nas cozinhas. A interação entre os jogadores é essencial, e as partidas se tornam incrivelmente desafiadoras e engraçadas à medida que o tempo passa e o estresse aumenta. Cada jogador precisa estar atento ao que os outros estão fazendo e ajustar suas ações para que tudo funcione em harmonia.

O jogo exige que os jogadores realizem tarefas específicas dentro de uma cozinha – como cortar ingredientes, cozinhar, montar pratos e entregar aos clientes. Ao mesmo tempo, há o constante movimento da cozinha (como pisos que se separam, elevadores, ou cozinhas flutuantes), o que exige adaptabilidade e uma boa comunicação para garantir que cada tarefa seja cumprida sem erros.

🔹 Novas Mecânicas e Ingredientes
Em relação ao primeiro jogo, Overcooked! 2 adiciona novas receitas, ingredientes e mecânicas de jogo, como a possibilidade de lançar ingredientes de um lado para o outro, uma mecânica que exige mais coordenação entre os jogadores. Além disso, o jogo introduz novos tipos de cozinhas, como cozinhas em movimento, de gelo, no espaço e até no fundo do mar, cada uma com suas próprias complexidades e obstáculos. Esses novos desafios mantêm o jogo fresco e oferecem uma variedade de dificuldades que podem ser enfrentadas pelos jogadores.

Um dos principais desafios do jogo é o tempo. A cada nível, você tem um tempo limitado para preparar e servir os pratos solicitados. O estresse aumenta à medida que mais pedidos aparecem na tela e os jogadores precisam gerenciar a pressão para cozinhar mais rápido e de forma eficiente. A velocidade e a comunicação entre os jogadores tornam-se essenciais para evitar que a cozinha se torne um caos completo.

🔹 Modos de Jogo
Além do modo tradicional cooperativo, Overcooked! 2 também oferece um modo competitivo, onde os jogadores podem competir uns contra os outros para ver quem faz mais pratos corretamente em um tempo limitado. Além disso, há um modo história onde você deve completar vários níveis para salvar o mundo da fome, mantendo a narrativa divertida e leve. O modo história oferece uma progressão estruturada, onde novos níveis são desbloqueados à medida que você avança e ganha estrelas, necessárias para desbloquear áreas adicionais.

🔹 Dificuldade e Acessibilidade
O jogo é desafiador, especialmente quando jogado com mais pessoas, pois a quantidade de tarefas e o ritmo frenético aumentam à medida que os níveis progridem. Isso pode ser uma experiência incrivelmente divertida, mas também pode causar frustração, especialmente quando os jogadores não se coordenam bem ou cometem muitos erros.

Em termos de acessibilidade, Overcooked! 2 é fácil de pegar e jogar, com controles simples e diretos. No entanto, a verdadeira dificuldade vem da coordenarão em equipe e a necessidade de manter um bom ritmo durante a partida. A curva de dificuldade é bem ajustada, com níveis iniciais sendo mais fáceis e os mais avançados exigindo muita habilidade e planejamento.

🏝 Gráficos e Estilo Visual
Overcooked! 2 tem um estilo visual cartunesco e colorido, com personagens fofos e ambientes animados. O design das cozinhas é diversificado e criativo, e a estética do jogo é acolhedora e divertida. Cada nível apresenta cenários e personagens distintos, o que mantém a jogabilidade interessante.

Os gráficos não são voltados para a realismo, mas sim para capturar o espírito alegre e caótico do jogo, com ambientes interativos e cenas de grande movimento, como ingredientes pulando fora das panelas ou clientes impacientes batendo na mesa. O estilo visual é definitivamente um dos destaques, proporcionando uma experiência alegre e descontraída.

🎶 Trilha Sonora e Áudio
A trilha sonora de Overcooked! 2 é animada e combina bem com a ação frenética do jogo. As músicas são enérgicas, ajudando a aumentar a tensão nos momentos mais caóticos da cozinha. Os efeitos sonoros também são bem feitos, com sons divertidos para cortar, cozinhar, fritar e até quando os ingredientes caem ou quando os jogadores cometem erros.

A interação entre os jogadores é fundamental, então, a dublagem dos personagens (que são geralmente apenas sons engraçados ou palavras simples) e a música ajudam a manter o jogo leve e sem muito estresse, mesmo nas situações mais complicadas.

⚖ Pontos Positivos:
Diversão cooperativa: O jogo brilha em sua experiência cooperativa, tornando-se uma excelente opção para jogar com amigos ou familiares.
Variedade de níveis e cozinhas: O jogo oferece diversidade nos tipos de cozinhas e desafios, mantendo o jogo fresco e interessante.
Novas mecânicas e receitas: A possibilidade de lançar ingredientes e as novas mecânicas de cozinhas dinâmicas são ótimas adições ao jogo.
Fácil de aprender, difícil de dominar: O jogo é simples o suficiente para ser acessível a novos jogadores, mas apresenta desafios para os mais experientes.
Estilo visual e trilha sonora divertidos: O visual é colorido, e a música é animada, criando uma atmosfera divertida e caótica.
⚖ Pontos Negativos:
Pode ser frustrante para iniciantes: Como o jogo exige muita coordenação, jogadores menos experientes podem se frustrar com a dificuldade crescente.
Repetitividade: Embora cada nível traga desafios novos, o jogo pode se tornar um pouco repetitivo após um tempo, especialmente em níveis mais avançados.
Pouca profundidade nas mecânicas: Apesar de ser divertido, o jogo não adiciona mecânicas muito inovadoras além do básico de cortar, cozinhar e servir, o que pode limitar a experiência a longo prazo.
💬 Conclusão
Overcooked! 2 é uma das melhores opções para quem busca uma experiência cooperativa divertida e caótica. Com seus desafios rápidos, requerendo comunicação e trabalho em equipe, o jogo é perfeito para jogar com amigos, seja no sofá ou online. Embora a dificuldade crescente e a repetitividade possam ser pontos negativos para alguns, a diversão proporcionada pelo jogo, especialmente em grupos, é inegável.

Se você gosta de jogos cooperativos que desafiam sua paciência, rapidez e habilidades de comunicação, Overcooked! 2 é uma excelente escolha para adicionar à sua coleção.

Nota Final: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (4/5)

I would give this game an 8/10 rating. In my experience, the other reviews about this game being buggy are mostly untrue. You just have to be careful with your roster management (if you redshirt too many players and then have injury issues, you might not have enough players to field a 'whole' team and the game bugs out when this happens, for example) and save often.

This is an incredibly fun basketball sim game, and for $5 it is definitely worth trying out! There are so many different ways to build a team based on how you want to run your offense and defense that it adds a ton of replay value in my opinion. Balancing personalities and playing time between your players can be an interesting challenge too, especially once your team gets to be a perennial top-25 team. Recruiting is also one of the most interesting aspects of the game, with many different ways of filtering through players and competing with other schools for the hidden gems in each class. If you're looking for a college basketball sim game that involves building a team from the ground up through recruiting, roster management, and scheme selection then this is the perfect game for you!

Lastly, definitely get the Bloomington's Real World Full Mod for this game! It adds in all real-world NCAA teams and their historical stats. Makes the game much more fun to play, especially if you have a favorite NCAA team that you want to use. Find it using this link:

https://www.draftdaysports.com/board/viewtopic.php?f=250&t=26598

TLDR: This game was a great experience for those looking for a college basketball sim game, with immersive recruiting and interesting team building dynamics. It's a bit buggy, so save often and make sure you always have plenty of players ready to go for each game (too many injuries and redshirted players might lead to a bug).

At the start, it seems like an original and well-designed game, with a semi-fresh approach to precision platformer genre. But check out the achievements page: not more than 20% of the players got to the fourth chapter, even less got to the finish. Why is that?

There are multiple problems that lead to that. First of all, novelty of design quickly vanishes. Chapters differ in color and some small sprites, but for player they almost look the same. What worse, the gameplay is also the same, with the addition of some small gimmick in each chapter; and these gimmicks are pretty basic, such as wind, lasers and shooting enemies. 

An interesting idea is the design of the narration that is literally the text that appears inside the levels alongside your movement. There are two problems with it. First, it looks silly as long as you backtrack or respawn (which you'll do hundreds of times). Second, it is nearly impossible to read after the second chapter, because gameplay becomes hard and quick enough that you just don't have any spare attention.

Oh, the gameplay. It is really constructed of just a couple of elements: Klaus "hacks" the consoles and K1 "crashes" them. Klaus jumps and is small, K1 "flies" and is big. Well, that is pretty everything you'll get, rinse and repeat. "Memory" bonus levels are somewhat original, but that's all.

And please, makers of "hard platformers", stop this approach of "one fail and respawn". Yes, there are checkpoints (in some games you have to replay all the screen or even an entire level); yes, it is clear and minimalistic; but it gets [b]too. freaking. repetitive![/b] It may be acceptable for "challenge" games like super meat boy, where there are virtually no plot and each screen is a "puzzle" to solve, but in a game with a long plot and characters speaking to each other through on-screen texts... It gets worse only in games with long cutscenes.

Now the story. This is even worse, because it does not hook you from the beginning. Amnesia, seriously? Many games start with something intriguing and then disappoint you with a weak ending. This is not the case: the life of Klaus ("ordinary office worker", "clone of a clone") is not interesting in the slightest, and his hysteria towards the player (!) is strange and off-putting. Seeing such a bland character, I thought he we transform, become someone interesting, gain powers, find himself in a complex surreal situation... But no, nothing like that. He... does not want to be ordinary and follow the order. Well, relatable, and? And nothing more, if you collect all the bonuses, he will "go outside" to "be on his own".

Just compare this game to "Thomas was alone". It is also a single-player puzzle-platformer with multiple characters, but it does not have most of the problems of "Klaus". The narration exist, but it has a voice over, not forcing you to read and jump at the same time. There are much more characters than just two. Minimalist design does not try to look complex, and looks good in result. Levels are shorter and the game does not stretch itself to 6-8 hours. Why be so long if you have so little to show for it? From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.

While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 100,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

[h1]200 character summary[/h1]
Bombfest is an amazing little brawler where you have to throw bombs at your friends in order to knock them off the level. It is local only but a whole lot of fun You can even customize your character.

[h1]Gamemodes [b]7/10[/b][/h1]
You can only play the game locally with up to 4 players, There is no online, You can add bots, but the real fun is in playing ths game with your friends, It has very simple controls it is just dive/roll and pickup/throw so even non gamers can easily jump in without getting too confused. It only has 1 gamemode but it is fun for the whole family.

[h1]Gameplay [b]9/10[/b][/h1]
The gameplay is very chaotic, Throwing bombs, diving away from the danger, Props that fly everywhere due to the explosions, Near misses, Insane explosions that blow you out of the map, or just amazing trickshots that you somehow survive. It really creates a lot of "wow did you see that?!?" moments. It is also very well suited for kids.

You will unlock new things after every game, Things like New levels, Outfits, Accessories, New Bombs, But also game modifiers which can drastically change the game, Like higher jumps, force rolling, big head mode, and a few more to spice things up, I personally prefer the stock game without the timer, But it is nice to be able to change the rules, You can even make it rain nukes right from the start. You can set the number of rounds, Set which bombs fall into the arena and how often, You can adjust the timer, bots, which levels are added to the pool, Almost everything can be adjusted. 

There are dozens of outfits and accesories you can mix and match to create your own unique character, There are also a whopping 14 different bombs, Some are sticky, Bouncy, Slidy, Some go up in the air or implode instead of explode. Some explode directly, there are mines and many many more, It is a blast to play this game, It creates some very tense and funny moments. The game can get a little stale after an hour or so. But it is just as fun next time you play it.

[h1]Aesthetics [b]9/10[/b][/h1]
You play as little wooden dolls and the arenas are all set in and around the house, On a table, on a carpet, in the sink or on a playmat. It looks very playful inviting, is easy to play and encourages rivalries. 

[h1]Performance [b]8/10[/b][/h1]
The performance is great, It is locked to your framerate but tt runs at a stable 120fps all the time. I had absolutely no issues, crashes or any other bad behavior.

[h1]Replayability [b]9/10[/b][/h1]
It is just so much fun if you have multiple controllers, You will unlock everything pretty early on, and there is not much more to do than throwing bombs at eachother, but it surely is a lot of fun.

[h1]Improvements[/h1]
I would love to see more gamemodes, games with a prop that must be forced out of the arena, Maybe protect your own and destroy enemy castles or something like that. Maybe even team modes. I would also love to see more different arenas, I think there is a good mix, but more levels would be very cool.

[h1]Conclusion [b]9/10[/b][/h1]
Overall Bombfest is an amazing little brawler It is perfect fun for short bursts of gameplay, I really enjoy it and I believe it is among the best local brawlers on Steam. If you have multiple controllers, Not having Bombfest is just a waste, If you like local brawlers you should definitely own this game.

Quick text review of BOMBFEST only:

-The only distractions are the unlocks but pleasantly you get something after every match until the well is dry (Exciting but the most exciting unlock, new arenas, are the least prevalent)
-Maybe the game could have done with arenas (Maybe derived from the rooms wherein the arenas are placed - you play as blocky dolls who throw bombs so there's a kind of army men battlefield going on with wood blocks and kitchen sinks)
-Thus, the arenas are compact, and this leads to some fun, fast paced, physics-based combat where you fling each other until ring out (Pleasantly the blocks scatter too and can even bury you)
-Has cute, kind of polygonal visuals displaying the toyroom and household places but some of the colour combos can be mildly grating and some of the arenas are less exciting than the rest of the room you find yourself in
-Good playful music that belongs in the toyroom yet is triumphant and competitive in its sound (For instance horns with triangle chime accents)
-Good sound design too (Booms and clicking wood)
-Maybe could have done with more arenas or something (Only takes 2 hours to unlock everything)

Practical concerns:

-Small download size as it takes up 329.12 Mb on the hard drive

I did get stuck at a couple for about 45 mins each but I never felt that I was never going to get it.  

Gameplay - divide the squares equally between the neighbours, by adding fences, making sure each has a person, house and eventually fruit in their area.  I really like that it has a level map so if you get stuck in a puzzle there are usually 2 other puzzles you can play.  There also is a change the view button,  you can turn and tilt it by moving it with mouse, even playing top down. You can zoom in and out using the scroll button on mouse.

Apart from fruit being added later to make it a bit harder, there are no new game mechanics introduced so it is a bit 'one note'. 

 It's fun, cute and there are 101 levels.  There are fun sayings on the loading scenes between the puzzles (one of them had a typo on it).  If you are looking for a hard puzzle game this isn't for you but for the rest of us who want to relax, take our time and get a few hours out of a casual game, this ticks all the boxes.

You need to allow 150mm for foundation mix and paving, and if you are laying directly next to a house then the finished patio should be at least 150mm below the damp proof course. This means you will need to dig out the area to a minimum depth of 300mm below the damp proof course.

To ensure that water does not collect on the paving, the foundation needs to have a fall of 1 in 60, which means one centimetre of fall for every 60 centimetres of width. So a 3m wide patio will need 5cm or 50mm of fall.

STEP 2: Preparing foundation base

To create the firm foundation, use a concrete mix of 6 parts all in one ballast with 1 part cement.

Mix and add enough water to dampen the mixture just enough so it binds together.

Cover the entire area with the mix to a depth of 75mm, level it out with a shovel and then tamp down using a length of timber or trample down with your boots.

STEP 3: Mortar preparation

Lay the paving slabs on a full mortar bed, which should support the whole slab, not just the corners.

Use a mortar mix of 6 parts sharp sand to 1 part cement.

Mix together with just enough water to make it damp and workable, but not overly wet and runny.

STEP 4: Laying the paving

First set up 2 taut string lines to guide both the line and the level of the paving. 1 line should run down the length of the patio and the second line side to side, with one including the fall for drainage.

Start from the corner and work your way out from there.

Spread out mortar to cover an area slightly larger than the paving slab you want to lay and high enough to allow you to tap down the flag to the correct level.

Lift and lower the slab into place careful not to catch the corners.

Using the rubber mallet, start to tap it down. Hit the paver, firmly but not too hard, at a point that is roughly midway between the centre of the paving slab and each corner along imaginary diagonals. Move around the paving, tapping in succession until the flag settles down to the correct level.

Check the paving is level with a spirit level and that you have included a fall, then start to lay the rest of the paving, leaving joints as required. 

Once laid, the patio should be left for around 24 hours to allow the bedding mortar to harden and should not be walked on. 

TEP 5: Jointing the paving

Use a mortar mix of 3 parts soft building sand to 1 part cement and mix it slowly adding a little water at a time to get a smooth, damp consistency - not wet or sloppy. A plasticiser can be added to make the mortar easier to work. 

Trowel the mortar into the joints, pressing it down and smoothing over using the pointing bar if necessary.

Take care to avoid any mortar going onto the surface of the paving slab. Surplus mortar can be scraped off, but its often best to leave these bits for a few hours until the mortar has started to harden.

Once the mortar has hardened, all you need to do is give the patio a good sweep - then that’s the job done!

Micro Miners isn't really a proper game, it's just a lazy 2D browser/Flash-tier "number incrementer" game where the object of the game is to increase the in-game currency by sometimes buying things that increase the rate at which your currency/score goes up.  It's an incredibly shallow game loop, to the point you might as well just run a program that does "i=i+1; print i" and watch the numbers go up automatically, and just watch it.  You'd get the exact same outcome.  If this sounds completely mindless, you're not wrong.

You do have to "rest" from time to time which makes this even worse than your average incrementer, and you don't even get to click to hurry the game up... not that "hurrying" would accomplish much given the sheer lack of incentive involved in "playing" this train wreck... you just unlock a bunch of horribly badly drawn "pets".  Is it possible for drawings to be of such bad quality that they're against the Geneva Convention?

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The artwork here is terrible, it's a hodge-podge of amateurish "My First Wacom Tablet" style drawings used instead professional looking game assets.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget to arrange someone who can create graphical assets properly, or lack of talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

For gameplay purposes, because the user interface for this game is mostly just 2D static images... it might as well be a browser game.  And we all know, Steam isn't here to compete with Chrome and Firefox.  If the game can be done in a web browser, it's just not rich or compelling enough to appeal to serious gamers on PC.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Micro Miners is relatively cheap at $1 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

Super Star Panda is the first game of Buk Games on Steam.

* What to expect?

It's a retro experience, like 80s / 90s arcade games on the big machines. They should really deliver a big red joystick with it, LOL! First impression: It reminds me a bit of "Asteroids" on the ATARI consoles that time.

* Graphics:

Yep, typical 80s / 90s graphics. Minimalistic, but functional. Retro-style, fits the game. Playfield could be a bit bigger though, lower third is for score only.

* Sound:

I like the soundtrack, it revives the retro-feeling.

* Controls:

A bit unusual at first, expected Asteroids-like control, but works for this game.

* Gameplay:

Harder than expected. Levels are simply-made but are a challenge anyway. Died a lot from rockets, spaceships, etc. For adults this is already a challenge, had no kid to hand to test it for kids here xD

* Power-Ups:

I love them. Would wish me even some more. My favorite is the shield and I like how it is visually displayed.

* Characters:

Very cute. Whether you love cats or pandas, you can have them all! :)

* Devs:

Are active and react to feedback, the way it should be.

* Suggested improvements:

Short ingame tutorial, found the "help" button in main menu long time after I startet playing. 

For 0,99 € or currently reduced 0,79 € this is a no-brainer if you are into this type of games and want to relive the old arcarde times. I found no bugs during play so far, which is great for that type of publisher / game, so the source code seems to be rock solid.

JunkerBot is an intriguing indie game with a pretty simple premise: car combat, without the chase, the checkpoints, the smashing... It's strictly weapons, from simple autocannons to mortars and "land torpedoes" and more. The action is indeed fast and furious, and there are some depth to the game, as successful combat and "decontamination" of of the area unlocks additional vehicles. However, the upgrade interface seems a bit weird, and the base construction interface needs to be better explained to make sense. 

The story is simple enough: a bunch of probes were dropped to decontaminate the planet from something. After the probe was deployed, it was out of power, and before it can deploy a solar panel and recharge, storm hit, and it was blown over, and bured in sand. Unknown amount of time later, sand blew away, and the probe woke up, and proceed to scan, dematerialize/recycle stuff, and built itself a basic vehicle, and recycled the initial probe body for storage. After getting away from the bad guys, which just showed up, it was able to find a spot and deploy a "headquarters", which becomes your base. 

Your base has a HQ area, and you'll need to deploy power and resources to keep the base running. You'll also need a TON of storage. You start with a "basic vehicle". Build a "replicator" to get more advanced vehicles. You need certain amount of power around the replicator to power it, Fortunately, you can move the modules around.  NOTE: You need to have the solar panels NEXT to the replicator (in the 4 compass directions for it to count. When you replicate larger vehicles, you'll need Solar 2.0 (+4 power) and 3.0 (+8 power) but you need special resources to build them.  

There are 3 resources in this game: metal (green), fuel (orange), and hydrogen/water (blue). The basic "1.0" vehicles don't need fuel, but the more advanced 2.0 and 3.0 vehicles do.  While you can capture thousands of units of resources by taking out a base, later, when you fight large groups of enemies, you can capture 2000+ units of metal in one battle if you end up taking out 8-9 enemies. You produce fuel by making a "refinery" and process metal and water. And you'll need a LOT of metal and water to make fuel. Some of the more advanced base modules and vehicles requires THOUSANDS of units in fuel. 

Your base is also doing "research" that gives you upgrades, like a larger base perimeter (instead of 4x4, you have a 5x5 base instead) or new modules, and so on. There's even "arty module" that will "shoot" you repair packs (you need to build them), or even another vehicle. But those will cost resources that you may not have. You can also accelertate research by converting extra resources to research points, but I don't personally recommend doing that. 

Any way, you travel in "real-time", but in overhead view, where you right click on a spot you want to go. (Or you can WASD your way too)  Press space to zoom out and see all the enemy bases and whatnot. When enemy vehicles gets near you, you go into combat mode. 

The different vehicles that you unlock have different weapons and thus different tactics altogether. Your starter "basic vehicle" is bulky, but has a 360 degree turret. The "attacker", almost like a cigar, has 2 front guns and a rear gun, so it requires a very different attack style if you replicate it. A "light bomber" is equipped with a short-range mortar that can hit you even when it's not facing you, but if you keep moving it's not that serious. An "attacker" is equipped with a "land torpedo" which seeks, but requires a manual detonation, so it's basically a short-range weapon useful against a bunch of enemies, but it seems to randomly veer off, so it doesn't "seek" much, and it has rear armor plate! Then there's the bomber, which has FOUR side armor plates, and TWO mortars in addition to the regular guns. But it's also a huge target. So each of these vehicles require a very different tactics. The fighter obviously requires slashing hit and runs, bombers cicle, attacker gets close. There are some uber-vehicles that requrie a ton of resources bo build, but they are VERY powerful indeed. 

The AI is decent, as they don't make too many stupid moves, but they do ENOUGH of it to give you a chance. Dropping shots in front of the enemies are not hard, but circle-strafing can be difficult. Your vehicles have aux thrusters to give a short burst of speed, but the basic version has VERY short duration and thus are not really "turbo" or "nitro" per se. The effect seems to barely last half a second. 

If you got enough H, and you got the teleporter wired up correctly, you can call in special help durign the fight. If you got your teleporter wired up to 16 units of power, you can call in kamikaze mini-cars If you got 32 units of power, you can call in stationary turrets. I personally found those to be way too gimmick-y because I was able to build one of the uber-vehicles (end-game "research") and have no need for the little things. 

If you built the teleporter, you can also build a "portable gate" with you, so you can return to base via the gate, rather than be forced to drive all the way back. 

To unlock the next crater, you need to defeat the enemy base, which is mounted on stilts. You need to destroy all four stilts, while you're under fire from the base's mortars, AND several enemy vehicles. 

Some of the bosses require other tactics, as the auto-turret doesn't always want to lock-on to them right. 

You can jump back to base as long as you're not in combat, but there's a chance to encounter enemies on the way, unless you spent some resources. But if you have the portable gate deployed you can skip that and go straight home. 

Graphics are pretty low-key, and runs on old machines pretty well. I can crank it up to almost 1080p, but not quite. There are 3 quality settings, but no optional frame counter. 

Once you "finished" the first cluster, you get to clear the craters again, when enemies came back and took over all except 1 crater. Now enemies will raid your HQ (unless you beat them off, then decontaminate it until it reads 0%).   You then engaged in artillery duel against the enemy units. If you are elsewhere at the time, go home, as each enemy hit takes resources from your storage. 

So what do I like about this game?

* Simple yet effective combat
* The factions of enemies do look different and act different
* Resource management is rather unique

So what do I NOT like about this game?

* Unclear background. The factions have names, but were never mentioned. 
* Unclear instructions. Some of the base modules are unexplained. You have to do trial and error. For example, the H-plant can be turned on/off in order to save fuel. You have to turn it on to make it work. Also, what exactly is the "
* End player vehicle too powerful

All in all, pretty good, and good value for the sale price.

Raji is a ARPG (isometric view) without loot elements or character build options. Instead, the game focuses on narrative taken from Indian mythology. The game features linear progression with visual cues to highlight the path forward. It features a mix of platforming elements and arena type combat sprinkled in with cutscene narration.

The game features a few weapons (spear, bow, sword + shield & chakram) which have minor variations in their light attacks & heavy attacks. Health recovery is through shrines and performing "finishers" on low health enemies. 
The game really shines in the world design and "artwork" spread across the game. Levels design is good but contains a few areas where your character can get "stuck". 

The story is good and the soundtrack really drives the atmosphere in combination with the artwork. Audio feedback from weapons are decent. Enemy variety is decent and spread across various levels however some enemy attacks can be very frustrating since they are relentless.

The weak aspects of the game are the the clunky controls (keyboard/mouse) in combat & certain parts of platforming. Certain enemy types also attack very frequently leaving little room for countering them. The perk system is very bare bones as well and could definitely be improved upon. 

I recommend playing on Normal difficulty for a balanced experience since Hard makes the game very frustrating due to frequent enemy attacks and lack of responsive controls to deal with them.

[u]TLDR: Raji: An Ancient Epic is a gorgeous game set in the Hindu mythos but could use some polishing for the combat/platforming aspects.[/u]

The premise of This is the President is simple: you’re a corrupt criminal who, somehow, inexplicably, becomes the President of the United States. How? Who knows. The game never really explains it, and it’s best not to think too hard about it. Your entire motivation? Passing a constitutional amendment that gives you lifetime immunity so you don’t get arrested the second you leave office. Totally normal stuff.

To pull off this ridiculous plan, you have to become wildly popular—winning over the public and Congress to push your insane amendment through. But then, in an absurd twist, you must become deeply unpopular and deliberately lose re-election… because… reasons? The logic behind this is as shaky as the game’s grasp on actual politics.

And that’s where things get weird. The game leans into a subtle liberal bias that quickly becomes frustrating. If you want to be popular? Do the “good” liberal thing. If you want to be unpopular? Either do something completely insane… or just enact conservative policies. Because apparently, in this world, conservatism is inherently unpopular, which anyone who works in actual politics knows is ridiculous.

Then there’s the forced backstory. The game gives your character random personal traits, like being bisexual, which feels oddly shoehorned in with no impact on the actual story. It’s as if the game wants to throw in edgy or “progressive” elements just for the sake of it.

As someone who works in professional politics, I found it really hard to suspend my disbelief. The political maneuvering, the absurd motivations, and the bizarre portrayal of public opinion make House of Cards look like a documentary. But despite all that, it’s still kind of fun in a wacky, B-movie sort of way. If you’re willing to embrace the nonsense, you might get a laugh out of it—but don’t expect any real political insight.

Note: My review for EXIT 3 will appear very similar to my review for the game, EXIT, from the same developer.  Why?  [i]Because the developer copy + pasted their entire game four times.[/i]  It provides little of value to gamers when developers try to get paid for the same game multiple times like this.

EXIT 3 - Painter is an older game from 2017.  It's a venerable 8 years old at the time of this review.  It's a simple "I can't believe it's not a mobile app" puzzle game, the type that's been done a hundred times or more, basically a ripoff of an old 2003 Flash game called "Orbox", the idea is that you push your ball in any of the cardinal directions and it moves until it stops.  Negotiate the puzzle levels to run over all the coins etc, touch the required points then land on the exit square.  The only differentiators here are a couple of special squares that push you in different directions, and some rather mediocre 3D graphics that aren't much better than the original Flash sprites of the game they're ripping off.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The game features low-polygon "retro" assets with cartoony, mobile app style shader effects, making this look like a barely functional mobile app from 15 years ago.  This visual style is a method that lazy devs often use when they have a lack of interest/capability to create highly detailed, high poly models and instead use shader effects to disguise that shortcoming under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It's far below the state of the art visuals gamers expect as a result of their decisions.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, left handed gamers or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes EXIT might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 2 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 110,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 110,000+ games on Steam?

EXIT 3 - Painter has the far too high price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

For comparison, the $5 asking price for this game could get you games like "Frostpunk", "Dragon Age: Origins" or "X-Com 2".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

Note: My review for EXIT 2 will appear very similar to my review for the game, EXIT, from the same developer.  Why?  [i]Because the developer copy + pasted their entire game four times.[/i]  It provides little of value to gamers when developers try to get paid for the same game multiple times like this.

EXIT 4 - Portal is an older game from 2018.  It's a venerable 7 years old at the time of this review.  It's a simple "I can't believe it's not a mobile app" puzzle game, the type that's been done a hundred times or more, basically a ripoff of an old 2003 Flash game called "Orbox", the idea is that you push your ball in any of the cardinal directions and it moves until it stops.  Negotiate the puzzle levels to run over all the coins etc, touch the required points then land on the exit square.  The only differentiators here are a couple of special squares that push you in different directions, and some rather mediocre 3D graphics that aren't much better than the original Flash sprites of the game they're ripping off.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The game features low-polygon "retro" assets with cartoony, mobile app style shader effects, making this look like a barely functional mobile app from 15 years ago.  This visual style is a method that lazy devs often use when they have a lack of interest/capability to create highly detailed, high poly models and instead use shader effects to disguise that shortcoming under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It's far below the state of the art visuals gamers expect as a result of their decisions.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, left handed gamers or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.  

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but I wasn't able to find it on the app stores.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes EXIT might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 2 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 110,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 110,000+ games on Steam?

EXIT 4 - Portal is overpriced at $5 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  This is also competing with over 14,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.

For comparison, the $5 asking price for this game could get you games like "Middle Earth - Shadow of Mordor", "Batman: Arkham Origins" or "X-Com: Enemy Unknown".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

Both myself and my co-op partner had never played a MOBA, and we thought that this title would give us an opportunity to familiarize ourselves with the genre under lower PvE stakes. I appreciate the attempt by developer Adam Thompson to create something new and different.

Players can pick one of four characters, each of which has two unique special abilities. Each character also has a standard grouping ability and clearing ability, although the shape differs by character. For instance, one character might shoot out what looks like a 20 x 5 grid of bubbles. As it approaches enemies, they are pulled into its formation. You can follow it up with an attack that is made up of a 20 x 5 grid of projectiles to clear the enemies.

I preferred to play with Dredrick, who has an ability to knock away swarming enemies and a chain lightning attack. My partner preferred Zica, who can one-shot certain towers and drop a cluster bomb.

Although we enjoyed our time with the game at first and liked the music and some of the humorous dialogue, we began to grow fatigued after a few levels. Each level plays more or less identically, with later levels involving more bad platforming and spongier enemies. The movement within the game never began to feel good for me – I just couldn’t get used to moving my character with right click. Although perhaps this would clash with the game’s MOBA roots, I think I’d prefer moving with left click or WASD and using the number keys up top to activate each ability.

The spongier enemies became tiresome, as you never gain any new abilities and your abilities never get any stronger. The game attempts to explain away your inability to upgrade through the game’s “story,” but this almost served to emphasize the problem. I actually felt while playing the game that I was a villain, and the paltry attempts to humanize Dredrick’s crew fell very flat for me.

Although we decided to finish the game, playing two levels per sitting before moving on to something more engaging, I can’t recommend it. Between the static abilities, repetitive levels, poor movement, and weak humor, you’re just better off spending your time elsewhere.

Unreal engine gives some amazing details to scenery and information displayed in the game - my favorite being several notebooks, maps, and whiteboards in the game which have clickable areas to open a pop-up window with -most- of the associated text displayed for scroll-able reading. But one can also right-click to zoom in on the documents directly and read an often more nuanced version of the information and also the diagrams associated with them. A couple of gorgeous scenes of a beach in the early part of the game - blue water, sandy beaches - but the rest of the time if was forced to portray the lifeless, brown, sand-storm prone world of the source material.
UI was frustrating for:
1. "look for the little circles/oval which show what you can interact with", coupled with the game not wanting to show them while you are "too far away", but forced to do it for distant objects it wants you to use the binoculars to look at.
2. when you're moving over uneven terrain - like moving to the edge of an area you need to climb down from - you can get too close to the edge and the circle doesn't display, so you have to learn -not- to move along the edge waiting for the circle to appear, but move back away from the edge far enough to let UI display the circle before you reach the edge.
3. need to climb a rock wall? you will probably have to click 5 or 6 times, and have an animation play for -each-  time you pull yourself up from one hand-hold to the next. Same for squeezing through a narrow passage in a rock wall.
4. Worse offender for me: vehicle controls. For someone like me who fell in love with the vehicle combat in Borderlands 2, the keyboard/mouse controls here are terribly frustrating. and the first time you get in a vehicle there is a big rainstorm at night and visibility out the windshield is lousy. UI kept throwing-up messages across paths i was trying to take. At one point displaying "No, No, No" in front of the tunnel I was trying to enter. gag me.
4a. Dishonorable mention: a series of rock ledges that needed to be climbed, and a small section of the face of each ledge was noticeably lighter-colored (almost white) than the rest of the rock = clearly giving away where each of the "climbing circles" would appear when I got "close enough".
TL:DR
Enjoyed Lem's ideas being played-out over the course of the game. Encountering something alien and not being able to understand it because it is truly alien to our concepts of life.
Frustrated by the game aspects which are the nature of the beast for this format. i.e  exploring areas not necessary to advance the game, and finding an object which could be used later. And then finding out - after I finished the game - that using that item ended the game before I reached additional content in a different ending. And during the ending I got, found out my character was carrying an item I didn't even know they picked-up.

The Invincible is a fantastic AtomPunk hard sci-fi adventure game, based on Stanislaw Lem's 1964 novel of the same name. It is atmospheric, evocative, visually stunning, and impeccably voice acted. The visual design of the game is rooted in 1950s era retro-futurism, and the alien planet of Regis III is starkly alien and beautiful. Re-Interpreted as a walking sim set during events preceding the novel, the game skillfully conveys the events and themes of the book with a deft balance of gradual reveals, naturalistic dialogue and environmental storytelling. If you're a fan of Golden Age Science Fiction, you owe it to yourself to experience this game.

Merv Reborn is yet another of literally thousands of 2D retro pixel platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere.  This one is bad, really bad.  It looks like a highschool project (and unfortunately not only did the student fail, they were held back a year as soon as the teachers saw this garbage).  This puzzle platformer painfully generic and features custom art assets (they're so bad they couldn't possibly be store bought assets), double jumping, and some limited object pushing and destruction.  All of which has been implemented in the most sloppy, garbage way possible.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The controls and game handling are notably very floaty and imprecise.  It's janky and unsatisfying to play... and any experienced gamer will tell you, the handling, responsiveness and general gameplay feel of the control scheme must be well polished for this kind of game to succeed.  Unfortunately, this is something the developer seems to have phoned in, with little to no apparent gameplay testing or polish done.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 2 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Merv Reborn is relatively cheap at $2 USD, but it's not worth it. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

This is a serious dungeon crawler game. You play as a blobby little character with a sword (of farting or some other bodily function), a pair of pants, and a hat. The character appears differently based on the equipment that you pick up in the game, which is an interesting twist to the normal pixel-based dungeon crawlers. 

You will hack your way through monsters and nests as you progress down the scrungeon. There will be occasional levels that are shops where you can often buy equipment that is worse than the RNG equipment that you find in the scrungeons.

One of the most interesting features that this game has to offer is the physics behind slain foes. If you kill off a bunch of baddies, they leave viscera around the floor, which will slow you down--the more chunks of bodies, the slower you move, which can often lead to death.

When you die, you can continue where you left off, without the awesome equipment that helped get you there, which often means continued runs will not go nearly as well.

The downside -- the monsters are very repetitive, with only a few models that you will encounter.
The upside(s) -- The developer is very active, and has already released a pretty big update to the game. It is also one of the most entertaining way to spend 15 minutes and get absolutely pissed off that you died when things were going so well.

Cave Brawlers is a very poorly made 2D retro pixel platformer (sigh) with a few minigames thrown in, so at least this isn't a simple matter of someone copying and pasting junk onto a basic Unity platformer pack.  Of course, with such a lacklustre technical implementation, all the work that went into this tongue-in-cheek comedy dungeon platformer brawler is completely wasted. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics.  It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.

While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.

The developers didn't design the game for modern gaming PCs, as such the display resolution caps out at 1080p, a very low resolution that became mainstream back in 2006 and became obsolete when 4K entered the mainstream in 2014.  The game simply won't look right on modern gaming displays due to this failure on the part of the developers.

The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers, or gamers using AZERTY or other international keyboard layouts.    To make matters worse, there's no mouse input, despite this being sold on PC as if it were a PC game.  This is unacceptable and somewhat insulting to PC gamers.  It's a good demonstration of the poor attitude the developer has towards PC gamers, and this attitude has resulted in yet another defect in this game.

While this is on PC, it has all the hallmarks and deficiencies of a console game, from the clunkier than needed control scheme to the less than cutting edge graphics.  There's 10's of thousands of PC games on Steam, and PC gamers deserve only the best.  This might not appeal to many gamers due to the lack of PC-centric design.  It's unclear why this game was never accepted on the video game console appliances it seems to have been designed for.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Cave Brawlers didn't appeal much to the people who own a copy of the game, either.  It has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game didn't really capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for re-entering the building you start out in, trivial to get, but less than 39 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  Hardly a success story, gamers just weren't all that interested in the game.

The poor quality of this game is also reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 2 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Hey there!! I'm an Idler enjoyer and I felt like I just needed to shine a teensy bit of light on this one in case you're wanting to buy it, possibly for a low-effort 100% achievements game!

It's rly hard to point out a lot about the game that rly stands out... Last 100% I reviewed was Kingdom Clicker and KC was the most barebones Idler I've played SINCE I started enjoying incrementals!

So, differentiating from that, Remaya is another fairly basic Idle game, focusing on both active/idle styles(and including a checkbox that doubles attack speed and disables mouse clicks, nice tiny QoL!).

You'll bump into various items that are chiefly focused around earning and drinking potions to increase your character's power+your click power. This system is quite neat in the first few rebirths but you quickly see how quickly the system hollows out once your Rebirth skill tree is maxxed out and Dungeon Orbs drop faster than you can use them!

You cannot fully Idle this game to 100%!! You will have to check on it and use up your potions or advance to boss stages if you don't clear it the first time automatically!

This didn't bother me TOO MUCH, I babysat the game while drawing and I 100%ed it after 3-4 days! I found it quite fine for an easy 100% to add to my Steam profile, but I can never in good conscience recommend Idlers to anyone that's a bit more "normalpilled."

I would definitely recommend picking this game up to play with 5 or 6 of your friends if you are tired of the toxic environment of gmod. Not a lot of polish but this game has great potential.

This is a good game, but it's a new game.  There is clearly still a lot of work to be done, but it's a much better version of the traditional prop-hunt.  If you're looking for a cheap game to enjoy playing with some friends off and on, this is a good one to pick up.   Here are some of my suggestions for the devs:

1.  Increase the damage that the Hunted take when shooting random props.  Since the hunted take so little damage when shooting props that aren't players, the hunted are essentially encouraged to shoot every single prop they suspect. I would suggest increasing the damage taken from 0.5 to 3; this will obviously require some playtesting, but the hunted should be punished for shooting non-player characters. 

2. The prop's nightvision should either be infinite or last longer.  It feels really bad to use, and it always seems you don't have nightvision when you need it.  

3. The explosive mine from the hunted seems a little out of place.  I'm not sure it needs to be in the game.  It might be better to change it to a more utility based mine.  

4. One of the biggest issues that the props face is that they do little to no damage when they are attacking. This might be intentional, but if it is, it should be more obvious that props are not meant to be attacking regularly.  There were many times that I was attacking a hunted, and it seemed I should be able to assassinate/kill them.  

5. Hit registration is a problem.  As a prop, you don't know whether or not you're hitting the enemy.  This leads to a lot of "I'm attacking this person and I think I'm doing damage but I don't know so hopefully they die soon".  Definitely needs to be fixed.  

Overall, I definitely recommend this game.  Support the devs and encourage them to keep updating and working on it.  This is definitely a game that I plan on revisiting and playing sporadically in the future.

This is a game that really makes me wish there was an ambivalent recommendation option, rather than just a straight out "yes" or "no".

Pimiko Plus is a simple part market sim part RPG game. It's the kind of game that lends itself to short, 15-ish minute sessions of play. The problems surrounding the game, though, arise from the simplicity of its core gameplay.

The market sim aspect is very barebones. It's what you'd expect- buy low, sell high- but there's not much more to it than that. The game flow is nothing more than just buying whatever's for cheap, and bumbling around any of the 8 locations in total to see where the price has skyrocketed to an absurd level so you can sell your goods. In only a few turns you might already see yourself with the best equipment and hauling around the more expensive goods. 

I'm not sure if I'm asking too much, but the game is just so painfully simple. I know that's part of the point of the game, but there's so much potential for something more. You follow the prices from whatever location you're in, it's rigid and there's no room for things like haggling; you just buy and sell. There's no rammification from what goods you decide to deal in, either- it's all basically random when it comes to the prices of items in any particular location no matter how much you buy or sell (though this is to be remedied in a new "realism" mode the developer is planning to put in). All of the locations are pretty much- no, rather- completely the same, with the equipment shops all dealing the same weapons and combat items, and there's no difference in what events or encounters that will occur no matter how far apart they are from another when you choose to travel from one place to another. There is a message at the end of your 30 turn session which discerns the implications of your (probably illicit) trading activities on the quality of life of the people in the game world, but that's about the extent of it, and I have never managed to get anything more than "nothing changed but at least you're richer".

The RPG systems in this game are also very sparse. As I said earlier, you'll find yourself bleeding cash, so in only a few turns you'll already be buying the best equipment. At this point, the random encounters with raiders will be completely inconsequential because you'll be able to deal with a group of three in combat with no problem. It just boils down to clicking the "fire" button because all of the other options in battle, such as throwing items, sweet talking, throwing sand in their eyes, even running away from battle itself are just suboptimal compared to just shooting them. It's nice that different options are there, but they don't hold much of a candle just to mindlessly blasting them until they're dead or flee. The fact that having a weapon weighs you down and that you pretty much want to be overencumbered with trade goods in order to get the most out of the market just exacerbates the idea that you should just be gunning everyone down. 

There is also an class system, with the class you pick enhancing a particular style of play, but not by much. You unlock these (as well as skins for Ruho) with tokens you get after a session, depending on how much money you make. The Junker is the best simply because you can save a lot of hassle by letting you see where items are the cheapest, thus netting you more money, which leads to encounters being a complete non-issue. The Raider can punch harder and can negotiate better with enemy raiders and the Doctor can use up a First Aid to get out of a battle for free, but why bother with any of that when you can just shoot everything to death, you know?

All I've been doing so far is harking on the game, so you're probably wondering why I recommend it. It's simple; I'm a sucker for this shit. Ruho is a super cute "plumpy mama" (game's words, not mine, I SWEAR!) and the doujinsoft style of it just drew me in. The UI is very simple and easy to grasp, and you can move it in the game space however you like, an enhance the overall sim feeling of the game. The pixel art, though not prominent, is really great, which I've come to expect from this developer based on their work on Amihailu. The soundtrack is absolutely killer. The short, coffee break nature of a single session speaks to me because I barely have enough time to sit down and really enjoy a full game of pretty much anything else. Though there's a great lack of variation in encounters and event types, the writing more than makes up for it. I really do like the world that's been put on display, and its a shame that there isn't much in the way of flavour text for the goods you're selling, the locations you're visiting and dialogue/descriptions for the equipment dealers or for Ruho herself, because I'd just eat it all up.

The developer is also actively working to iron out the kinks and plans on making major updates on the game, too. To me, the game was worth the five dollars I spent on it. A lot of it just hits the right strings, at least, for me. If anything sticks out to you about this game, it might be well worth the pick-up for you. I definitely look forward to this game's future.

[b]Introduction[/b]
So, where to begin with this. It's a nice idea. I've been itching for a market simulator without the city management aspect or what-have-you. But there are many, many flaws with this game that just makes it... meh.

[b]The Negatives[/b]

[b]The Price[/b]
This game is normally priced at $4.99. Four. Ninety. Nine. Even with the 15% off sale going on right now, it is nowhere near worth that price in its current state, if it's state were to even change at this point. If you can manage to get it at a price of $1.29 - $1.99, I would say it's a decent price, with $2.49 even pushing it. It is simply not worth the price.

[b]The Market System[/b]
Think of the market system in this game not like a gamble, but like a boulder at the top of a hill. You don't even have to know what you're doing and you will likely make over 2 million RMD, or whatever the currency is, without even trying. Once the boulder starts rolling, there is no stopping it. With nearly zero risk and near infinite reward, this isn't a market you really want to get involved in.

[b]The Encounters[/b]
The encounters are fairly straight forward. You shoot things. Things die. Things flee. You flee. You know, the usual stuff. Expecting to find varying encounters of increasing difficulty? Don't. In my 1.5 hours spent on this game, I have only seen three types of encounters, all of which were the same enemies either solo, pairs, or triplets.

[b]The Token System[/b]
Surprise! This game has replay value (kind of) in the form of a Token Shop. You earn tokens based on your performance in the run, which you can use to unlock three classes along with three unique skins which serve no purpose besides changing how your character looks. Considering how gameplay is mostly the same for all classes, I really see no real reason to play as the other classes. I personally would just stick with the Junker class.

[b]The Shop System[/b]
Considering how simple it is to purchase the best weapon in the game, alongside the fact that every town in this game sells the same items in the equipment shop, the shop is only used to gain back health, seducing, or robbing mid-late game. I have seen no need to purchase any of the equipment items from the shop, or Mercenaries and Travellers as well. Once you get the best Rifle from the shop and keep taking the Shopkeeper out to lunch, you are basically invincible.

But don't worry, the game isn't all that bad. There are some prevailing factors that keep this title from entering into the depths of Gaming Hell.

[b]The Positives[/b]

[b]The UI[/b]
I like the ability to move around the windows and such, but refocusing on the window prior to interracting with them, combined with the fact that the Player Stats screen resets the position you set it to after every encounter is keeping this attribute from being well done.

[b]The Art Style[/b]
Simple and clean 2D Pixel Art. Nothing too spectacular about it, but it's at least nice to look at.

[b]The Sountrack[/b]
It's okay. I never felt as though I wanted to mute the music and play my own through my 1.5 hours.

[b]Summary[/b]
Overall, it's a semi-decent title with a rediculous price tag. Don't expect much out of it at its current state, but with updates and some changes, it can become a decent title worthy of a price tag like that. If you want a semi-fun/interesting title, this is a must... when more content comes and the price changes.
