I am not fond of SteelWool as a developer, it does not surprise me that this VR studio could not handle a full open world type game, and tbh I think it would be dumb to assume that they could.
I do not want to come across as "punching SteelWool just because" but having recently replayed this game I cannot help but think "What the hell did they even patch?"
I played this game when it came out and honestly.. what did they do? Like yeah sure they did obviously do a lot, just take a look at their patch logs. But it feels like nothing has changed..

This game, at the point of this review, is still insanely buggy and has game breaking glitches that seemingly will never get patched. The last time they rolled out a Patch was in August 2023 and it looks like they moved on from SB, leaving it in this state and still charging 34€ for this game.
Thankfully this is not a 60/70€ title, but they better be working in silence on this game because despite all the patches, despite the RUIN DLC, I still feel ripped off..
I am not saying that they "Have to stick with this game forever" or anything, but didn't they say that they will give SB long term support?

The level design is also such a hit or miss, some parts, like Fazerblast look great, whereas the Maze gives me PTSD.
The Maze is easily the worst location in the entire game and I do not understand why they included it.
I love the idea of this game. an open world FNAF sounds like a dream and I remember back in 2015 thinking how cool this could be, well I think I now understand that a "open world FNAF" is not a good idea just because it needs to be done right, and that is no easy task.
I love the aesthetic this game has, the theme of the Pizzaplex is great and is easily one of the game's strong suits. However.. it is hard to enjoy this area when it is not scary at all, everything being lit up makes the map look good, but it also makes the game a cakewalk to go through.

Not to mention the horrible AI in this game, chases are easily avoided thanks to Freddy, but then sometimes the game just glitches out and suddenly you have animatronics teleporting behind you constantly for a while while you are trying to walk through a STAFF Bot infested Mall.
The amount of STAFF Bots they added to this game is just criminal, they knew that having just 3 Animatronics chase you sometimes is too boring so they opted to spam the maps with countless of "HAH GOT YOU" Jumpscare machines that get old after the second one.

The Animatronics having a personality is fine on the surface, it just makes me dislike 2 out of the 3 enemy animatronics, aka Roxy and Monty.
It feels like they poured a ton of time into Roxy, making her insanely self obsessed and unlikable (tbh I only like her in Ruin), meanwhile Monty has "I am angry, raaaaa" as a personality. I rather just take the silent animatronics out of FNAF 1.
Or a more fair comparison, Sister Location, those animatronics also talked and had personality, and it was done right.
A bold choice to remove Bonny and Foxy from the roster, as they easily are the most liked ones.
Now if this was a choice by SteelWool or Scott, I do not know, but I mean HEY LETS BRING BACK AFTON RIGHT?

Let me briefly talk about the DLC..
RUIN is for sure the better game, it removes the Open World for a more linear experience and I think this is the way forward for them, they can actually make a decent experience with linear levels.
SteelWool seems to have ideas, but as we know from the 10 Year Anniversary from Scott, he (Scott) did not communicate properly with SteelWool and the Director of this game had to piece all of this together.
Ruin works, I have less issues with this DLC..

But let's get back to Security Breach. The multiple endings I feel like was added purely because "Well, FNAF has multiple endings, so we have to". But they took this and cranked that up to 900% with endings that just do not really make sense, look bad and made people confused as to what the canon ending even was. Some are comic strips and some are fully animated. Which made people (and me) assume that endings like the Afton ending were canon, but apparently no, the Princess Quest ending comic strip is the actual one.
Vanny/Vanessa was also such a joke, what a way to ruin FNAF's next antagonist. Vanny had so much potential, but they fumbled the bag with her to the extent that they seemingly want to make the Mimic the next big bad evil guy.
I will admit, I am not good with the FNAF lore, I pretty much stopped looking at the lore after FNAF 4 and only know the key details from SL and FNAF 6. I have 0 clue about the books and ngl, I do not wish to get into those xD

Lawnmower Game 2: Drifter is where the core mechanics really start to define the series, and being cheaper than both its predecessors AND successors, it is definitely worth the price. I cannot recommend this game more if you're looking for a gateway into the Lawnmower Game community. I have never felt more insignificant than I do now after having finished the story mode of this experience. If you're interested in space, then you already know about the vastness of the universe. However, it's one thing to know this and quite another to get to experience it first-hand through the power of VR.

You grow up and you're confined to your personal perception of the universe. That the earth is huge and the sun seems to be grandiose at the center of our universe. Yet it's but a speck in the galaxy and even smaller one in the universe. There's not much remarkable about our solar system or our place in the galaxy. The speed of light seems fast, but across these vast distances it seems to go at a snail's pace. It's well-illustrated here.

The power of gravity and space and time is never more abundantly clear. The story experience is 32 minutes long. It it an eye-opening experience to say the least. The visuals are top-notch and realistic. The ambient sounds are also nicely done. I think the narrators could have been voiced better although they do present very concise, an informative narrative to the experience.

Rate 9/10. I couldn't help but shed a tear at the end for my own insignificance and for that of all mankind and sit in awe of the vastness of the universe. No Gods or Kings, only man? No not even man. It may seem pricey, but it is not. You will want to share this with anybody who will listen/view, especially that religious nut relative you may have.

If you have Elite, that game already gives a sense of scale, and better than this one. This game has no point of reference for those who get motion sick so this is also a rather motion-intense experience,.

A must have if you own a VR system. Launch it, select play all, put the controllers aside, and enjoy the ride. Sometimes I was walking around the room and looking at things up close, other times I would just lay down and look up. It's amazing. I've used it several times when I want to relax and clear my head. It makes you think a lot of crazy thoughts about time, life, distance, and our place in the cosmos.

$20 for this? They must be joking. This is not worth even $5. Despite their claim, there is no sense of real scale; everything appears as if it were a miniature model. The narrator has a pleasant voice, but the script reads like a dry Wikipidea article. The pace is slow, the animations trivial, and the planet textures uninteresting.

I love the topic of outer space, but I bailed out of this "experience" after 10 minutes.

If you really want to deflate your ego this program will definitely put everything into focus.  This makes you really understand how insignificant our little planet really is.  We may think where the center of the universe but this will definitely let you know you are not.  Extremely well done and you can lose yourself for many hours in this program looking at amazing things that we will never experience in our lifetime.  Things like flying through the rings of Saturn are watching our earth changing from a night time to day from the Moon general location and even closer.  After spending over an hour using and without any problems (that they have only scratched the surface) it is deftly worth the money and if you have any interest in space this is definitely a wonderful program to have in your library.

I am reposting this from a review I wrote on Reddit last week:  I saw the the title of Overview in the Steam Store and added it to my wish list a few weeks back. Most people may have heard about the overview effect that astronauts all share when they look down at the earth from so far away and it makes them realize how small we are in the grand scheme of things. So. when it was on sale recently I grabbed it and was excited to try it.

It’s basically a single sequence that lasts about 30 minutes with another explore our solar system feature as well (which is good but underwhelming if I’m honest). The sequence is the star of the show but it too starts s bit slow. At first I found myself a bit disappointed- sure the graphics were gorgeous but it just wasn’t thrilling to me-I wanted the earth to be bigger in my perspective. I was missing the point I suppose!

If you’ve ever watched and enjoyed Breaking bad you can appreciate the slow build concept. No show did it better IMHO with the crescendo happening in the last few episodes and really packing a wallop. This app is the same. It really starts to build with chapter 5 - the Milky Way. The sense of scale and the soundtrack both hit me that by the end I was overwhelmed. The credit sequence is in my opinion worth the price of admission alone. I got goosebumps at the end of the story and the credits went on for about 3 minutes and I still had the goosebumps at the end of them. Just... wow. I think I totally experienced the Overview effect- and that’s not a joke. Very profound feeling.

Did I mention I watched this on Ultra graphics setting with an Odyssey+. I don’t think there is a better headset out there for this experience- the darkest of blacks are needed and the lack of SDE make it so stunning to watch.

If anyone you know has even a mild interest in space this makes a great demo app- just crank up the sound and let them at it.

I highly recommend this app. It is very short for the money so wait for a sale if you’re stretched for cash. I hope the app sells well though as I’d love to see what else they come up with! Hope you like it as much as I did.

In other words, if you look at real life photos from space, if the camera's pointed toward an object that's being lit up by the sun (or towards the sun itself) then you won't see the arc of the milky way/other stars in the background. One of the things that makes Space Engine the most realistic-looking space simulation out there is that it implemented auto-exposure properly so that, instead of it just looking like a simulation where you can be staring at the sun and still see the galaxy/nebulas etc. in the background, the visuals of Space Engine actually represent the starkly beautiful aesthetic of space.
Anyhow, I'm really glad to see the software put to such good use. Bring on Space Engine 1.0!

Many games present you with a mystery and challenge you to find the answers. Outer Wilds does something far more special: it doesn’t just make you search for answers, it makes you discover the very questions you need to ask. Instead of offering a single, central mystery, it provides a small, intricate solar system filled with fragments of history, unexplained phenomena, and hidden connections, all waiting for you to explore at your own pace.

What’s also truly unique is that the only progress you can make toward the end is through gaining knowledge. In other words the only thing standing between you and the ending of the game is your lack of knowledge on how to reach the ending. Given this design, it makes sense why so many recommend going in completely blind. Every discovery feels satisfying when you uncover it yourself. I also want to mention that the game’s physics simulation is impressive. Every planet in the solar system spins and orbits the sun in real time, so every object in the game including the player is constantly moving all the time which sounds like a nightmare to design/program.

The downside to this unique approach of Outer Wilds storytelling is the missing initial hook. Not everyone is intrinsically motivated to explore purely for exploration's sake. Additionally, some aspects of the game (especially in the DLC) can be pretty convoluted to figure out. I admit I didn’t have the patience to complete everything on my own, luckily there are some good resources that provide hints without spoiling too much.

While I genuinely appreciated the overall experience of Outer Wilds and mostly had a good time, there were also times when I was bored or frustrated. In the end, it’s not exactly my type of game, but it might be for you. If the premise sounds interesting, you should give it a try. But if you suspect that its slow-paced, discovery-driven nature might not be for you, there is a good chance you are right.

(no spoilers)

I've never, ever felt so much like I wasted my time playing a game. It's genuinely not at all the developers' fault. The game is not awful, or broken, or anything like that. What went wrong is that the game is so overwhelmingly positively reviewed, that I felt like I had to try it and play it to the end. And... it's not for me. At various points throughout the game I felt bored, annoyed, and like I generally wasn't getting drawn in to the game as much as I would hope. But there is such a positive narrative around this game, people LITERALLY say that it changed their lives and they thought about it for months afterward. And, no one shares any details or spoilers to give you a better idea, because that would take away from the game. So, it seemed well worth playing it to the end and seeing what it was all about, but for me, it was not.

I like space, I like exploration, I like puzzles, I like lore. There were a lot of cool and unique elements in this game in those veins. My favorite parts were where you finally unraveled something that you had found dozens of loose threads for, and you could finally see how some part of the story fit together. Besides that, the physics, the mechanics of the planets, the writing, and the music are good.

But there were also significant negatives.

1) The game is SLOW. There are many parts of the game that literally require waiting. You can speed this up to various extents, but you still have to wait. If you die or mess something up, have fun waiting again. And again. 

2) Without being too specific, there are a couple places where there are semi-random placements of entities that can kill you, and there's not much you can do about it if you get unlucky. 

3) Most of the many little puzzles and things to figure out have good, clear hints. But there are probably around 5 critical things that do not have good hints at all, and it is possible to get stuck for hours. That is not fun puzzle time, either. It's just being completely stuck, wasting your time trying things that are never going to work. There are a lot of things you might try since they seem to make sense based on other elements of the game, but no. The solution is a completely different direction. Mostly very simple, but if you don't head in the right direction to solve it in the first place, good luck. Hopefully you look it up before you waste too much of your time. 

4) Also, the ending. The ending sucks, in my opinion. Everything interesting in the game comes earlier, as you figure things out such as the history of the game and how things fit together. Then the ending is the biggest let down of the whole game, since you're expecting something interesting and great. And then there's nothing. It's slow, and boring, and if you die in the final sequence (which requires multiple steps after you've figured it all out) have fun repeating the whole process to get to it, as with everything else in the game.

If this game had not been hyped up so, so much, I would have probably played for ~5 hours before gradually losing hope that it was going to fully hook me, and moving on to something I liked better. But because it was hyped up so much, in combination with no detail sharing by anyone, I played on. If you're interested in this game, great. You'll probably like it. But if you're playing it and getting bored, or not sure if it's for you: consider this your permission to drop it. It's not life changing for everyone.

Despite the tone of this review, overall, the game is fine. Good, even. But bear in mind that it's a small indie game and it's not perfectly polished. If you go in with reasonable expectations, you're far more likely to enjoy it.

Outer Wilds is an undeniably ambitious and artistically stunning game, one that has earned a devoted following for its unique approach to exploration and storytelling. However, while I can appreciate its strengths, I found myself more frustrated than enthralled by its mechanics and structure. The handcrafted planets, each with their own distinct character and mysteries, showcase an art direction that is both whimsical and hauntingly beautiful. Whether drifting through space or stepping onto a crumbling planet, the aesthetic choices reinforce the sense of cosmic wonder and existential loneliness that the game thrives on. The music, too, is a standout feature, perfectly complementing the atmosphere with haunting melodies and quiet, reflective moments that elevate the game’s emotional weight.

Unfortunately, my appreciation for its world was constantly hindered by the controls. Navigating a spaceship and maneuvering in zero gravity should feel intuitive, but instead, I often found myself battling against unresponsive or floaty controls that refused to do what I intended. Whether landing on a planet or trying to make precise movements in space, I felt like I was fighting the game more than engaging with it. This added unnecessary frustration, especially in a game that demands repetition and precise execution. The narrative, while conceptually intriguing, didn’t land for me. I understand that many players found deep meaning in its existential themes and the mysteries of the universe, but I never fully connected with it. The story felt more like an overarching stage for the gameplay rather than something that pulled me in on an emotional level. It’s not that the game lacks depth—there are certainly big ideas at play—but the way they were presented didn’t resonate with me personally.

A major reason for my disconnect is my general dislike for time-loop mechanics. While I recognize that Outer Wilds uses the loop in a creative way, I’ve always found time loops to be a restriction rather than an engaging mechanic. There’s an opportunity cost when a game forces you to experience its world in bite-sized increments, constantly resetting progress and forcing repetition. Instead of being able to take in the game’s universe at my own pace, I was constantly racing against the clock, which only heightened my frustrations with the controls. I understand why Outer Wilds is beloved—it’s a deeply atmospheric, cleverly designed game that offers a unique experience in the gaming landscape. However, for me, its frustrations outweighed its brilliance. The art and sound design deserve all the praise they get, but the unrefined controls, underwhelming narrative delivery, and time-loop structure kept me from truly enjoying it. If you love open-ended exploration and don’t mind a bit of repetition, it might be a game worth experiencing. But if time loops feel like a burden rather than a thrill, it might leave you more exasperated than enlightened.

So this is the game that made Dawko's blood boil. That alone should've been enough an indicator of what I signed up for; but it ended up being so much worse than I could've imagined.
Let's just address the elephant in the room first. Whether you wanna call this game a FNaF ripoff or a paid FNaF fan game, or even something else; there's no denying the similarities in concept, so there is absolutely a debate to be had there. However, even if you throw all that out the window; I care whether or not a game plays well. This game does not play well.
For starters; this game is cryptic as all hell in all the wrong ways. This game tells you very little in regards to what you're supposed to do; and even if it does give you a vague hint sometimes the hint is misleading. Other games are generous to let you figure out what you're supposed to do in an intuitive fashion; but this game just throws you in pretty much blind. Phase 3's flashlight mechanic felt like it was seriously broken; and gives you very little idea of your objective. Even now I don't know what I did to win. After that comes Phase 4; which is one of the most tedious sections of any game I've played thus far. It honestly wouldn't be so bad if you were allowed a little more leeway to avoid the Woodens and it wasn't SIX MINUTES LONG tbh. There's virtually no difference between any of the endings either (and yes, there are multiple endings); nor is there some elaborate setup to attain either one. [spoiler] All you do is a multiple choice dialogue box and boom, different ending. [/spoiler]
Just about the only positive I can give this game is that some of the animations are pretty fluid, and aside from the wires section in Phase 3, isn't horrible to look at.

To summarize; this game isn't worth $8. FNaF is a lot cheaper and gives you a much more polished play experience. Heck, even a lot of free fangames seem to have more effort and care put into them than this. I personally don't care as much that it's based on FNaF (or it seems like that at least); but the bad gameplay is a serious turnoff.

TL:DR:
Reminds me a lot of the FNaF series to some extent.  Some translation errors, but a decent gaming experience.  Lots of Puzzles, some harder than others.  Artwork is pretty good, sound is awesome, and the atmosphere is effective.  Seems worth it for the short amount of time I've played it so far.

First Impression Gameplay: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SYn0HNqDACM&index=90&list=PL0ChqurHdrD4GDyzfEWF1egV0jL1CVSbq

The story is that you are a janitor called in to fix some kind of light and gas problem in the auditorium of an art college.  Things start off creepy right away when you start to hear voices and see thing which don't quite make sense.

Right off the bad, your treated to an awesome soundtrack.  Props to the dev team for putting great audio into a scary/horror game.  Audio is so important in order to give immersion to the environment and rope you into the story and surroundings.  They did a great job there.

Graphics/artwork are basically what you see in the store screenshots.  I think they are good, and seeing how this is basically a point and click, it works well.  Also, there are animated objects in the game, not everything is purely static.

Once again, they did an excellent job on the atmosphere.  The audio, setting, story, and artwork all work together to give immersion to the player and really bring impact to what is going on in the game world.  Jump scares do exist, so be warned if that is not your thing.

Puzzles are pretty much the meat of the game, with scenery creating a bridge between them.   Some are hard, some are easy; not going to give away any spoilers.  

Controls can vary between each room you visit, sometime utilizing a key commands to intact with objects, sometime just the mouse.  Some rooms allow you to pan around by moving the mouse, others are static.  Nothing really major to note there.

All in all, the game is pretty decent.  At least I enjoyed it for the time I've played it.  Pricing feels a bit on the high side, but if you're into these kinds of game and feel interested, don't be afraid to grab it.

So, 3% of players have beaten the second boss. And there's a reason for this.

Treachery is a semi turn based brawler. You navigate a city map, get into scuffles, and during fights you can pause time and program in strings of attacks.

Problem #1 - Nearly everything you do can be countered, and enemy counter rates are based on their current hp. This means you need to whittle them with low damage high acc attacks before you start opening up, but sometimes they just counter the low damage high acc attack and it's rng.

Problem #2 - Resources are limited, maps are big, and movement is ungodly slow. You might think I'm exaggerating, but half of the reason I burned out of this game on my second hour (and 97% of players burned out before then) is because walking between two points on the map takes a genuinely comical amount of time. Backtracking to grab more items from a side route feels like a punishment for being thorough.

Problem #3 - The writing feels like an episode of Archer, but only in a bad way. And there's a ton of it. And the provocation for most fights is that there's a character being annoying. This means you're spending most of your time reading, and you're specifically reading about characters being annoying. If it bothers you even a little, it'll wear through faster than flesh touching pavement at 75mph.

Despite all of this, I do think there's a good *idea* in here. A lot of thought has gone into the mechanics, and if the game clicks with you there's a ton of content. It did not click with me, and it did not click with 97% of players, but who knows. Maybe you'll be the one.

[h2]Finally found the old school nostalgia hit I've been looking for![/h2]

Treachery in Beatdown City takes me back to the days of Double Dragon, River City Ransom, Bad Dudes, and all the other NES-era beat 'em ups with some OG Final Fantasy under the hood to create a sweet 8-bit fighting RPG. For the first time in literal decades, I found a game that [b][i]feels[/i][/b] exactly like ones I'd played in the 80s, but also has new elements added that make it interesting and fun.

The gameplay starts out with basic moves and combos that are unique to each of the three playable characters. Aside from certain story-mode fights, you can choose any character/fighting style and rock your enemies in a number of different ways. You can find items along your journey that will aid you in battle. The writing is extremely tongue-in-cheek, never takes itself seriously, lampoons just about everyone and everything, and (again) really feels like writing you'd find in any old NES game. 

As the story progresses, the complexity of battles and combos ramps up alongside a level of difficulty that is expertly dialed in. Fights start out very easy to allow you to find your way, but become increasingly more challenging. While the going gets quite tough toward the end, nothing in this game ever feels impossible. If you died, it was your fault. I like this because the game is a challenging enough to be engaging - it never gets boring because it's too easy nor does it get frustratingly difficult of sadism. 

In addition to great balance/difficulty, I have to shout out the items and inventory system. Each item is single-use and you can only find them along the way, preventing item hoarders like me from stockpiling ungodly amounts of items and ruining the gameplay balance. Instead, players have to be judicious about when and where to use items to maximum effect or when to take the L and rotate to another character. By the end, I had [i]just enough[/i] items on hand to beat the last few encounters.

The addition of hidden combo techniques keeps fights interesting as well. You can inflict additional status effects that are more or less effective depending on enemy types. The list of possible moves accumulated by end allows for a staggering amount of different combinations. I still haven't found all of the hidden techniques as of the time of this review and something I plan to do using the chapter select unlocked by beating the game.

The banter between characters will either land with you or not. Some jokes made me laugh out loud and some fell a bit flat, but the overall style and content kept me entertained throughout the whole game and was another area where I felt the nostalgia shine through. It felt like I was reading text that would be in an 80s game: direct and to the point, somewhat ham-fisted and goofy, but updated with modern references. If it's not your jam, you can always just skip the text, but there are some good gems in there worth reading.

Soundtrack is bangin!

Lastly, this game is perfect on the Steamdeck. Even though TiBC is not fully verified as of the time of this review, I had [b]zero[/b] issues playing on the deck. The turn-based nature of the combat in this game made it easy to enter a game-and-chill flow state on couch with some TV on in the background, making it a ultimate relaxing nostalgic gaming experience.

The game isn't bad by any means, but it was way too repetitive for me to finish it. The overworld is almost pointless and the game really just boils down to walking from one fight to another with the same enemy types and same strategies over and over again. Once you figure out an optimal series of moves, there is almost no reason to deviate from that and breeze through most fights. As for the dialogue, it is occasionally funny but more often than not, it overstays its welcome too, constantly making the same types of social commentary jokes over and over again.

If it was just a quick 2 hour game for a few bucks, I feel it would be a much easier sell

From the anthemic slogan "Beatdown City -- we gon' whoop your ass!" to the epic trailers and artstyle-defying promotional material, Treachery in Beatdown City forebodes a world full of pixelated punches.

It follows good game design by easing in mechanics, enemy types, and difficulty. With that said, the "tutorial" is a tad too long, arguably it could be cut to a third of its length and still be effective. The multitude of short battles (each 1-5 minutes in length) can feel repetitive, but the variety in enemies and tactics required in overcoming them keep it fresh.

A special note to keep in mind: one time my save file got corrupted via Steam Cloud, I let the dev know, and they sent me a backup save file. That was incredibly kind of them to do.

Outside of fighting, the writing's some of the most hilarious American social commentary you've seen in a video game. Nobody's spared the rod of "social justice", everyone gets whacked with it a few times for good measure.

This is definitely a love letter to older games and it's made with passion. It's neither too difficult or too easy, and its unique charm in the realm of beat-em-ups will keep you coming back for another fight.

[b]Reasons to buy[/b]
- Important game from a minority creator
- Shows what it's like to face racism around every corner (literally)
- Great scrolling beat-em-up, which innovates by merging the genre with RPG tactical combat
- The RPG influence extends to the world map and narrative, creating a long-lasting and immersive singleplayer experience
- 8-bit loveliness in the graphics, sounds and animation

[b]More detail[/b]
Love this game. I like scrolling beat 'em ups, but I always feel a sense of shallowness and repetitiveness after a while - the narratives always feel kinda optional, and after a while the combat feels samey.

Enter Treachery in Beatdown City, which brings some RPGness into the mix and gives the genre the much needed longevity I've been missing. There's a whole world map to explore, tons of character dialogue that is sharp and funny and dripping with satirical social commentary. Hell, I heard about this game through a website encouraging people to support Black developers, following the killing of George Floyd, and right away in the first few areas there's a scene depicting police brutality. It's a great game, but also important insight for white players like myself to see how far racism is etched into society.

The game uses an RPG-like combat system: you can punch enemies outright, but the meat of the combat comes from dipping into the menus to choose and chain together a wide variety of moves (whose roster increases as you level up) in interesting ways. Navigating the menus pauses the game, and makes you stop and strategise your next move, considering the enemy type and your own health and action points.

That might sound overwhelming, but fights, at least so far, are nearly always one on one. It's not technically a "scrolling" beat-'em-up in that the level doesn't scroll with you as you progress. You traverse from point to point on the world map, and at the destination enter into a one-on-one fight (sometimes two-on-one so far, and looking at the screenshots, even-more-on-one later) - but it's not Street Fighter 2; you still have the depth of the screen to move in and out of, and move around. So the fights play out more like the Duel/Battle mode in Streets of Rage 2 (and possibly in the new SOR4, though I've not unlocked that mode yet - I'm actually spending more time on this game instead). Position is very important, as you sometimes need to step back while your action points recharge, though be careful you don't get attacked from behind!

I don't know how long the game is, but it feels like the story is only just beginning; and looking at the screenshots, there are clearly new enemy types, locations and moves I haven't even seen yet. The story is pulling me along, and I want to keep playing to see where it goes. I've just reached unlocking the third playable character, and each time the story swaps them in you get another point of view on the story; I genuinely feel like I'm getting to know these people. It definitely feels more like a long-play RPG than an arcadey beat'-em-up, and that's a positive turn for the genre in my eyes.

The 8-bit graphics look gorgeous on my 4k monitor, and the music and sound effects are totally on point.

I really don't have any areas I would have liked to see improvements. At first I missed the use of WASD for directional control, but it soon becomes clear the game's keyboard layout is well-suited, with arrow keys for movement, and the WASD area used for navigating the combat menus. The subtitles in the intro movie were too fast for me to read, though I got the gist of the backstory; with repeat watches though (it plays each time you launch the game), I was soon able to read them. (The subtitles in-game are player-forwarded which is cool.)

The tutorial prompts are extensive, and even now 1.7 hours in they are still teaching me new things. But they are drip fed at a good pace for me to take everything in, and coming back to the game each time I feel like I can remember what to do - the info has clearly sunk in.

It's a blast of nostalgia to classic scrolling beat-em-ups, with a modern genre-bending and social sensibilities.

Wow, what a blast from the past. 

For the uninitiated, the original slime sports games are simple, browser-based games that pit two or more slimes against each other in a variety of sports. They used simple physics and graphics, but the end result was a very fun time-waster that was a blast to play against friends or the surprisingly robust AI. I remember wasting hours of time in middle school computer labs slacking off and playing these games versus my friends. Over the years, I had all but forgotten about them until stumbling across this game.

Featuring three sports: soccer, racketball, and volleyball, Slime Sports brings back the exact feeling of those silly old browser games with even more added replay value. The graphics are simple, but suit the game well. The music is fun, albeit a little repetitive until you unlock some additional maps. And, the gameplay and physics are a great representation of how the old games felt to control. Game modes include Quick Match, Arcade, and Tournament, all of which can be played with some amount of local multiplayer partners or opponents.

The best update to the formula has to be the whole host of slimes with unique abilities that affect movement and the ball's trajectory. This opens up a ton of new strategies that give the game a depth that the browser games could never hope to achieve. Along with interactive maps and tons of unlockables and achievements, this is a game I can see myself coming back to. Anyone who is a fan of wacky local multiplayer titles like Gang Beasts or similar, would definitely enjoying checking this one out.

So far, after 12 hours I am not far from the start of the game, and will update my review as I spend more time on this game.

The steam achievements are also well made as well. I spend 12 hours and managed to get only 4 achievements, so the game really makes me work for them. That is great.

Anyway, for 99 cents, this is definitely a game worth getting. That I have no doubt.

I forced myself to endure this game for 22 hours, hoping it would get better. It never did.

If you're looking for a game similar to Grounded, this is not it. The combat is terrible and not fun whatsoever. Every encounter is extremely easy yet unnecessarily long. Parrying is wildly inconsistent; some attacks come out in a few frames, making them nearly impossible to react to, while others take ages.

Progression becomes repetitive almost immediately. You’re forced to grind the same tasks over and over just to get armor with slightly higher defense or weapons with marginally better damage. Unlike other survival games, where different gear provides unique buffs or playstyles, this game lacks variety. There are no unique builds, just a linear progression path that stifles creativity.

The map had the potential to be great. There are plenty of remnants from past civilizations, which add detail and atmosphere to the world. However, these points of interest serve no real purpose, making exploration feel pointless and unrewarding.

Boss fights are laughably easy. Their attack patterns are predictable, and the only challenge comes from their bloated health bars, which just make fights drag on rather than feel engaging.

Crafting and fuel mechanics are tedious, but luckily, you can turn them off, which says a lot about their design.

Building is decent except for the structural support system, which is completely broken. The only thing that provides support is the foundation. Pillars and other supports do absolutely nothing, making the entire system feel useless.

The price of this game is ridiculous. Selling it for $50 CAD is absurd considering the lack of depth and quality. There are so many better games you could get for the same price, so don’t waste your money on this one.

Look, I'm just going to be brutally honest here in the most unbiased fashion as possible. And if it triggers you then well, so be it

To start off with, the game has some 'good' points. Scenery can be pretty nice, the bugs make the most adorable noises, and the world 'kinda' does a good job at giving you a feel of perspective scope. Though I say 'kinda' because some items in the world don't exactly add up in this perspective when you actually put the size of the model to scale an dpit it against others. How a bird bath is as tall as a slide, or how a slide is as tall as 2 water spigots, etc etc. And the weather is a bit interesting, even if you only have in truth, 2 seasons. 

Mounts are a bit dumb and unrewarding. You can ride a damselfly and a blue tit, but can't ride a dragonfly? Can ride a lizard yet not a toad? etc etc. The inventory on them, if they have one, is accessed by inspecting them, then clicking on inventory, which is a bit irritating. Just give them an inventory tab with a hotkey ... not that hard people. Learn from your predecessors if you'r that inept.  

Cooking can be okay at best, yet honestly the better foods don't really do anything that mind-blowing for you in comparison to the very starter meals you make. Only exception is the ones that give you a better cold weather buff. Besides that it felt like a wasted mechanic since you'll just reasonably stick to making the fast and easy starter food anyway for convenience and simplicity. Why make stuff that uses flour, honey crumble, and other bs when I literally can get the same effect from a grilled mushroom or soup? 

Base building is a bit rough. sure things snap, and you get most of the building variants ... but despite grass, wood, stone, metal .... they're all just the same. It's just to stare at with no real function. Only one that did have a function, is the bed, and you'll never use it at home. You can just teleport to your tree base and use the beds a sa fast die to travel to other areas.

Tames are very few, and very disappointing. Adorable to some degree sure! But disappointing. Even after the 'overhaul'. I am happy that the bait system was changed to the trap /egg hatch for sure. give credit where it's due, but thats as best as it gets. You'll never reasonably use them, maybe once or twice, but once you get a damselfly and later on a blue tit, why bother? Answer is, that realistically, you won't ever use the other bugs. Because the game mechanics and traversal pretty much makes you lean very heavily to just flying around. at least ARK gave every tame a function that encouraged the use of other species. 

And ending by the way that I found to be completely BS. You go to fight the guy on a giant firewatch tower, who by the way is easy AF to beat with minimal effort and not so much grinding to be done, and you don't even ge to kill him, the bird falling on him kills him .... I've played a lot of games since like Sega Gen and NES ... and I have to say, This is probably the 3rd game with the most disgustingly disappointing end-boss fight I have ever had to get too. Felt exceptionally disheartening and disappointing. You work your way up to him and he just kills himself for you. The weapon reward for it is also pretty bad in comparison to the last actual crafted sword you unlock previously. 


All in all, despite many many many issues not yet put in, but you can clearly see other people having, is that this game had some decent potential, and instead of feels like one lazy halfhearted waste of time after another. Even Grounded, a game that this one was supposed to replace, is somehow better ...
Even the story and NPC's felt like a snoozefest. Not because they were bad ... in a way? I actually liked a couple of them/ But because they came off as being thrown in there, input quick objective module tie, and then move on. They lacked any real weight to them, they don't even move around, they have nothing about them thats important aside from the objectives and free gear. 

Even the factions, which you grind out for, don't give you anything special. VERY MINOR companion buffs, which you don't even need. and the rest is purely cosmetic. That's it ...

All in all I honestly wouldn't recommend this game to anyone, at least not anymore and not at this current point in time. Maybe if the team gets its act together and it gets fleshed out a lot better I will revisit this and re-post a positive review. But right now it's a hard no.

A fair amount of work has gone into this game. Quite nice graphics, good but simple concept and some reasonably good puzzles. Basically, you are alone on a ship that is littered with dead bodies and you need to find out how they all died. Sadly, the English version suffered from a few problems due to the translation from Chinese (?). E.g. the text overlapping with the graphics in some of the pages of the books and I believe it also might be missing dialogue that is in the original version (although I didn't feel I missed anything). I had to refer to the in-game walk-through a fair amount and sadly, my version ran out about 5 pages before the end (another translation problem perhaps) but I found a walk-though on-line that had all of it so I did manage to complete the game. I think my main problem was getting about on the ship because it wasn't always intuitive and I don't have much patience for wandering round looking for the right doorway when they all look so alike. There was a bug which others have mentioned whereby you collect 3 torn bits of a piece of paper which you have to combine and which is essential to moving forward in the game. If you attempt to combine 2 of the pages before you have picked up the 3rd page, the 2nd page disappears. It happened to me and the only thing to do was start the game from scratch (there is an option to obliterate any saved data so that you start with a clean sheet). Thankfully, this bug is near the beginning so it wasn't too much of a problem. If this is a trial run by this developer before embarking on something a little more ambitious, then it is a good start and I wish them well. Hopefully, there will be someone to test the English version for any problems before it is released.

This has to have been one of the most innovative gaming experiences of my life. The gameplay is remarkably immersive - you really feel like a zomby who is also a soldier - and the disparity in the levels adds to this as well. The numerous locations where you have to kill the red men to find the blood potion brilliantly reflects the lore without too aggressively shoving it down the player's throat. This game also breaks away from standard shooter molds with its unique gameplay. Why restrict melee attacks to enemies that are near by you when you can occasionally melee attack enemies twenty feet away? Such paradigms have been stifling the shooter genre and this game does away with them boldly. Instead of Doom's glory kills, Zomby Soldier introduces a new mechanism to make combat more intense and visceral: seizure kills. Killing enemies causes them to enter into a seizure, a primeval yet rewarding effect. Headshots are the most enjoyable types of shots, so in Zomby Soldier the designers made these the only way to kill enemies with a gun. I could continue on about the spikes that kill you even when retracted, the immeasurable lag, the floating ammo, but I think you get the idea - these features break away from traditional molds and greatly enhance the gameplay experience. Buy this game immediately; for me, it has been one of the best gaming experiences of the year. I can't recommend it enough.

This game is a pizza making simulator. The customer gives you the order, you make pizza based on that order. Simple enough. At the start, orders are fairly simple since you only have few ingredients, later as game progresses, you will get more ingredients and you will have more challenging orders, and I'll come back to that later, because I have a special gripe with the orders.

Now the game currency of this game is green money, or cash. You use this cash to pay rent, pay upkeep for your ovens, buy upgrades, new ingredients, and sometimes keeping the place bug or thief free and ingredients. The customers will pay you enough to cover the expenses for the ingredients, and if you bring them pizza in a short amount of time, you get a bonus tip, but if you screw up the order, you will have to refund them. So the idea is pretty simple, but the game isn't just make pizza, earn money, buy upgrades... because there is also a story, yes this game has a story, a pretty wacky story, because the entire world in this game revolves around pizza puns. These stories are divided in chapters, and as of writing this review, there are 5 chapters, but from what I hear the devs are developing a sixth chapter which should come out soon... I will probably not be reviewing that chapter because I am not returning to this game again, but negatives aside, the game does have pretty funny story, with some twists and turns and the system itself is pretty simple and casual: Progress the story, make pizzas, earn money, buy upgrades rinse and repeat.

The first four chapters of this game are in my opinion great. I think my favorite was the first one where you rival Alicante who is trying to be as much of a bully to you it's kind of funny IMO, like he tells you to make a pepperoni pizza, you make it correctly and he can't admit it and says "Great... that was the worst pizza I ever tasted!". From chapter 2, the game sort of becomes a puzzle game, because as you gain more ingredients, you will start to notice that the orders... start to become a bit puzzle like, for example one of the orders is "Ding dong" which you are supposed to make bell pepper pizza, because it has the word Bell... get it? This can be both good and bad, good part is when you get these orders the first time, you have to put your thinking cap, but of course you can always just ask them "What?" and they will be more specific, though that will reduce their tip as a result. So overall, the entire experience is pretty cool, it's a good game if you want to be a pizza maker for a few minutes, and the upgrades are overall decent.

Another cool thing about this game is limited time events. Depending on whether Valentinte;s day, Halloween or Christmas day comes, you can participate in special events where they introduce new orders and new ingredients. This is pretty cool, I like this. It's a bit FOMO though, I wish they had a separate DLC where you can buy to participate these events at any time, but it is what it is. They are cool, I liked it.

And that's probably all the positives I am going to say about the game. Time for my main gripes and why I am giving a negative review.

The music is absolutely repetitive, and the entire game has only few soundtracks. They get old pretty fast, and even the special even music becomes repetitive. Overall, the music department sucks, I would say it's even depressive in a way, I wish they had a bit more cheerful italian pizzeria music than... whatever they were playing... I do like Alicante's theme though, that's the only OST I like.

Now I said that the puzzle orders can be good and bad. The good part is the first time you get them... the bad part is when you keep getting them. I probably got Sponge Bob and Little Mermaid reference a dozens of times over my 170 days of in game playthrough and honestly some of the orders start to get extremely annoying. "No pain no grain" is a pretty good example, because it's basically "put everything on the pizza except corn", and that takes a lot of time by the way. A little more variety wouldn't hurt.

If these were the only problems, I would probably give thumbs up of this game... but notice that I said I liked the first four chapters and I mentioned that there are 5 chapters... Oh yes, the main reason why this game is getting thumbs down is... CHAPTER 5.

Chapter 5 is when devs here decided that: "You know what... we are not making enough money from MTX from this game... so let's make chapter 5 waste as much gems as possible". Gems are premium currency that you only get in this version of the game from quests and achievements. In the first four chapters, gems are only used to speed up the plants that grow in the garden (That you get in chapter 4) and buying cosmetics... and then Chapter 5 came. This is a spoiler, but I don't really care because chapter 5 made me absolutely despise this game. So chapter 5 is... have you guys ever played Phoenix Wright Ace Attorney? Do you know that detective part of Phoenix Wright where you go around talk to people, collect clues? This is exactly that, but the devs made a little trick... for you see, you have to visit certain shops and either interact with the shopkeepers or collect clues around their shop... but you can only do once per game day. If you want to enter another shop or re enter the shop... you have to spend gems... and the first time it costs 2 gems... then 4 gems, then 8 gems etc... The cost actually resets to 2 the next IRL day, so the game is basically doing the same bullshit mobile games do: Either pay up premium currency or waste more time, Entered the wrong shop? Too bad, spend a day taking orders and wait for the next in game day... AND THEY DO THIS IN THE PAID VERSION OF THE GAME. This is my main problem, you cannot port a game to PC, charge it, and then leave this scummy premium currency bullshit that other mobile games do as well.


Devs, this is completely unnacceptable. And I did actually finish Chapter 5, and low and behold... only 0.8% of players actually finished it. Why? Because what I said above, Chapter 5 is not only in my opinion really badly made, because without a guide, you will constantly enter wrong shops and have to wait the next game day or spend hard earned gems to progress the story, but it's also made with bad intention to waste your gems... except the devs did it in the mobile port so you can buy more gems, and on PC they just didn't care. 

You want to play a pizza simulator? Play Papa's Pizzeria Deluxe. It's based off the old flash game, and it came before this game, and let me tell you... it's better than this game. Forget about this game. Until the devs remove the gem barriers in chapter 5, which I don't think they will, I don't really care about Chapter 6, nor do I care for returning this game.

5/10, mediocre mobile port, play Papa's Pizzeria Deluxe instead.

I really wanted to like Fimbul. Was waiting since I originally read about it, I think a good few months or so before its release.
The game delivers pretty well on the narrative & Norse mythology. The comic book style delivery of the narrative isn’t necessarily something I’m into but it works. Unfortunately, everything else seems to fall flat. 

The gameplay is interesting for the first 10 minutes, but then starts to drag on. An hour later and there doesn’t seem to be anything new, just some special skills that are fairly uninteresting, albeit it useful. 

Combat is stale and repetitive. I did like that you could throw a spear to either break an enemy’s shield, knock them to the ground or kill them. But the nature of the enemies surrounding you doesn’t leave much room for it to be a regular thing. This is also an issue in and of itself. Too many enemies surround you and often attack you midway through your attacks with no ability for you to cancel out. This can be considered part of the challenge but in a modern era where fluidity in combat is (or should be) the norm, it’s a fairly jarring & annoying experience.

There are boss fights that are fairly underwhelming and because of the limited combat, it introduces nothing exciting. It’s pretty much just the same combat & mechanics, but the boss is a spongier & stronger version of the lesser enemies.

Visually the game doesn’t do much, it’s okay & appealing but the animations, often during cutscenes, are embarrassingly mediocre. The best way to describe it; the character looks like they’re doing a fake walk during cutscenes. 

The camera system is also annoying. It feels almost like tank controls, especially when moving around in some buildings. But worse off, the camera is fixed in different positions in different scenes or areas. It makes it fairly difficult to navigate some of the areas & further increase frustrating during combat.

I couldn’t really stomach much more of it hence the reason I had to stop my playthrough short. I could finish it given that the game isn’t too hard but excitement the game invokes is non-existent. I’m lucky I only paid about $6AU for it and while I don’t regret it, I’m not satisfied with it either. I want to recommend this game but I can’t. If I could give it a neutral review I would but since I’m more doubtful than sure people would enjoy it, I can only give it a negative/thumbs down. There was a good effort made though, you can tell Zaxis didn’t just slap a few textures together, throw it on Steam & call it a day. But it’s sadly not enough to keep me playing.

If you like Norse mythology and you’re looking for a cheap game to fill some void of Norse games, then this should kind of fill it. It has a good narrative that would have probably been better off as an actual comic book rather than a game.

[i]"While Fimbul is only a game I'd recommend on a deep sale and struggles to find its identity with the combat mechanics, it still shows a bit of heart with unique comic storytelling and a decent story."[/i]

Fimbul is an interesting idea.  I imagined it sounded even better on paper.  Take a story and wrap it around comic storytelling where you play out most of the adventure and combat scenes in 3d.  Where this game starts to completely fall apart however is in its core mechanics.  I imagine this game won't be for many, and if the achievements are a telling story, then most people only played a bit of the first encounter and stopped.  However, if you look at the trailer, the art style and the comic pages and it looks interesting to you and in addition you can accept that it is a short, probably 2 1/2 hr play through for you with only decent at best movement and fighting mechanics, this game might be for you at a low enough price drop/sale.  I got it on sale at .99 cents USD and it was worth my time.

[h1]Pros[/h1]

[list]
[*]The artwork and storytelling on the comic pages is very well done.  The artist here did an amazing job.
[*]There is some good music within the game.
[*]I like the simplistic style the developers chose to go with for the models and animations.
[*]Personally speaking, I like the enviornment and some of the stories that are being told here about what is going on in the background.
[*]I think it has a pretty decent story that made me want to find out as many details as I could all the way up until the end.
[*]I enjoy the characters and setting.
[*]There are moments where you will choose options during the story.  Based on the achievements, it appears that some of those, if not all made a difference in my story/ending.
[*]Shields and helms can be picked up and equipped quickly and can also break.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]

[list]
[*]The fighting mechanics are passable at best.  They don't feel terrible but someone definitely wasn't listening to feedback about these as anyone who plays the game could give feedback that I'm sure would make the combat more enjoyable.
[*]Blocking works great, but you need to face the enemy.  So.... there are no perfect blocks, and also if there are multiple enemies it is better to dodge or run away than attempt to block.  This is what you'll do most of the game, unfortunately leaving blocking only for desperation.  If the block system had been more thought out this fighting system would be way more interesting, especially considering shields can break and new ones can be picked up.
[*]There are 4 specials you can use by building up a combo meter but most of the time you'll always feel that one of them is best in your given situation making the combat feel limited in variety or attempting to try to make it look fancy.
[*]The camera angle is fixed so at times trees will block your vision.  Luckily, most of the time this won't affect you aside from annoyance and it never got in the way of any of my fights.
[*]While having choices during certain sections of the story is a nice touch, I don't know if you can tell enough distinction in the choices you made in order to warrant a second playthrough.
[*]All dialogue is not spoken, so outside of some limited ambiance, sounds for combat and music, the game is overall a fairly quiet experience.
[*]There are only a handful of different enemies.
[*]The game is only about 2 1/2 hours long.  However, at least it didn't outstay its welcome with both new things to show you and a story that stretched on too long.
[/list]

[h1]Bugs[/h1]

The only bug I experienced was not being able to get my Xbox One controller to work, despite it listing full controller support.  I just went into Steam Controller settings and changed the default to mouse and keyboard and manually assigned my buttons so I could play with a controller.  Even still, it was a disappointment that native controller support that was listed on the Steam Store page was non-functional for myself.  Aside from the controller issue I ran into no other bugs or glitches within the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Do you like what you see in the trailer?  Are you okay with only decent combat?  Can you deal with a fixed camera?  Are you okay with a shorter game?  Are you a fan of this mythology?  Do you like the art style?  If so... I'd say at a very deep sale price you'll probably enjoy this game well enough.  I'd DEFINTELY recommend against it at full price.  I really appreciate what the developer, Zaxis was trying to do here and I wish them nothing but success with their future titles.

I honestly did not enjoy playing this game.  It has some of the poorest implemented combat and platforming mechanics I've even seen from a combat/platforming game.  The combat is unsatisfying and incredibly easy, and the platforming is frustrating and boring.  I could beat most bosses within 2-3 tries and they can all realistically be damaged tanked if the player even slightly uses the right build.

On the topic of builds, the game's progression isn't that great either.  For the first half of the game, your build does not matter.  The tools you have affect so little, the difference between using them or not is meaningless.  That is, until you get the late game items allowing you to backtrack and collect 50+% of the total items at once.

I would also argue this is not a metroidvania.  The movement/ability "upgrades" within the game are purely optional.  Unless you are trying to collect every item in the game like me, I do not believe you will ever be locked out of an area because you lack an upgrade.  On top of this, the upgrades they give do not affect base gameplay.  No air dodge, no double jump; just items that let you collect other items in very specific areas.

The quest design is poor as well.  Nearly every quest in the game has a fail condition that is not explained and very easy to encounter without even knowing.  I completed 90% of my first run before finding that a boss I killed 15 hours previously locked me out of an ending and the ENTIRE DLC SECTION (the dlc was free, I didn't miss payed content outside the base cost of the game).  This was never explained, I would have needed to break normal pathing to avoid this outcome, and if I didn't look it up I wouldn't have known how to fix this in my next playthrough.

The only small complement I can give to Blasphemous is that I love a good dark fantasy.  Should having a good setting be an excuse for everything else being bad?  I don't think so.  If not for the sunk-cost fallacy and my need to 100% games, I would not have finished this game.

A gorgeous, souls-like metroidvania that punishes the player for exploring with janky controls, lots of instant deaths, mediocre combat, and massive amounts of repetition and backtracking.  

The game improves immensely once you donate 20k tears to the church and unlock fast travel from save points but the game never tells you about this. 

5/10 - barely not recommended


PROS:
-Gorgeous pixel art
-Really cool setting
-Good voice acting
-Dialogue is mostly gibberish, but it sounds cool. 
-Music was good, especially the guitar. 


NEUTRALS:
-There are some shortcut paths that can be enabled once you've made it through so you don't have to repeat everything.
-Non-linear level design (this is usually a good thing, but quests can be failed without you knowing it if you sequence break)
-Many interesting bizarre characters, but their personality doesn't match their characters.


CONS: 
A metroidvania that punishes you for exploring just doesn't work. 
-The game has LOTS of platforming elements with instant death traps and janky controls. If you die, you have to repeat large sections again. Good luck beating the controls when grabbing ladders over spike pits.
-Quest design is almost nonexistant; you have to take various items to various places but there is nothing indicating what goes where. You just interact with things and hope it lets you offer a quest item. 
-You can fail certain quests without knowing. 
-You can be PERMANENTLY locked out of the "true" ending without your knowledge (requiring you to start a new playthrough).  
-Most of the quest related things are NOT marked on your map. Why??? At least you can put your own markers.
-There are few fast travel locations (because you unlock fast travel via save points after donating 20,000 tears to the church - but the game never tells you that, not even after donating the 20k!). 
-Until you unlock fast travel from save points, if you want to explore a different location, you'll have to navigate large portions of the map, getting past all the traps again. This gets tedious fast.
-If you die, you leave behind a "guilt fragment" that you now need to recover (meaning you have to go back the same way again) which further punishes you from wanting to explore a different path.
-Non-linear map design (which is usually a good thing) combined with this immense punishment for trying to explore and a complete lack of any direction whatsoever to guide the player just doesn't work. 

Combat is almost entirely trial and error.
-Can you block that attack? Only way to find out is to try, die, and just remember that one can't be blocked. 
-Can you dodge through an enemy? Sometimes!
-Chain knock back hits. 
-Your character will randomly change direction sometimes when swinging the sword for no apparent reason.
-Enemies have massive HP pools, but you can upgrade your sword several times. Once upgraded, the earlier enemies become trivial, but later enemies still take forever to kill. For example, in the DLC area, there is one regular enemy that takes SIXTEEN fully upgraded attacks to kill. 
-You have to "unlock" combat skills by using currency earned by farming enemies after upgrading the sword itself. What is the point of this added farm? Devs needed more things to spend your tears on?   

Controls are jank - platform elements don't work
-You need to equip the movement abilities, but you can only equip 3 at a time. This makes absolutely no sense, adds nothing to the game, and requires you to constantly change out your movement items. 
-The most awkward double jump mechanic you've ever seen (you don't ever need it)

Bugs:
-If you try to slide (dodge) while on a moving platform as it reaches the bottom of its descent, your character will immediately turn around and slide in the opposite direction. Why would I know such a specific bug?  Because one of the timed challenge rooms requires you to do exactly that at least twice. 
-the snake boss bugged out on me in the third phase and I couldn't move left or right (but I could jump and attack). 
-if you fall over a ladder, sometimes your character will slow in the air and show a bugged animation
-Most of the time you will grab a ladder in the air (over a spike pit). Sometimes he won't though. 

-Nothing is explained. None of the map icons are described anywhere. There is no quest log. The items only include vague descriptions. I get leaving things for the player to discover, but there is so little information ingame that you will invariably have to google just to figure out what items do. 
-Plot is nonsense/gibberish. 
-No ingame method for tracking collectibles, even in the post game. 
-Numerous powerups are behind breakable walls with no indication that the wall can be broken. There are no items or skills that will reveal this either.
-Lore and mechanics text are mixed together. Most items do not clearly tell you what they do. The vast majority of items are useless.

Absolutely phenomenal. There's a love/hate relationship I have with this game. 

The Great
- The Gothic haunting visuals are an absolute treat, the bleak hopelessness of Cvstodia is brought out with visual clarity with every passing level
- The soundtracks are perfect for each new landscape, they go well with the monsters that inhabit these lands
- Bosses are absolutely breathtaking, I absolutely loved how much real life references has gone into creating each of them, while they aren't particularly challenging, every boss battle was a visual spectacle
- Unlike the Souls series where bosses dictated difficulty, in this game traversing through the terrain itself is a challenge and the checkpoints are spread just enough to give you a frustrating yet rewarding experience once overcome
- The voice acting is top notch, every twisted monstrosity or meaningful character you encounter were voiced to perfection

The Good
- I love the map elements in the game, instead of adding many layers, it simply shows up as one large world map, makes it easier to navigate and mark secret locations and hidden power-ups.
- The entire system of rosary beads, hearts, prayers, relics, etc. come together as a nice way to build player power and the difference between having the best build is apparent when changing between builds
- Every monster feels fresh and different, going through levels, each monster adds a new level of frustration and feels rewarding when conquered

The Bad
- While I love the visuals, the messages from the corpses or clues to the hidden puzzles were vague and out of context, not a complaint for the game's grim layers, I absolutely love that but crucial game aspects need to be respected and stay relevant 
- The Mea Culpa upgrade system is terribly boring and felt one-dimensional, there isn't a caster/ranged/summoner playstyle, it's melee all the way with a few ranged options, makes going through NG+ boring
- While backtracking is alright since the game itself isn't long, NG+ feels extremely stale and the game doesn't feel necessarily difficult the 2nd time around, I usually prefer an added layer of challenge after completing a game 
- Starting a NG+ run will also not give you many bonus items to collect, there's about 8-10 items to collect and it feels truly repetitive
- The DLC content doesn't add too much weight, it's also easily miss-able depending on the route you take which means you have to start a new NG+ to continue

The Ugly
- The atrocious double jump is unnecessarily made difficult, it almost becomes a gamble to get right when rushing through the notorious crystal levels (timed)
- The controls aren't responsive, the input time feels clunky
- When combined with the bad controls, jumping can feel extremely clumsy as you can randomly cling to surfaces when you weren't intending to and other times, fall off, when u intend to cling 

Overall, the game is magnificent and appealing to play. I absolutely loved and hated this game on my way to 100% completion + plat trophy. Blasphemous is up there among my favourite games and it hits the nail when it comes to merging atmosphere and gameplay.

Blasphemous is a very competent metroidvania with an incredibly unique setting. Combat feels wonderful and I found myself hooked on deciphering the lore. Bosses and enemies are extremely fairly designed, making you feel accomplished when beating one or getting through an area, rather than slogging your way through an unbalanced, unfun hellhole (although that can occasionally happen via bad timing). Platforming is by far Blasphemous' biggest weakness, with controls lacking the polish seen in the combat system. Like other metroidvanias, Blasphemous rewards backtracking but is done significantly more tastefully than others. The time at review is after a casual first playthrough which hooked me enough into 100%ing it.

Tl;dr If you're looking for a polished metroidvania with fair and rewarding combat, a unique setting, and more of a soulslike approach than other games in the genre, give Blasphemous a go. You will not regret it.

Crab Champions Review: A Shell of a Good Time
Crab Champions is a fast-paced roguelike shooter that proves crabs aren’t just for the beach—they’re for bullet-dodging, loot-collecting mayhem too. Developed by Noisestorm, the game takes the simple premise of crustacean combat and transforms it into an addictive, high-energy experience that keeps players coming back for more.

Gameplay: Every Run Feels Fresh
At its core, Crab Champions is a roguelike, meaning no two runs are ever the same. Whether you're diving into solo play or teaming up with friends in co-op, every session brings a different combination of weapons, abilities, and challenges. The game throws waves of enemies at you, from aggressive sea creatures to mechanical threats, all while rewarding you with power-ups that stack in ridiculous and creative ways.

The movement is fluid and surprisingly deep—dashing, sliding, and double-jumping as a crab feels incredibly satisfying. Mastering movement and aiming is key, as every fight turns into a high-speed dance of dodging enemy fire while unloading your own.

Combat and Upgrades: The Right Kind of Chaotic
Weapons range from basic pistols to shotguns and explosive launchers, each feeling unique and responsive. The true fun comes from the perks you collect along the way—modifiers that can turn your crab into an unstoppable force. One run, you might have a rapid-fire sniper build that melts enemies from a distance; the next, you could be a melee juggernaut dealing electrified ground slams.

Synergy between upgrades is where Crab Champions really shines. The game rewards experimentation, and you’ll constantly discover absurdly overpowered combinations that make you feel unstoppable—until you hit the next difficulty spike and get humbled in an instant.

Replayability: Endless Fun in Bite-Sized Runs
Each run is relatively short, making Crab Champions the perfect game for quick sessions or long playthroughs. Even when you lose, it's hard to be frustrated because every run feels like an opportunity to try new builds. The different biomes, enemy types, and randomly generated upgrades ensure you’ll never get bored.

The difficulty ramps up in a way that keeps things engaging, and with leaderboards and challenges, there’s always a reason to jump back in. The game’s soundtrack—composed by Noisestorm himself—is a high-energy mix that keeps the adrenaline pumping as you blast through hordes of enemies.

Final Verdict: A Hidden Gem Worth Playing
Crab Champions is one of those games that’s easy to pick up but hard to put down. Whether you’re looking for a solo challenge or a fun game to play with friends, it delivers an exciting and unpredictable experience every time.

Pros:
✔️ Fast, smooth, and addictive gameplay
✔️ Highly replayable with endless build variety
✔️ Fun solo or in co-op with friends
✔️ Satisfying movement and combat mechanics
✔️ Great music that keeps the energy high

Cons:
❌ Visuals can get chaotic, making it hard to track enemies
❌ Some upgrades feel stronger than others, leading to imbalance

Score: 9/10
If you love roguelikes, bullet-hell action, and absurdly fun combat, Crab Champions is a must-play. It’s a game where every session is different, and no matter how many times you get knocked down, you’ll want to jump right back in for another round. 🦀💥

However, while a story is nice, it's not essential.  Ultimately it comes down to the puzzles.  And yes, the puzzles are fun.  I would even venture to say they're 1.99 fun.  BUT! All in all, this is disappointing as this game has potential to be one of the better moving block puzzles out there.  To be honest, I'm torn about the game as it is and the game as it could be.  Ultimately, I have to rate the game as it is, and the lower price doesn't give much hope that there will be further development.  I STILL will be recommending the game despite the lack of story, lack of ending (you just finish the last puzzle, there's no indication the game is done) and rather simplistic game play because *I* feel (and yes, this is a judgement call here, take this review with a grain of salt) this game is still worth the 1.99 asking price.  Lord knows I've paid more for less on Steam.  I do hold out hope that if this game starts to make some money the developer will give this game the attention it rightly deserves. I really wish there was a "neutral" review option. TL;DR: It's a fun time sink with mountains of potential but the dev seems to have gone AWOL.

This game seems to do a better job than any of its competitors at giving players freedom to build all sorts of aircraft (and cars!) with an easy to use fuselage and wing editor. Both are straightforward if you're comfortable messing with 3D shapes by cross section and by pulling 'handles' to move points in 3D space. 

Engines take a little (a lot) more effort but are also satisfying once you get them right. All in all, it's a decently fun game and a solid time sink. I'd say it's a bit like X-Plane 9's Plane Maker but with a better UI and prettier looking aircraft coming out of the other end.

However:

It feels like it's been abandoned. No updates or even news on steam for the best part of 9 months at the time of writing. There's lots of nice-to-have features that are missing -- not just the undo function which, if you [i]really[/i] get stuck into this game, you'll probably learn to live without (the game's super-regular autosave feature really helps here). Mods paper over some of the cracks but it's really not the same as having these features included from the start.

I will change this to a positive overall review if the dev breaks radio silence but otherwise, buyer beware.

Each city and village seems to have been modeled individually, creating a huge variety of battlefields to work with. The logistics/supply system is less nuanced than in ROTK, but the addition of stances (March, encamp, ambush, normal) adds an additional level of depth to the world map.

Compared to ROTK XI, this game especially excels in the ability to play real-time battles with real stakes (Iron man). Compared to Shogun 2, this game has richer diplomacy, more nuanced city management, and more variety in how generals/characters work.
